Then they are in favor of free trade. For example, the United Kingdom adopted free trade after the Industrial Revolution. After 1945, the United States became the world’s leading power and did just that. They used their economic power to force other countries to open up their protected markets. 

Today, China is the main supporter of free trade. On the other hand, the United States has turned to protectionism for the first time since the 1930s. Trade wars can sometimes turn into military conflicts. But they do not always. 

In the case of Donald Trump, however, protectionism has been combined with isolationism. But this alone does not fully explain the imperialist position of the United States. Trump may want to stay away from war, given the failed wars of the last generation of the United States. But he is by no means a pacifist. 

Trump wants to focus on China. He has a deep hostility towards Iran. When he makes disparaging remarks about NATO, it is actually a tactic to pressure European powers to increase their military spending. This tactic was quite successful in his first term. Trump has demanded that European NATO members spend 5 percent of their gross domestic product (GDP) on weapons. While the United States itself spends 3.5 percent. 

All of this is a clear sign of the decline of US dominance in the world. The United States, the core of empire, is now failing to maintain its military superiority. So he is demanding more and more economic and military support from his subordinate states. 

Permanent preparation for war 
Trump may have wanted and probably could have established a temporary peace between the war-weary parties in Ukraine. This would have brought temporary peace. But it is not certain that instability will not start again in the future. 

The war in Ukraine has pushed NATO powers towards permanent preparation for war. It has strengthened Russian President Vladimir Putin’s alliance with China and others. But US influence is declining in other places besides Ukraine. The situation in the Middle East tells a similar story. 

US position in the Middle East 
First, the US may want to reduce its responsibilities in the Middle East. Otherwise, it will not be able to focus on East Asia. 

But it is practically impossible to withdraw from the Middle East completely. The world’s most profitable oil fields are in the Middle East. The Houthis have recently proven beyond doubt how important the Red Sea-Suez Canal shipping route is for world trade. 

Moreover, the political instability in the region always has a global impact. It is never just a regional issue. 

The role of the United States and Israel 
In the Middle East, the United States' ally Israel has destroyed Gaza, reduced the effectiveness of Hezbollah, and brought down the Bashar al-Assad regime in Syria. 

The political significance of these events is enormous. Israel, widely accused of genocide, has become a state-unwelcome state. Its prime minister is a man indicted for war crimes in 124 countries. It is not clear whether this rebel state is fully under the control of its imperialist master. 

It is true that the United States has avoided a full-scale regional war by ordering Israel not to attack Iranian oil facilities or nuclear weapons sites. 

However, so far, Israel has often violated the limits set by the United States. The latest example is Israel's seizure of the Golan Heights and further Syrian territory. Even Trump has acknowledged that the political environment in post-Assad Syria will have a greater impact on it than the US, which is an ally of the new Syrian government, Turkey. 

Finally, China 
It is difficult for the US imperialist power to completely withdraw from Europe and the Middle East. At the same time, it must be prepared to face the new challenge of global power from China. 

The US has no other choice in a competitive world market. No matter how much it talks about peaceful coexistence between China and the West, this is not possible for the global imperialist system. 

A weak imperialist power 
It has long been apparent that China's growth rate has slowed. The Chinese Communist Party rulers have understood this. They are trying to expand the domestic market. Many industrializing countries have done this before. 

However, this rapid economic change will inevitably lead to social unrest. It could create economic and political challenges that China's leaders have never faced before. 

This will not reduce international tensions; rather, it will increase them. Empire and internal unrest are companions of each other. The ruling classes of Britain and the United States know this from experience. 

Outlook for 2025 
By 2025, the world will see a weakened imperialist United States. Led by a president who, for the first time in nearly 100 years, will use a combination of protectionism, isolationism, and third-party dependency to govern the empire. In such a situation, governments often try to push their problems outward. 

Its main challenger, China, may have already left its years of spectacular growth behind. The most serious internal problems that growth has created lie ahead for China.

Headline_English: Why India, Russia and Israel are happy with Trump's return
Content_Enlish:
Donald Trump's surprise and landslide victory in the US presidential election has also given birth to a diplomatic ring. It can be called the 'Trump axis'. The rise of this axis will have a serious impact on the world order. Trump's axis includes Russia, Israel and India. These countries have been viewing the US more favorably since Trump's return. 

Biden's disastrous foreign policy 
In August 2021, US President Joe Biden withdrew troops from Afghanistan. Since then, the US has been involved in two hot wars. They do not seem to have any control over them. Wars have been going on in Europe for almost three years and in the Middle East for more than a year. The dominant Western narrative portrays the leaders of countries that challenge them as arrogant tyrants. Russia's Vladimir Putin and Iran's Ali Khamenei are shown as people who are determined to cause trouble abroad and tyranny at home. 

According to the Western narrative, they are solely responsible for the wars. But many observers, including US political scientist John Mearsheimer, admit that these wars were started at the initiative of Biden to expand US influence through the expansion of NATO in Europe and the Trump-era expansionist policy in the Middle East. Before this, a status quo was established that favored the United States. Instead of being satisfied with that, Biden wanted more. 

Myths of Empire is a classic book by Zack Snyder. There he said that empires have believed in a myth throughout history. The myth is that security can only be ensured through expansion. And in doing this expansion, they bring harm to themselves. That is what happened in Biden's case. Instead of security, he brought destructive war while expanding. 

India thinks that Trump will be more friendly towards India than Biden. The Modi government and the Biden administration have put some pressure on each other over the horrific treatment of religious minorities and press freedom. Many Indians are now convinced that Trump will not put any more pressure on them. 
In both wars, human rights groups have accused Russia and Israel of genocide. But they fail to mention how the global order has broken down in at least two regions critical to US national interests under Biden. US allies are no longer able to deter their enemies. 

Multilateral institutions like the UN Security Council have been rendered powerless and ineffective. This is largely due to the US’s arbitrary use of its veto power. Russia and Iran have not succeeded in expelling the US from their neighbourhoods. But they have certainly shown the limits of US power. The resulting breakdown of order is likely beyond repair. 

Biden has decades of experience in foreign policy. Yet his tenure has not been a good one for US interests. The US withdrawal from Afghanistan has been disastrous. It has set off a series of US setbacks in each of the three regions that Washington is so focused on. US allies in Europe, Ukraine and the Middle East are fighting a desperate battle with Israel. 

This war threatens their very existence. Failure in Europe and the Middle East will only weaken the Indo-Pacific. Biden’s foreign policy will be marked by a colossal failure as his term ends. But Trump’s victory has abruptly changed the international landscape. 

Both sides—friends and foes—will now suddenly be assessing their relationship with the US differently. Leaders are flocking to Trump’s home just months before he is sworn in as the 47th president of the United States. 

Israel 
Consider Israel. Since Hamas’s attacks on Israelis, the Israeli government has responded with relentless brutality. It has killed thousands of civilians. It has made Gaza uninhabitable. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has done all this with the unwavering support of the United States. Biden has given Israel billions of dollars in aid, a steady supply of weapons, and Biden’s unrelenting diplomatic support. But now, after Trump’s victory, relations between the two countries have suddenly soured. 

Trump has appointed a few pro-Israeli appointees to his administration. Like Senator Marco Rubio and Governor Mike Huckabee. Netanyahu is so elated by Trump’s victory that he is offering the president-elect a ceasefire in Lebanon. A ceasefire as a gift! 

Trump has promised peace in the Middle East. Is Israel afraid of upsetting Trump’s grand plans? Will Israel adjust its goals accordingly? While there is unwavering support from Biden, there is no guarantee that it will come from Trump. 

India 
Indian institutions are also thrilled with Donald Trump’s return. India considers Trump's nominee for national security adviser Michael Waltz and his nominee for director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to be its friends. Many in India believe that Gabbard and Vivek Ramaswamy, who are Hindus, will be more loyal to India. 

People also remember the friendly relationship that Trump and Modi talked about during their bilateral meeting during Trump's first term as president. India thinks that Trump will be friendlier to India than Biden. The Modi government's terrible treatment of religious minorities and press freedoms has been somewhat pressured by the Biden administration. Many Indians are now convinced that Trump will not apply even a little pressure again.

Headline_English: The significance of three zeros in environmental conservation in Bangladesh
Content_Enlish:
Dr. Muhammad Yunus, the chief advisor to the interim government of Bangladesh, has presented a transformative but simple concept for addressing global challenges. In this, the importance of formulating urgent policies in the context of the ‘three zeros’ framework has been emphasized. The three zeros are: a) zero poverty, b) zero unemployment and c) zero carbon emissions. If these are not ensured, the world will not be able to move towards sustainable development. 

Inspired by this vision, individuals and organizations can set the ‘three zeros’ according to their priorities. For the environmental development of Bangladesh, attention should be paid to zero plastic, zero noise pollution and zero lead. If these policies are effectively incorporated into the environmental program, Bangladesh will be able to move towards building a healthy, environmentally friendly and sustainable nation by 2025. 

9.2 billion tons of plastic waste are generated worldwide. Of this, 7 billion tons are landfilled or discarded carelessly. This plastic waste is a major environmental crisis. Especially for Bangladesh. 

Plastic pollution creates environmental degradation, public health risks, and social and economic challenges. It also has detrimental effects on climate change and ecosystem dysfunction. According to the World Bank’s 2021 data, Bangladesh ranks among the top countries in plastic pollution, mainly due to inadequate waste management. The annual per capita plastic consumption in Dhaka is 22.25 kg. 

This amount is three times higher than in rural areas. It is understood that environmental pressures are much higher in urban areas. Plastic bags have been banned recently. But the effectiveness of these initiatives is low due to weak implementation. Bangladesh is facing the impact of climate change. The presence of these microplastics has exacerbated this crisis. 

Accelerating environmental damage. A completely plastic-free future is not realistic at the moment. However, Bangladesh needs to work towards significantly reducing plastic use and eliminating pollution. It is important that sustainable plastic management becomes the basis of the nation’s environmental strategy, with a goal of reducing plastic pollution by 2025 through a comprehensive and integrated approach. 

Another major environmental problem in Bangladesh, along with plastic, is noise pollution. This pollution is having a serious impact on public health. Recently, Dhaka was identified as the most noisy city among the 61 most densely populated cities in the world. According to a report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the average noise level in Dhaka has reached 119 decibels. 

This level is more than double the tolerable level. 65 percent of traffic police in the capital have reported hearing and sleep disturbances due to chronic high noise levels. Citizens are suffering from health risks due to chronic noise exposure. These include annoyance, sleep disturbances and more serious consequences. Such as heart disease and metabolic disorders. In addition, long-term exposure of children to noise pollution causes cognitive and intellectual disabilities in them. 

Solving these problems should be a national priority. With the aim of creating a noise-free Bangladesh by 2025, there is an urgent need to formulate strong policies, increase public awareness and effectively implement laws related to noise pollution. 

By adopting the ‘plastic zero, noise zero and lead zero’ framework, Bangladesh can unlock its full potential. Through this, it can reduce health risks and align with achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 
Lead pollution is a growing threat to public health and the environment in Bangladesh. The rapid spread of three-wheeled electric vehicles (such as easy bikes and e-rickshaws) has revolutionized urban mobility. 3 to 4 million vehicles in Bangladesh transport more than 112 million passengers every day. This number is more than the global Tesla fleet. 

However, the reliance on lead-acid batteries (LABs) used to power these vehicles poses serious environmental and health challenges. The main reasons for this are the lack of sustainable management and informal recycling of used lead-acid batteries (ULABs). Each vehicle uses 4 to 5 LABs, which carry 125 kg of lead per vehicle. 

Worryingly, only 10-20 percent of these batteries are recycled through formal channels. The remaining 80 percent is recycled informally, which is responsible for the generation of an estimated 167,000 metric tons of lead waste annually. This informal recycling sector has created a silent, but devastating health crisis. 

A recent study in The Lancet journal found that two out of three children in Bangladesh have high levels of lead in their blood, which has a detrimental effect on their cognitive development, attention, and educational outcomes. Lead poisoning reduces IQ levels, income potential, and quality of life. Cardiovascular diseases associated with lead exposure have become an urgent public health concern. An estimated 60,000 people die from heart disease each year, a number that is likely to increase to 138,054. Bangladesh has taken significant steps to address lead pollution, such as reclamation projects, source identification, and capacity-building initiatives. 

Specialized training programs, such as the Benchmarking Assessment Tool (BAT), Environmentally Sound Management (ESM) and App-based Implementation Strategies, will strengthen regulatory practices and enhance the knowledge of government officials. This effort will present a promising path to reduce lead pollution, stimulate sustainable recovery and build resilience within society. 

Despite the challenges, taking action to address plastic, noise and lead pollution can lead Bangladesh to economic growth, innovation and healthy lifestyles. Replacing plastic with sustainable alternatives, reducing noise for better health and transforming the electric vehicle sector can collectively help in the recovery and progress. By adopting the ‘

Zero Plastic, Zero Noise and Zero Lead’ framework, Bangladesh can unlock its full potential. Through this, it can reduce health risks and align with achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A strong policy framework and social engagement can create sustainable ecosystems. Through this, environmental, economic, and climate adaptation will be facilitated. These are essential for the people of Bangladesh to move towards a healthier and more sustainable future.

Headline_English: The biggest victory in Bashar's fall is Turkey's
Content_Enlish:
The overthrow of Bashar al-Assad and his flight to Moscow ended nearly 60 years of Baathist rule in Syria. 

Syria sided with Iran during the invasion of Saddam Hussein. In return, Iran stood by Bashar al-Assad’s government against the Islamic State and al-Qaeda attacks in Syria and Iraq from 2011–17. 

A coalition of Russia, Iran, and pro-Iranian armed groups known as the Axis of Resistance defeated the Islamist armed groups and protected the sovereignty of the two Arab countries. 

In any case, there was no trace of democracy with the Assad government. Western and Arab leaders were frightened and angered by the large presence of Iran and Russia in Syria. By any measure, the change in the Syrian political system has brought about major changes in the geopolitics of the Middle East. 

In the short term, Iran, Russia, Iraq, and the Axis of Iranian Resistance are the main losers in Assad’s fall. The fall of Assad has weakened Iran’s geopolitical influence in the Middle East. 

Syria is the only route for Iran to supply Hezbollah with weapons and supplies by road. As a result, the disruption of this supply route not only poses a strategic challenge for Hezbollah, but also weakens Iran’s leverage over the Palestinian issue. 

Now that the enemy has been overthrown, their differences will come to the fore. As a result, uncertainty remains about how to resolve their differences. 

The fall of the Assad regime in Syria also poses a major threat to Iraq’s security. This is true for both the Kurdish-dominated regions of Iraq and the Sunni-majority regions. 

In the short term, Israel has an opportunity to further weaken Hezbollah and the Iranian axis in the region. 

In any case, the activities of new Islamist armed groups in neighboring countries, Syria’s possible future position on the Palestinian issue, and the dispute over the Golan Heights all pose long-term security threats to Israel. 

In the short term, the fall of Assad would be a win for the United States and the West, as it would greatly reduce the influence of Russia and Iran in the region. 

It is still uncertain what the long-term impact of the fall of a secular government in Syria and the rise of Islamists will be on U.S. interests. The different views of the United States and Turkey on the Kurdish issue, the uncertainty about what the Syrian rebels will do in the future, and the potential for further instability in the region make it impossible to say. 

Turkey is the main winner in this event. Turkey can now hope to resolve the Syrian refugee crisis in its country, establish more effective control over the Kurdish region, play a stronger role in the Palestinian issue, and build stronger alliances with like-minded countries in the Middle East. 

While Arab countries are pleased with the decline of Iranian influence in Syria, Turkey has organized operations against Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) and other armed groups. These groups are associated with the Muslim Brotherhood. 

Several Arab countries, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan, are opposed to the Muslim Brotherhood and its ideology. As a result, Turkey’s influence in the Middle East is expanding and the Brotherhood will dominate Syria—which some Arab countries may consider a new threat. 

There are two possible scenarios for Syria’s political future. The first is a peaceful transition to a new order. The second is the outcome of the Libya or Sudan model. 

A peaceful transition is only possible if the Syrian rebels who ousted Assad adopt a moderate stance in word and deed. After all, they come from different groups. They have come together to eliminate a common enemy. 

Now that that enemy has been overthrown, their differences will come to the fore. As a result, there is uncertainty about how to resolve their differences. 

Even if the opposing parties can reduce their differences to zero, their conflict with the Kurds and Turkey’s position will still be the biggest obstacles to building a consensus. This could plunge Syria into a long-term political and security crisis, like Libya and Sudan.

Headline_English: The Assad era is over, how will the new Syria be formed?
Content_Enlish:
The fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad is the result of years of weak rule, economic crisis, and social problems. Even his own Alawite supporters have not come forward to fight for him. Another reason for Assad's fall is the loss of support from key allies like Russia and Iran. The war in Ukraine has weakened Russia. On the other hand, Israel's campaign against Hamas and Hezbollah has also weakened Iran's position. 

The Syrian people will not mourn Assad. Because he was a harsh ruler who failed his people in every way. Now many are taking to the streets to express joy. Those who fled the country and were in refugee camps are starting to return home. Assad's fall could have a positive impact not only inside Syria, but also across the region. Assad's rule facilitated the flow of weapons from Iran to Hezbollah. New leadership could help reduce this influence and build a stable regional order. 

The fall of strong rulers in the Middle East has usually been followed by violent chaos. Ultimately, a stable and inclusive government was not established. During Assad’s rule, the minority Alawite community ruled over the majority Sunni population. This created the fear of reprisals and assassinations. In addition, Syria’s diverse population could be subject to the politics of ethnic and sectarian division. 

The civil war left different parts of the country under the control of different rival groups. Among them, the Syrian Kurds are affiliated with the PKK (Kurdistan Workers’ Party). The PKK is considered a terrorist organization in Turkey. Turkey also occupied a large part of northern Syria. In this existing division, extremist groups could take advantage of the fall of Assad and the resulting instability. As in 2014, the Islamic State (IS) could once again try to seize large parts of the country. That is why Israel is creating a “safe zone” outside Syria’s borders and destroying Syrian weapons caches to prevent them from falling into the hands of groups hostile to Israel. 

The group that ousted Bashar al-Assad, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was originally formed as an al-Qaeda affiliate and is still listed as a terrorist organization by many countries, including the United States. Although HTS leaders have pledged restraint and inclusive policies aimed at forming a national government, they have a history of repression. In addition, rival groups in Syria may not agree to work together and seek revenge among themselves. 

On the other hand, Iran’s influence in Syria may be greatly reduced, but Iran will still try to maintain its power. In particular, Iran’s old ally, the Alawite sect, may fight its rivals for power. For these reasons, concerns remain about Syria’s future. In order to rebuild a viable state, the country’s territorial integrity must first be restored. This is only possible if the various groups agree to share power in the interests of national unity, while giving up some of their autonomy. 

In addition, a new social contract must be created that will provide the people with adequate security and economic opportunities. Although the main responsibility for this reconstruction lies with the Syrians. But the role of the international community is also important here. Learning from the experience of Iraq, external forces can put pressure on the Syrian opposition. 

Turkey and the United States must put pressure on their allies in Syria to cooperate with the new interim government; at least not to oppose it. External forces can also play a role in protecting the Syrian state and economy from further collapse. A lasting post-conflict solution there will be difficult to achieve if the standard of living deteriorates further. It was in such a hostile environment that the rise of extremism and state failure occurred after the regime change in Iraq. The next few months are crucial for Syria. Because the history of attempts to stabilize post-conflict societies is full of failures. Syria, Afghanistan, Iraq and Libya in the last 13 years are examples of that. That is why the reconstruction of Syria must be done properly. The time to do that is now.

Headline_English: Why is BNP not happy with Yunus' speech?
Content_Enlish:
In his speech on the occasion of 100 days of the interim government, Chief Advisor Dr. Muhammad Yunus said that the election train has started its journey with the formation of the Election Commission. It will not stop. 

Despite this assurance from the Chief Advisor, there was apprehension and uncertainty about the elections among people from different walks of life, including political parties. Many people asked why the government was not announcing the possible date of the elections? 

The political parties, especially the leaders of the BNP, pressured the government almost every day to announce the election roadmap. Again, each of the advisors was giving different hints. 

We thought that after receiving the reports of the six reform commissions by December 31, the countrymen might get some good news about the elections at the beginning of the new year. But the Chief Advisor announced the possible date of the elections in his speech to the nation on Victory Day on December 16. He said, ‘The national election will be held in the country between the end of 2025 and the first half of 2026 next year.’ 

However, here too, the chief advisor has put ‘if’ and ‘but’. He said, ‘If the election is to be completed on the basis of making a few reforms and preparing the voter list accurately, then it may be possible to hold the election by the end of 2025. And if we add to this the expected level of reforms in the light of the recommendations of the electoral process and the Electoral Reform Commission and based on national consensus, then it may take at least six more months of additional time. Roughly speaking, the election time can be set between the end of 2025 and the first half of 2026.’ 

The BNP was not happy with the chief advisor’s announcement. BNP standing committee member Salahuddin Ahmed said that the chief advisor has given an idea about the election time. But there is no clear roadmap in it. It is not clear from the chief advisor’s statement how much time is needed for reforms in some necessary areas. Hasnat Qayyum, the leader and coordinator of the State Reform Movement, also said that the government should give a roadmap for reforms before the elections. 

Wishing the countrymen a happy Victory Day, Professor Yunus said, "The first and biggest task is to update the voter list. This is already a difficult task. Now the task is even more difficult because voters did not have the opportunity to participate in the last three elections." 

The words of the chief advisor seem to indicate that the government does not want to end its responsibilities by handing over power to the people's representatives with just one election; they also want to ensure their participation in the process of political reform by forming a national consensus building commission. Another problem here is that the commissions formed earlier are not part of the government. The members of the commissions formed by the government are appointed persons. But if the national consensus commission is formed under the leadership of the chief advisor, it will become an essential part of the government. 
In fact, the task is not very difficult. A member of the Election Reform Commission said that every citizen aged 18 years and above has a national identity card, based on which there should be no problem in making an accurate voter list. The people who could not vote in the last three elections were not due to discrepancies in the voter list, but because the elections were not competitive. Even though the young people who were the first voters in the last three elections did not vote, they have national identity cards. As a result, those who explained to the chief advisor that the task of compiling an accurate voter list is very difficult did not give the right advice. 

Stating that the voting of the youth will be a memorable event, Professor Yunus said, ‘All arrangements must be made to smooth this experience. My sincere wish is that the young people who are the first to vote in this election create a tradition by voting in numbers close to 100 percent.’ Voting is compulsory in many countries, including Australia. If you do not vote without a valid reason, you have to pay a fine. The chief advisor did not say whether the interim government is thinking of enacting such a law in Bangladesh. The 2008 election is proof that democracy is not sustainable even if there are many voters. 

The chief advisor said, ‘Political consensus is needed to undertake any reform work. The interim government has formed six reform commissions in the first phase. I hope they will submit their final reports soon. We are moving towards establishing a “National Consensus Building Commission” with the chairmen of these six commissions. Its job will be to identify the issues on which consensus will be established by exchanging views with all parties, including political parties, and make recommendations for implementation. 

While the task of preparing the voters’ list is not difficult, establishing a national consensus on other reforms, including elections, will be a very difficult task. There are fierce disputes among political parties on various issues. Although Jamaat-e-Islami and the left parties are interested in proportional representation elections, BNP is strongly opposed. The left parties are also expressing a general agreement on the four fundamental principles of the state; but opposition is coming from the Islamic parties. There is also no consensus among all parties on whether there will be a bicameral or unicameral parliament. 

However, everyone agrees on one issue. And that is to hold national elections under a non-partisan caretaker government. There is no disagreement that the current interim government will play a supervisory role in the next election. However, there will be a problem if any of the government's advisors want to participate in the election. 

The ordinance approved in principle by the Advisory Council on the interim government states that no one from the government will be able to participate in the next election. Many people have raised questions because it has not been issued in the form of an ordinance even after several days have passed since the approval by the Advisory Council. The government's position should be clarified on this issue as well. 

The Chief Advisor's words seem to indicate that the government does not want to end its responsibilities by simply handing over power to the people's representatives through an election; they also want to ensure their participation in the process of political reform by forming a national consensus-building commission. Another problem here is that the commissions formed earlier are not part of the government. Members of the commissions formed by the government are appointed persons. But if there is a national consensus commission formed under the leadership of the Chief Advisor, it will become an essential part of the government. 

Although the Chief Advisor said that there will be an election train, he did not disclose which election train will come first. Some quarters have demanded that local government elections be held before the national elections. At the same time, there is a push to form new parties. 

We welcome the election roadmap announced by the Chief Advisor. However, the question remains as to how much his proposed National Consensus Commission will be able to unite the nation.

Headline_English: We wanted such a fearless celebration.
Content_Enlish:
Just before Victory Day, I was talking to a media person in Dhaka on the phone last Saturday night. In the midst of various conversations, he said that Victory Day celebrations have begun in Dhaka. After listening to him, I asked him how he views this Victory Day as a media person. 

In response, the journalist said, "After a long time, we are celebrating Victory Day in a free environment. Everyone in the country is celebrating the great achievements of the Liberation War in a fearless environment. As such, this Victory Day has brought a different atmosphere to us. The joy of Victory Day has also been added to the joy of freeing the country from fascism. Now we no longer have to speak with extreme caution. There is no need to whisper and whisper in a low voice while sitting in a cafe." 

The main thing about this year's Victory Day is this fearless environment. The joy of Victory Day does not belong to any specific party or political statement. This joy belongs to everyone. But in the past 16 years, the liberation war, the victory of the war, was based on a kind of exclusive narrative that it was the victory of the Awami League and the Bengalis. During this time, Victory Day had to be celebrated under various restrictions. There was no normal atmosphere at all across the country. 

Yet, the main spirit of our liberation war was to form a liberal and tolerant state and society. But by subverting the main idea of ​​the liberation war, an atmosphere was created that stifled and stifled, where there was no opportunity to even criticize politics normally. We know what would have happened to those who wanted to speak out even in an extremely controlled environment. Writer and activist Mushtaq Ahmed was killed inside the prison. 

A report by the Commission on Disappearances, published just a day before Victory Day, details these atrocities by the government forces. The report, titled ‘Unfolding the Truth’, said that the lips of living people were sewn shut and taken away. They were killed and tied to cement bags and thrown into the river. They even killed and threw the bodies on the railway tracks. The moving train would tear the bodies to pieces. The commission has not yet given a full report. However, for now, we have learned about the chilling details of torture from that report. In an independent country, the Awami League was no less than the Pakistanis in terms of torture. The Awami League chose a path as brutal as the Pakistanis to suppress opposition. 

This Victory Day is free from the monopoly of the Awami League and Bengalis. The victory of August 5 has given us an opportunity to liberate the victory of 1971. We have to realize the achievements of August 5. In the light of ’71 and ’24, Bangladesh must be made a state for all. Bangladesh is not a country of a single nation or religion. 
By suppressing and oppressing, the Awami League not only enslaved the entire country, but also the Liberation War. The narrative made by the Awami League about the Liberation War was the last word. The Awami League used to decide who was a freedom fighter and who was anti-liberation. During their rule, they made many freedom fighters anti-liberation. And they made anti-liberation freedom fighters. They did not even spare their own party's minister, freedom fighter Khandaker AK Karim, due to his dissent. He was vilified as a Razakar and anti-liberation. The Awami League also took the initiative to cancel the Liberation War charter of former President Ziaur Rahman. 

But the Liberation War as a political party is not the Awami League's alone. Except for a few anti-liberationists in 1971, the people of the entire country joined the war in the fight to liberate the country. Where there was no ethnic, political, religious and cultural division. Everyone joined the fight to form Bangladesh from their own political understanding. 

But in the past, the great Liberation War was promoted as a victory of Bengalis alone, thereby making everyone's achievements a private matter. Due to the majority, the contribution and participation of Bengalis in the Liberation War was certainly greater. But along with this, other ethnicities and language speakers also participated. They also made significant contributions to our liberation struggle. The achievement of a collective struggle is not continued as the victory of the majority alone in the modern state system. There is no scope for the majority to be given priority in an inclusive state. 

The victory of 1971 is the fruit of the collective sacrifice of all nations and groups. Therefore, it is not just the victory of Bengalis; this victory belongs to all of Bangladesh. To every nation, group and religion living in the territory of Bangladesh. Even the smallest ethnic group, even if its population is only one, must also share in this success and victory.

To take Bangladesh forward, we must build an inclusive society. To do this, we must first come out of the idea of ​​identifying the victory of 1971 as the victory of the Bengalis. Our motto will be Bangladesh first.

Headline_English: Why did Iran also turn its back on Assad?
Content_Enlish:
After 14 years of popular uprising and 13 years of devastating civil war, the fall of the Assad regime was a matter of time. 

The images and videos that have emerged of prisoners, including children, have been likened to medieval dungeons. Social media is awash with images and videos of Syrians celebrating their newfound freedom from the brutal rule of the Assad family. 

However, others may learn something from the fall of the most brutal ruler in the history of the Middle East. For Assad’s desire to hold on to power at all costs not only reduced Syria to ruins, but also sowed the seeds of his own downfall. 

The clearest lesson from Assad’s fall is that relying on foreign patrons and believing that their support will never end is a big mistake. In the case of Bashar al-Assad, this was an inevitable outcome. Assad received extensive support from Iran. He was confident that he was an indispensable part of the axis of resistance. 

For example, Iran has invested more than $30-50 billion in Syria over the past 13 years. This is 7.5 to 12.5 percent of Iran’s total GDP in 2023. This is certainly a huge amount for a country under sanctions. 

We have seen some of the top Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officers killed in Syria. In most cases, Israelis targeted them. In 2016, 1,000 Iranian soldiers were killed. In 2019, 2,300 were killed. 

This huge investment created an illusion in Assad of his indispensability. Assad thought his position was secure. That is why he began to try to distance himself from Iran and re-integrate himself into the Arab world. Assad thought that investment from the Gulf countries would flood Syria. 

In fact, Assad refrained from taking an active part in the conflict between Iran and Israel. Even as senior Iranian commanders were being killed on Syrian soil, Iran expressed concern that intelligence was being leaked from the Syrian security forces. 

Assad’s army was the guarantor of his power. But Assad paid his soldiers very little, leaving them dependent on widespread corruption to survive. This failed to transform the army into an effective fighting force and paved the way for his downfall. 

This was a huge miscalculation for Assad. Without Iran’s additional military support, the Syrian army quickly collapsed under the onslaught of the rebels. 

External support can never be unlimited or unconditional, especially when the sponsoring country has its own challenges to overcome. 

For example, Russia was involved in the war in Ukraine. This was evident in Russia’s failure to prevent the fall of Aleppo. Russia had reserved most of its warplanes for the war in Ukraine. 

The second lesson is that failure to reform properly will lead to your downfall. It is undeniable that the fall of Aleppo to the Assad regime and its allies in 2016 completely turned the tide of the Syrian civil war in Assad’s favor. 

Then in 2018, in Daraa and Eastern Ghouta, rebel groups surrendered under heavy shelling by Assad and his allies. 

As a result, the grip of power came under Assad’s control. Yet it was considered the right time to start a political process. In any case, Assad did not move towards any kind of compromise. He did not start any political process that could include the opposition. 

A widespread pattern of repression developed. This included confiscation of property, demolition of houses, torture, and arbitrary detention of thousands of people. 

The agreement that had been reached to reduce tensions in Idlib was clearly violated. 

Assad also consistently refused to normalize Syria’s relations with Turkey, which was mediated by Russia. 

Assad’s failure to reach an agreement with his opponents at home and with his rivals abroad paved the way for his downfall. In fact, if Assad had been able to normalize relations with Ankara, it would have been much harder for the opposition to launch an attack without Turkey’s strategic support and approval. 

On the other hand, if he had been able to bring the opposition into the political process, the attack that brought him down would have been much less likely. 

Perhaps the most important factor in the fall of the Assad regime was that he had lost the support of even his most loyal supporters. 

When Assad fell, 90 percent of Syrians had fallen below the poverty line. Inflation had risen to 120 percent by April 2024. There had been a major devaluation of the currency. The GDP had shrunk from $67 billion in 2011 to about $9 billion in 2021. 

To address these crises, Assad turned Syria into a narco-state. Syria became a hub for the production and export of Captagon-like drugs. In 2021, Syria’s Captagon drug economy was worth an estimated $5.7 billion. 

In other words, Assad sacrificed the country’s economic life to stay in power. As a result, the Assad regime gifted the country endless civil war and endless deaths in poverty. 

Assad’s army was the guarantor of his power. But Assad paid his soldiers very little. As a result, they became dependent on widespread corruption to survive. This failed to transform the army into an effective fighting force and paved the way for his downfall. 

Other dictators in the region and their patrons are likely to ignore these lessons. 

The most obvious example is Egypt’s Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. He is the president of a country that is extremely financially dependent on other countries. He is strongly anti-reform and dependent on suppressing the people. He is rarely concerned about alleviating the financial hardship of ordinary people (even those who support his government).

Headline_English: How can BNP's proposal for a bicameral parliament be implemented?
Content_Enlish:
The opportunity has come to make major changes in the politics and state structure of Bangladesh. After the July mass uprising and the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government, vigorous discussions have begun on state system reforms. 

The sincerity in the discussions on what kind of changes can be brought to the state structure from both sides - political parties and the interim government - is noticeable. Although there are differences among the political parties on how and when these reforms will be carried out, no one doubts that changes to the state structure are necessary. 

One of the 31-point proposals announced by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its like-minded parties for state reforms is the formation of a bicameral legislature. 

According to this proposal by the BNP, experts from various professions will be given the opportunity to play a role in lawmaking in the upper house, along with the existing parliamentary structure. They believe that it will be possible to bring a balance of power in the governance of the state by utilizing the special knowledge and experience of these experts. 

BNP Acting Chairman Tarique Rahman said in a recent speech, ‘There are countless knowledgeable, talented teachers, artists-literate people, journalists, researchers, doctors, technical experts, and human rights activists in the country who are not involved in traditional politics but want to participate in the formation, development, and governance of the country; but in the current constitutional framework, there is no opportunity for them to contribute as members of parliament. To utilize their services and contributions for the benefit of the country, BNP wants to see a bicameral parliament system with an upper house included in the constitution in our country like many other countries in the world’ (September 4, The Daily Star). 

The United States is one of the countries that has a system of electing members of the upper house through elections. Two members of the upper house, that is, the Senate, are elected from each of the 50 states of the United States. The total number of members of the Senate is therefore 100. It is worth noting here that all states, whether large or small in population or area, have two senators. This system has been put in place with the aim of giving equal importance to small states.

Apart from the United States, Argentina, Switzerland and Australia also have a system of electing members of the upper house through elections. Some countries elect members of the upper house not by direct vote of the people, but by indirect vote through elected representatives of the people or state representatives. Germany, Austria and France are among these countries. 

In our neighboring country India, 238 members of the upper house Rajya Sabha are elected by the votes of the state and union territory legislatures under the proportional representation system through 'single transferable' votes. However, the President of India can appoint 12 people who have made special contributions to art, literature, science and social service as members. In that regard, it is a mixed system. 

The upper house system is necessary to ensure that the legislature of Bangladesh does not depend solely on the whim of the ruling party. Along with this, if Article 70 of the Constitution is repealed in both houses, the power of the members of parliament to give their own opinions beyond the party decisions will be created. It is difficult to make and get approval from arbitrary laws in a bicameral legislature. 
One of the most traditional examples of bicameral legislatures is the British House of Commons and the House of Lords. The legislature began in the 11th century and the bicameral legislature was fully introduced in the United Kingdom from the 13th century. The members of the upper house, the House of Lords, are not directly or indirectly elected by the people, but are appointed through lineage, political and religious importance. Lords, barons, earls, etc. are members of the lineage and religious representatives such as archbishops and bishops. However, political considerations also have a major influence on these appointments. 

There are examples of members of the upper house of parliament being appointed from representatives of different professions and tribes in society. The National Council of Slovenia is composed of representatives of different languages, nationalities and indigenous peoples. There are also representatives of various professions including teachers, doctors, researchers, workers, farmers. 

Direct election, indirect election, appointment of lineage and religious influential people and social representative appointment - basically, members of the upper house are elected in different countries by these four methods. A mixed system could be considered for Bangladesh. 

The most influential political party in Bangladesh, the BNP, and its like-minded parties do not want a proportional representation system in the lower house. On the other hand, Jamaat-e-Islami and some smaller parties are in favor of this system. There are some major complications in introducing a proportional representation system in the lower house, and there is even a possibility of rehabilitating the authoritarian Awami League through it. 

On the other hand, a proportional representation system in the upper house could benefit both the BNP and the smaller parties. If the current ‘first past the post’ system in the lower house is kept and a proportional representation system is introduced in the upper house, on the one hand, the people will have the power to elect their own representatives through direct votes, and on the other hand, small parties and important figures from civil society will also have the opportunity to participate in the country’s lawmaking and scrutiny. 

According to this proposal, political parties can elect their members of the upper house in two ways. First, members of the upper house can be elected through indirect votes. After the members of the lower house are elected, the political parties will nominate their members of the upper house in that proportion. 

The second method is that the people will vote separately for the upper house by voting directly for the lower house along with another ballot (which may be of a different color) only for the party symbol. Along with this, the President may have the authority to appoint five to six members of the upper house, who can be appointed with special consideration without the nomination of any political party. It must be ensured that the nominations of the members that the political parties will nominate in a proportional ratio include representation of different sections of the country and society. 

Women, youth, ethnic and religious minorities, and backward regions must be represented. In addition, it is important to have representation of various professions, such as doctors, engineers, teachers, researchers, former government officials, former army officers, lawyers, artists, writers, journalists, farmers, workers, etc. in the upper house. 

Political parties must prepare their lists for the upper house by ensuring the representation of these classes and professions. Meanwhile, the BNP has mentioned the election of members based on profession among the major parties, which is clear from the statement of the acting chairman of the party. Political parties and civil society should come to a consensus on the process of electing members of the upper house before the elections. 

The upper house system is necessary to ensure that the legislature of Bangladesh does not depend solely on the whims of the ruling party. Along with this, repealing Article 70 of the Constitution in both houses will create the power of members of parliament to give their own opinions beyond party decisions. 

It is difficult to make and get approval for arbitrary laws in a bicameral legislature. In addition, along with the leaders of major political parties, leaders of small political parties and representatives of civil society will also be members of the upper house, through which the representation of different classes and professions of society will increase, as well as the balance of power will be created.

Headline_English: How can the banking sector turn around?
Content_Enlish:
The characteristic of all the best and successful private commercial banks in the world is that they work independently, with the cooperation, supervision and audit of the board of directors. There is no unwanted or unreasonable interference in these supervisions, which are carried out according to specific rules. The main decisions of the strategic and operational procedures of these profit-oriented financial institutions are finally implemented after proper audit, review and diligence by the board of directors. 

After close observation, it has been seen that behind the success of many banks, many independent directors play a major role, who work thinking about the progress and achievements of the bank outside of personal interests. The matter of concern is that most of the commercial banks in Bangladesh are not independent or autonomous. Out of more than fifty commercial banks, only a few banks are partially autonomous with the right guidance and cooperation from the board of directors. Needless to say, these handful of banks are the most successful, strong and praised in the country. 

On the other hand, the banks controlled by the ‘Board of Directors’ of Bangladesh are run by them on a daily basis; but there is a lack of balance and compromise between the Board of Directors and the Management Board in implementing the policies. The reason for this lack of compromise and balance is that the Board of Directors of commercial banks in Bangladesh is more authoritative. In the Board of Directors of our commercial banks, people directly associated with their ownership, political leaders, and even close relatives of the owners are considered influential. 

Due to this situation, it is seen that influence is exerted in the process of making bank activities and policies in the hope of personal gain. It can be said that many times the entire process is corrupted and the banks are run in the wrong direction. The directors of the banks themselves are not independent, moreover, various unethical interventions come through them. The primary infrastructure of these commercial banks is full of mistakes and various complications arise in the policies. 

In the history of commercial bank management, the work of directors working with executive responsibilities has been more fruitful than that of people associated with ownership or parties. These directors do not have any direct relationship with the bank and therefore their primary objective is to improve the bank through their work. 

JPMorgan Chase emphasizes a balance of professionalism and industry knowledge, business, financial expertise, senior management, and diversity of representation among the members of its board of directors. Following this principle, the board of directors is appointed from among people with experience in leadership, business management, JPMorgan Chase and its businesses, and those who are interested in taking on challenges; judgment, achievement, integrity, and judgment. According to the company's management policy, at least two-thirds of the board members must be independent. 
In this method, directors are brought out of business-related thinking, so that they can create new plans and ideas while keeping their profit-making perspective in mind and turn them into work through rules and regulations. 

According to this method, to become a bank director, even if he does not have much experience in the banking sector, he needs to have a good idea about how this sector works. In addition, these independent directors can learn the necessary practical ideas and technical tasks from other executive directors. Because it is necessary to know about the rules, structure and procedures of an organization. 

Another important thing is that they must also have human qualities. Because through this, it will be easier to understand the logic or perspective of other members. In addition, if such directors have good communication or acquaintance with the outside world, they are able to further integrate the organization by creating diversity in the mix of markets, industries and people. Since the directors are not associated with the bank, they can easily raise various questions and even challenge decisions. As a result, unilateral decisions cannot be made or questions that arise due to mistakes can be corrected. 

JPMorgan Chase emphasizes the balance of professionalism and sector knowledge, business, financial skills, high-level management, as well as the diversity of these presentations among the members of the board of directors. In accordance with this principle, the Board of Directors is appointed from among those with experience in leadership, business management, JPMorgan Chase and its businesses, and those who are willing to take on challenges; They are appointed from among those with experience in leadership, business management, JPMorgan Chase and its businesses, and those who are willing to take on challenges; They are appointed from among those with experience in judgment, achievement, integrity and a desire to take on challenges. According to the company's governing policy, at least two-thirds of the board members must be independent. 

According to some of the inclusion criteria, candidates who have shown particular evidence of ethics; Have served as chairman, chief executive officer, chief operating officer or equivalent policymaker of a business, professional organization; Are skilled in a particular field or have been previously employed by members; Have financial skills that allow them to monitor various issues; Work with everyone with integrity and are willing to question various issues of management; Such people are included. 

According to the policy of HSBC Holdings, its board should be dominated by independent executive directors, whose job is to monitor and challenge the management of the company, as well as help improve strategic matters. They are also responsible for assessing the risks of the company and communicating the policies and management adopted. Some of the regional banks, such as Singapore's Development Bank of Singapore (DBS) or United Overseas Bank (UOB); India's HDFC or ICICI Bank, follow a similar ideology. 

The boards of directors of these banks are primarily run by independent directors. Most of the directors are highly respected in relevant matters and as independent directors, they literally influence the strategy and management of the bank. Their remuneration is also designed to reflect their enthusiasm and performance. Based on these, it can be said that most of the world's international banks, and even many regional banks, have given special importance to the appointment of independent executive directors.

Headline_English: When will the chaos in public transport in Narayanganj end?
Content_Enlish:
Kings come and kings come, but the face of anarchy in many things in the country never changes. The places of irregularities never remain empty. Somehow or the other, they are filled. Markets, ghats, markets, sidewalks, extortion in transport, encroachment of rivers, encroachment of government land and property—these things change hands. These can never be kept free from encroachment or extortion. When one group leaves, another group fills that place. These extortionists or encroachments are always from the government party. The administration helps them. In some places, the administration and all these encroachments and extortionists continue this work together. The picture of this anarchy in transport is horrific. 

For ages, an anarchic situation has prevailed in the entire country regarding public transport. The government forms a syndicate in transport to provide immoral benefits to its party members. The syndicate keeps ordinary passengers hostage year after year. This anarchy has increased terribly during the previous rule of the Sheikh Hasina government. 

According to information published in various national dailies on October 22, former Shipping Minister Shahjahan Khan alone has extorted Tk 24,000 crore from the transport sector in the last 15 years. Recently, Transparency International (TIB) said in a study that corruption worth Tk 29,000 to 50,000 crore has been committed in the construction of road and highway projects alone in the last 14 years. They said that the extent and depth of extortion in the road and transport sector is very high. This sector is hostage to politics. 

Sheikh Hasina's government has always been against the people and has always irrationally set the fare per kilometer for public transport. The owners have always maintained dominance in the fare-setting meetings. The fare has been set the way they wanted. In line with this anti-people policy of the government, the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) has also set the fares of various places ignoring the interests of the people. 

The anarchy over transport in Narayanganj has been going on for a long time. During the Awami League regime, the transport sector, like other sectors, was one of the sources of extortion by the Osman family. The local BRTA and administration have always helped them in arbitrarily increasing the fare and creating suffering for the people. 

In June 2011, a movement was formed in Narayanganj when the bus fare on the Dhaka-Narayanganj route was increased from Tk 22 to Tk 32. At that time, the 'Passenger Rights Protection Forum' was formed by local social, political and cultural organizations to protect the rights of passengers in Narayanganj. A few days ago, the local transport owners had written to the local RAB to get rid of the extortion. In the letter, they mentioned how Shamim Osman and Nasim Osman were paid extortion every month. At that time, the fare was reduced to Tk 27 in the face of the movement. 

On August 5, some of the Narayanganj transport syndicate left the country along with Sheikh Hasina, while others went into hiding. In the changing reality of the country, the general public of Narayanganj has now demanded that this transport sector should not be captured by another extortionist or godfather. No new godfather should be able to flourish by taking people's pockets and holding them hostage. And that is why there is a demand to reduce the fares of all routes from Narayanganj to Dhaka to a reasonable level after August 5 and to quickly implement half the fare for students. 

To that end, BRTA, transport owners and leaders of the Passenger Rights Protection Forum have held several joint meetings with the local District Administrator, but no effective initiative has been observed to implement the demand. On April 2, 2024, BRTA issued a notification regarding bus fares on the Narayanganj route. Although the notification was to protect the interests of the owners, the owners did not accept that notification. They have been collecting additional fares year after year, going beyond the notification. The district administration or BRTA has no role in stopping this. 

The notification shows the distance between Dhaka and Narayanganj as 19.5 kilometers (2.32 taka per kilometer), the fare is shown as 45 taka, the flyover toll is 5 taka and the Sanarpar U-turn is 3 taka, and the total fare on this route is 53 taka. The same notification also states that the fare for Dhaka-Narayanganj will be 54 taka. But in reality, 55 taka is being charged. The notification shows that if a passenger gets off at Narayanganj Terminal, the fare is 45 taka (excluding flyover and U-turn), 42 taka if he gets off at Chashara, 40 taka from Notun Court, 37 taka from Shibu Market, 31 taka from Jalkuri, etc. But the fare is being charged at 45 taka from all places. 

The notification shows the distance from Motijheel to Shapla Chattar as 19.5 kilometers. But the reality is that no bus travels around Shapla Chattar. According to the calculation, the current distance is 17 kilometers. Even though the government reduced the price of diesel by Tk 1.50 per liter on August 30 and later by Tk 0.50, BRTA or the administration did not take any initiative to reduce the fare. The district administration and BRTA did not take any effective steps to resolve these discrepancies despite knowing them. On the other hand, the long-standing demand for half the fare for students is also unresolved. 

In such a reality, demands are being raised to reduce the Dhaka-Narayanganj fare to Tk 45, the fare of CNG-powered buses on all routes from Narayanganj to a reasonable level, half the fare for students, and to make BRTC buses Tk 60 and private buses Tk 65. 

Various local social, cultural and political organizations have already expressed solidarity with these demands. Local BNP, left parties and Islamic parties have expressed solidarity. The Passenger Rights Protection Forum has set a deadline of November 15 for implementing the demands. The people of Narayanganj believe that the Deputy Commissioner will respect the public demands of the people of Narayanganj and implement them.

Headline_English: What is the way to increase the number of seats in universities?
Content_Enlish:
First of all, higher education is not for everyone. Especially, where the rate of highly educated unemployed in the country is increasing alarmingly. However, the state cannot avoid responsibility by talking about unemployment. Just as the state has to create new jobs, it also has to provide opportunities for higher education for all those interested. It is important to discuss how this is possible in the current infrastructure. 

This year, more than 1.331 million candidates appeared for the HSC and equivalent examinations in 11 education boards. The pass rate is 77.78. That means that more than 1.035 million students have passed. It is estimated that some of these students will no longer be in education. A large number of the remaining students will take the admission tests in universities and other higher educational institutions with the hope of higher education. But very few students will be able to get admission in their desired places. 

Students start preparing for admission to medical, BUET and universities after HSC. Coaching centers try to convince students and parents that the admission test means crossing a turbulent sea. In reality, students and parents see how several times more students are fighting for a single seat every year. Many students who fail in this fight lose interest in studying for the rest of their academic lives. 

First, we need to think about whether we really want to increase the number of seats in universities. We need to ask first, and then the means or plans will be clarified through discussion. 

In the latest 2023-24 academic year, 1 lakh 22 thousand 80 people applied for the undergraduate program admission test of the Science Unit at Dhaka University against 1 thousand 851 seats. That means, 66 people competed against one seat. In the last few years, the number of seats at Dhaka University has not increased. Seats have decreased in most departments. This means that competition has increased day by day. It can be seen that fewer students are getting admission in Dhaka University than they were four-five years ago. Students also have to compete fiercely for admission in the other three autonomous universities. 

Every year, the university has to verify its capacity to admit students. Before opening the online application process, each department is asked centrally how many students they can admit. The departments determine the number of students by considering the existing situation. In this case, the number of seats in the classroom is very important. Although there is a high demand, more students are given admission than there are seats. 

Dhaka University is the main place of interest for most students seeking admission. Apart from this, students have to compete fiercely in the other three autonomous universities. However, it is surprising that the students who try their best to get admitted die within a few days of starting classes in the university. Most of the admitted students are not seen to be focused on academic studies. 

It is surprising that the students who try their best to get admitted die within a few days of starting classes in the university. Most of the admitted students are not seen to be focused on academic studies. In this case, some systematic changes need to be made so that students focus on university classes and exams. In this case, universities need to get out of the policy that students must pass their undergraduate or postgraduate exams at any cost. Because, public universities provide huge subsidies against the education expenses of each student. 

The best way to increase seats in universities is to introduce two shifts instead of one shift. There are also departments in Dhaka University where 100 to 150 students sit together in classes. Teachers end classes with lectures like giving speeches to a mass gathering. There is not enough opportunity for students to discuss each other, do group work, or give class presentations in class activities. However, simply taking classes in two shifts can make the entire program more productive. 

If classes can be taken in two shifts, it is also possible to increase the number of student admissions. In this case, some additional problems may arise. For example, there will be additional pressure on teachers for more classes. For this, it may be necessary to increase the number of teachers. Or they may have to be given additional honorarium. Pressure will also increase in the area of ​​hall accommodation, transportation, library seats and other areas. 

Some measures can be taken immediately. For example, a portion of the admitted students will be those who will confirm in the admission form at the time of application that they will not take up residential facilities. The number of vehicles or the number of vehicle trips for transportation will have to be increased. If the shift system is introduced in the library, the tendency of occupying a chair continuously and studying 'BCS' will also decrease. However, it will definitely be necessary to increase various infrastructural facilities. No changes can be made suddenly. 

Half of the students' studies can be made completely online. The skills of teachers and students have been developed in this work during the Covid period. It can be seen that all such facilities are available online, which are almost impossible to get in a direct classroom. For example, it is very easy to discuss online by presenting PDF copies of books or showing slides made by the teacher himself. 

Currently, most government universities have classes five days a week. If this can be done, there will be two direct classes a week and two online classes, but the pressure on teachers' classes can be reduced. The remaining day can be kept for group work, class presentations, project work, library work, assignment preparation and continuous assessment by the students. 

To reduce the 'highly educated unemployed', at least half of the master's level students should be involved in research work. Their research topics and areas should be determined taking into account the needs of the society. Students should also be associated with various institutions through various projects. In this way, they can make themselves more skilled and competent. 

In short, we should first think about whether we really want to increase the number of seats in universities. We should ask first, and then the means or planning aspects will also be clarified through discussion.

Headline_English: Imran Khan's 'final call' in Pakistani politics
Content_Enlish:
On November 24, PTI chief Imran Khan gave a ‘final call’. His workers and supporters in Islamabad will protest against the ‘snatched mandate’, unjust arrests and the 26th Constitutional Amendment in the capital Islamabad. 

A major reason for the popularity of Tehreek-e-Insaf is the failure and poor performance of the Pakistan Muslim League (N) and Pakistan Peoples Party governments. This problem was also Imran Khan’s own. He was rapidly losing popularity during his three and a half years in power, especially in Punjab. A ‘no-confidence’ motion was brought against him in March 2022. His government got a new lease of life for a short time. 

The axis of politics did not change between April 2022 and November 2024. 80 percent of the media’s news and comments were only about Khan Sahib. Excluding the results of the last February 8, 90 percent of the ‘independent’ candidates who won in the party-based elections had ties to the PTI. I ask my democratic friends, what would have been the outcome if PTI had been allotted their election symbol? 

However, despite Imran’s popularity, why PTI has yet to launch a successful protest movement, why Khan Sahib had to give a ‘final call’, is a matter worth pondering. And it is something that his own party needs to ponder as well. This call is a challenge for his party; and a big risk for Imran Khan himself. 

Why does PTI feel ‘alone’ in this movement? Imran Khan himself is also a ‘victim of isolation’. And that is because of his strategy. On the one hand, he himself has formed a six-party alliance. But before giving the ‘final call’, he did not trust or talk to any party. Where are the leaders of his alliances? Why is PTI silent on all this? There is another reason for Khan’s isolation. 

Many of his trusted colleagues have left him in these difficult times. Perhaps because he no longer trusts those whom he himself nominated and appointed to high positions. Today, his wife Bushra Bibi and sister have practically entered politics. Sister Aleema Khan has announced a 'final call' despite not holding any party position.
