Headline_English: Why this year's climate conference is important for Bangladesh
Content_Enlish:
The World Climate Conference (COP-29) will be held in Baku, Azerbaijan from November 11-22, 2014. Like every year, a delegation from Bangladesh will attend. Bangladesh has some good achievements at COP-28. Bangladesh has played a leading role in promoting climate resilience, access to finance and fair access to climate-vulnerable countries. 

Bangladesh has been largely successful in negotiating climate finance for a balanced allocation of funds between adaptation and mitigation. Bangladesh highlighted the need for developed countries to meet their annual commitments of $100 billion. Bangladesh also spoke about the complexity of accessing the climate fund. 

The establishment of a $700 million loss and damage fund was a key achievement of COP-28. Bangladesh, as the country most affected by climate-related disasters, welcomed this development. 

Bangladesh, which leads the countries most affected by climate change, has been working for fair international financing. As a result of continued efforts, new financing mechanisms have also laid the foundation for ensuring effective and easy access. It is hoped that the benefits will be seen soon. 

Situation in Bangladesh 
Bangladesh is going to this conference in a radically changed political context. On the other hand, global temperatures are rising, biodiversity is being lost and natural disasters are becoming a regular occurrence. Support for Bangladesh to address these challenges and achieve climate resilience is essential. 

COP 29 is important for Bangladesh. The conference is an important opportunity for Bangladesh to ensure the necessary support for adaptation, mitigation and financing for losses and damages. Bangladesh is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. As such, Bangladesh deserves global action at COP 29 to achieve ambitious climate-related challenges. 

A Climate Vulnerability Assessment was conducted to assess the damage due to climate change. This document review shows that the central and coastal flood-prone areas are vulnerable to flooding and river erosion due to heavy rainfall and sea level rise. Annual monsoon floods affect about 18 percent of Bangladesh’s total land area. This affects agriculture, infrastructure and livelihoods, especially in low-lying floodplains. 

The northwestern region of Bangladesh faces severe water shortages during drought-prone, dry seasons. The coastal regions of Bangladesh are at high risk of cyclones. These events have intensified in recent years. Sea level rise is causing salinity intrusion into coastal areas, polluting freshwater resources and arable land. Food security and healthcare for people in southern Bangladesh are under serious threat. Rising temperatures in the country are likely to increase the frequency of extreme heat events, especially in urban areas. This trend increases health risks for vulnerable populations. The study found that unless climate action is scaled up, Bangladesh could lose 2 percent of its annual GDP by 2050 due to climate impacts. 

Bangladesh’s lack of skilled negotiators often makes it difficult to present its case in the appropriate forums. However, Bangladesh has made significant progress in climate policy. In 2021, it updated its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), which sets out ambitious targets for greenhouse gas reductions. These include renewable energy, energy efficiency and sustainable agriculture. 

Achieving these targets depends on substantial financial support and technology transfer from developed countries. This has therefore been included in the central agenda of COP29. 

Bangladesh’s priorities at COP29 
Bangladesh’s agenda at COP29 revolves around three main agendas: climate finance, adaptation implementation and operationalization of the damage fund. 

Bangladesh seeks a new global climate finance package beyond the $100 billion annual target pledged by developed countries in 2009. About $90 billion is needed to meet climate adaptation and mitigation needs by 2030. Therefore, financial support from international sources is crucial. COP29 is an appropriate platform for Bangladesh to negotiate for accessible and adequate climate finance. 

Bangladesh’s climate resilience plans emphasize coastal afforestation, improved water management and climate-resilient agricultural practices. COP29 will emphasize the implementation of National Adaptation Plans (NAPS) and provide necessary support for the implementation of infrastructure projects designed to protect people from the impacts of climate change. Bangladesh is expected to push for additional commitments to the Adaptation Fund. 

COP29 will review and revise the Loss and Damage Fund. This fund has helped Bangladesh address displacement and loss of arable land from sea level rise. The conference will also advocate for a strong financing mechanism to support the most vulnerable populations affected by climate change. Bangladesh will continue to work with the view that countries that contribute the least to global emissions will receive priority in compensation. Bangladesh’s inclusion in this issue is a significant step forward. 

Bangladesh’s Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change is working to include nature-based solutions such as mangrove afforestation and wetland restoration in its climate action plan. These initiatives, while reducing carbon emissions, protect biodiversity and help ecosystems become sustainable. These initiatives are crucial for Bangladesh’s coastal and rural areas. At COP29, Bangladesh will work with other countries to highlight the importance of biodiversity conservation and implement land use policies that are environmentally sustainable and climate-resilient. 

Bangladesh’s urban centers, including Dhaka, face severe climate threats due to heat waves, air pollution and waterlogging. Effective participation in COP29 on sustainable urban development and climate-resilient infrastructure could provide an opportunity for Bangladesh. 

Ahmed Shamim Al Razi, Former Additional Secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change

Headline_English: Why did so many students fail the English department of Chittagong University?
Content_Enlish:
An initiative to re-evaluate answer sheets in violation of the existing rules has created controversy at Chittagong University. The decision taken in the recent emergency meeting of the syndicate to re-evaluate the answer sheets of the English department's postgraduate examination is considered by some to be an admission of the administration's policy under pressure from some unsuccessful students. They also consider this decision to be a bad precedent for the future. 

117 people participated in the English department's postgraduate examination (2021-2022). Of them, 39 failed. The students say that some teachers in the department underestimated the answer sheets, which is why so many candidates failed. 

The university's vice-chancellor formed a four-member investigation committee to find out the validity of this claim of the students. After verifying the sample selected through simple random selection, the investigation committee confirmed that the results of the postgraduate 2021 year are 100% accurate. There is no justification for re-evaluating the results, and in addition, it is also commented in the investigation report that it is in conflict with the university's laws. 

But the syndicate did not take into account these opinions of the investigation committee. An emergency meeting approved the decision to cancel the results of the exam and re-evaluate. A new committee was also formed. 

The chairman of the examination committee for that academic year is angry with this decision. The teacher considers the formation of another committee to re-evaluate the answer sheets to be insulting to them, since the investigation committee did not question their honesty or competence. He expressed his reaction in a letter to the Vice-Chancellor and sought the cancellation of the newly formed committee. 

The big proof that the decision of the syndicate meeting did not have enough logical force is that the acting registrar of the university said in this regard, ‘This has been considered as a special case (incident). It cannot be shown as an example in the future.’ Isn’t a decision that is not accepted as an example for the future a weak decision? 

Now let’s talk about the unsuccessful students. It is naturally assumed that English is one of the preferred subjects for the front-runners in the merit list of the admission test for the faculty of arts. But we know that the amount of English a student takes in higher secondary is not enough for studying English literature. As a result, the results of these students in the first year of university are not as expected. Many of them continue to have this deficiency in subsequent years. 

One has to wonder, is there much difference between a student who failed with 38-39 and a student who passed with 40? Or how much difference is there between a student who got 59 marks and got B minus and a student who got 60 marks and got B, especially in literature and theoretical subjects? 
Since two years ago, 30 marks have been allocated for attendance and internal assessment in every 100-mark course, and the exam results have improved. But the batches that are in the old system are deprived of this opportunity. The question arises, how normal is it for a large number of postgraduate students to fail the exam after completing a five-year course in seven-eight years? Are the teachers not responsible here? 

There are relatively more complaints against teachers of the Faculty of Arts in universities for not taking classes regularly. As I said earlier, relatively talented students qualify for the English department. Therefore, teachers cannot completely avoid the responsibility of their disastrous results. I don't know how many teachers remember that the fate and future of students are related to their own skills, qualifications and sincere efforts. The allegations of extra income from classes in private universities are also old. 

The examination committee may not be responsible for the good or bad results of the exam, but can't some responsibilities be fulfilled even for humane reasons? For example, if students fail for one or two marks or are deprived of a good grade, can't the examination committee give special consideration in that case? If it can't be done according to the rules, then a way needs to be found out after discussion with the university authorities. 

We know that when we were students of this university, a student was given grace up to 3 marks to get first class. There may not be such a system in the grading system. But if the examination committee wants, it can come to a solution after discussion with the concerned examiners. If the matter was mathematics, this might not have been said. But in literature or similar theoretical subjects, examiners basically evaluate subjectively. As a result, the evaluation of one examiner differs from another. In other words, the student's literary sense is evaluated by not just judging the answer to this question as correct or incorrect. 

One has to think, is there much difference between a student who failed with 38-39 and a student who passed with 40? Or how much difference is there between a student who got 59 marks and got B minus and a student who got 60 marks and got B, especially in literature and theoretical subjects? 

Keeping these issues in mind, the university authorities can give the examination committee the right to give grace marks as before. The biggest question is why can't students challenge or appeal if they are dissatisfied with the results? The logic in this case is that if there is a difference in the marks of two examiners on the answer sheet, it goes to a third examiner. But in that case, the difference must be at least 15 marks. Where fate is decided for one or two marks, how effective is it to rely on a third examiner?

Headline_English: The lock that the government must break to conquer fear
Content_Enlish:
A group of capable and intelligent people got together and decided that they would build an ideal city. This group includes urban planners, architects, engineers, contractors, investors, bankers, landscapers, environmentalists. Everyone who is needed to build an ideal city is there. They are sitting in a large hall. The door of the house is locked from the outside, they cannot leave this house even if they want to. 

The architect gets frustrated while designing the city. What will happen after designing? We cannot leave this house, how will we build a city? However, he keeps his mind focused and focuses on the work of taking a break. 

The landscaper thinks of a flowing river, the river will circle the city. A beautiful road will run along both banks of the river. There will be rows of black-capped trees on both sides of the road. Birds will sit on the trees and sing. Inland, parallel to the road, more and more beautiful elevated walkways will run, city dwellers will walk along those well-decorated floating walkways in the gentle breeze in the morning and afternoon. Suddenly, he thinks, "Oh my God, what will happen to all these beautiful plans? We won't be able to leave this house, how will we build a city?" 

An investor is plunged into despair while creating a great project, "We won't be able to leave here, how will we build a city?" 

The same question is asked by engineers, bankers, and environmentalists. They work for a while, then stop, and every now and then they think, "What's the point of all this planning? Will we ever be able to leave here?" 

The situation of our interim government is much like this now. They have taken initiatives for all these wonderful reforms, but every now and then they wonder whether these are constitutional? The existing constitution is that huge lock on the prison hall. The government must first break this lock, otherwise they will not be able to do anything. They have entered this house by breaking a huge lock. Then someone came and put another lock from outside. Now they are afraid to break the lock again and get out. 

They must now overcome their fear and break the lock. Because, if they cannot get out, the Bangladesh of the people's dreams will not be built. They must be much braver now than before, ignoring all obstacles and dangers, they must break the lock called 'Constitution' and come out into the open wilderness. They must understand that about 180 million people of the country are looking at their faces, if they fail, this nation will no longer get the opportunity to build the Bangladesh of their dreams, a Bangladesh without discrimination, a Bangladesh of justice and fairness. 

The main task of this government is to write a constitution that reflects the hopes and aspirations of the people. Many are saying that reform is an ongoing process. Yes, it is true, Bangladesh needs to make many reforms, such as revamping the income tax system, reforming the education system, massive reforms in the medical system, reforms in countless sectors, and once the reforms are done, new reforms will be needed to make it compatible with the future, with the changing world. This process will continue, it has no end. But this government will have to decide how much reform it will leave. 

By forming six reform commissions in the beginning, they have clearly defined their boundaries. Although several more reform commissions have been formed later. So they should not back down from this place. If we can carry out reforms in these sectors properly, we will reach the dream that the young students and people of this country have shown us, a fascism-free Bangladesh, a discrimination-free Bangladesh. 

A major obstacle to fully dedicating ourselves to this work is the 1972 constitution. You will not be able to go far by maintaining it even after revoking some amendments. Therefore, we will have to completely repeal this constitution and move forward on an alternative path. If the current President has to be removed and a new President appointed, then do so. 

Do whatever you have to do to make your job easier and hassle-free. We all need to remember that it is not right to compromise the aspirations of the nation because of the Constitution; rather, the Constitution itself must be adjusted to keep in line with the aspirations of the nation. This is the right path.

Headline_English: How will a disoriented Europe deal with Trump?
Content_Enlish:
The return of Donald Trump to the White House has brought European leaders face to face with a new reality. They now face two major pitfalls or mistakes. One is to panic about Trump’s possible policies, and the other is to avoid the situation altogether without facing reality. They must avoid falling into both traps. 

The problem is that it will not be easy for European leaders to avoid falling into this trap; and if they fail to avoid this trap, Europe could face grave consequences. 

The reasons for the panic over Trump’s return are clear. 

It is difficult to predict in advance what Trump will do, and he is an incredibly stubborn man. 

However, there is no doubt that Trump’s political instincts and announced plans will shake the pillars of Europe’s security, economic, and political systems. 

There is ample reason for Europeans to be alarmed on security issues. 

First, Trump’s proposed “peace plan” for Ukraine could violate Ukraine’s territorial integrity and disarm the country and permanently exclude it from NATO. 

After Trump takes office, the United States will significantly reduce its participation in NATO and shift the responsibility for military command and spending to the Europeans. As a result, NATO itself may become “inactive.” 

Europeans are rightly concerned about the Middle East issue. Because Trump’s “peace-making” plan in the Middle East means supporting the expansionist plans of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist coalition. Trump’s plan may even include measures such as expelling Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank and resettling them in Egypt and Jordan. 

Europe’s second biggest challenge will be trade. If Trump imposes tariffs on all imports as he has promised, a trade war between the EU and its largest export market is inevitable. In that case, the EU will have to prepare to retaliate against the US and try to expand trade with the rest of the world. 
The economic situation is likely to worsen after Trump takes office. 

Trump has said he will impose a general import tariff of 10 to 20 percent on goods imported into the US from other countries. He has also said that a 60 percent tariff will be imposed on Chinese goods. 

Trump's policy could trigger a global trade war. If such a trade war breaks out, other governments will take countermeasures against the US to protect themselves from economic damage. 

If Trump's tough tariff policy pushes China out of the US market, Europeans will be more vulnerable than before. Because the impact of China's excess production capacity (overcapacity) will be greater on Europeans. 

The situation in Europe could be even more complicated. Because, with Trump as president, Europe will not be able to take united countermeasures. Behind their inability to unite, a so-called international coalition called the ‘illiberal international’ will be at work. That coalition includes Trump’s close allies, Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. These leaders show an anti-liberal mentality in their policies, which could weaken Europe’s overall political and strategic response. 

For these reasons, European leaders are on the verge of panic and are tempted to rush to Washington to make bilateral agreements—as many did during Trump’s first term. But if they work separately with the United States, it will directly damage European unity. 

The second mistake is equally dangerous. 

If European leaders do not face or deny the kind of threat that Trump can pose, then in the end it will be seen that they have not been able to organize themselves enough to deal with the situation on their own. 

For four years, European leaders have known that Trump could return, and they have taken steps to address the possibility. They have also taken steps to address their new geopolitical vulnerabilities. They have increased defense spending (Europeans collectively now spend more than 2 percent of their GDP on defense) and reduced their reliance on Russian gas. But overall, they have been moving too slowly. 

Meanwhile, some European leaders are basking in a false sense of confidence. They think that since they survived Trump’s first term, they can survive another. 

But they need to remember that there are many differences between the Trump of 2017-20 and the Trump of today. The Trump of the first term was a man outside politics, who surprised himself by winning the election and was eager to gain institutional recognition. 

This time, Trump is experienced. He is determined to take revenge on the institutions that hindered him in his previous term. European leaders should take this seriously and prepare themselves accordingly. 

The most urgent task for European leaders is to agree on their common interests and find ways to protect them in the 70 days between now and January 20, 2025. If it can be done together with the United States, that is fine; if not, they will have to do it on their own. 

This means preparing a coherent plan to protect Europe from security and economic pressures. 

The most immediate concern for Europe is Ukraine. It must first ensure that any agreement to disarm Ukraine and keep it out of NATO is not reached. It must also ensure that Ukraine can be supplied with uninterrupted ammunition and air defense systems in the short term. It must also guarantee Ukraine reliable security in the long term. It must also find ways to spend more efficiently on defense. NATO and the European Union must increase the number of combat-ready forces; and, if necessary, strengthen their own nuclear deterrent. 

The second biggest challenge for Europe will be trade. If Trump follows through on his promise to impose tariffs on all imports, a trade war between the EU and its biggest export market is inevitable. The EU will need to prepare to retaliate against the US and seek to expand trade with the rest of the world. 

Trump’s victory is completely changing the landscape of the UK’s relationship with the EU. Now the EU should come up with a big and bold offer to the UK, so that they can work together to build a new kind of partnership. 

UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer should commit to working for a stronger and more united Europe. 

To make this happen, EU member states – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Spain – will need to rise above their own domestic politics and forge a pan-European consensus. 

Europe’s response to Trump’s return will require creativity, resilience and a strong commitment to defending its own interests. 

They should remember that every crisis brings an opportunity. The Trump crisis has also presented Europeans with an opportunity to build a stronger and more self-reliant bloc.

Headline_English: Are the constitution and laws only a matter for lawyers?
Content_Enlish:
The Indian subcontinent became ‘independent’ in 1947 thanks to the hands of the British Labour Prime Minister Clement Attlee. He once said of the French World War II general and later head of state Charles de Gaulle, ‘He may have been a very good general, but a very poor politician.’ 

The response that Charles de Gaulle made to this brick has now become a proverb in political literature. De Gaulle said, ‘Politics is such a serious matter that it is not safe to leave it in the hands of politicians alone.’ 

The same applies to the laws, the court system, the constitution of the state, and justice of a country. These are also so important that they are not safe to leave it in the hands of lawyers alone. It is very important for citizens, professionals, and a section of the population of the country as a whole to be closely involved in and pay attention to them. Yet, the opposite is happening in our country. 

In our country, there seems to be a conscious or subconscious attitude among our civil society or intellectuals to avoid the legal system, considering it incomprehensible or inaccessible or 'absolutely untenable'. But these issues touch us every day in our daily lives. 

I would like to take refuge in the postmodern theorist Jürgen Habermas. He says that law, on the one hand, functions as the primary means of social cohesion in the modern era. On the other hand, its role is as power; the power with which the obedience and obedience of the governed is obtained. Because, in modern society, power alone cannot guarantee its legitimacy. Law legitimizes power only by obtaining the consent of the governed. 

I don't know if you have heard such bad things about law! I haven't. Yet these are very true. The 'lingua franca' or state language of power is law. The state, government, and power all speak this language. Now, if we don't understand this language or at least don't make a conscious effort to understand it, how will the people understand the state's 'clockwork orchestra'? 

It's not like we can get by avoiding the state or power. At this stage in human history, we have no way of ignoring it. We have to establish ourselves within it. At the very least, we can form a better state. Again, suppose that power, politics, the state, the government—in all of these, citizens have a fair share. How can you or I understand that right from the state? 

Through laws, regulations, the judiciary and other 'state apparatuses', the state or various authorities and corporations keep an eye on you and me all the time like big brothers. On the one hand, they keep our eyes and brains busy by producing and distributing various ideologies. On the other hand, they keep various electronic gadgets and apps on the internet all the time like big brothers. 

As a poison on the palate, today's artificial intelligence, through big data analysis, follows us, tries to understand our minds and behavior. If we can get a fair amount of knowledge and throw us into their trap once, the fortress will be breached. But now, I or you, unknowingly, come forward and become subscribers, fans, followers of their ideas, thoughts, doctrines, and methods of work. 

From within this endless legal and secret surveillance, we must keep the state and power on counter-surveillance by continuously studying, reviewing, and constructing new discourses on our legal and judicial systems. If we cannot understand the language of power, read the mind of the state, and engage in dialogue with the state, the state gets a 'walkover'. It understands that you are not capable of dealing with it. And once the power understands that you are 'milk rice'; If you can keep yourself busy with gossip, gossip or gossip, then you will not be able to reach him. 

Among the various reasons for the tendency of the law courts to bypass us, two reasons seem particularly significant to me. The reason why the common people want to bypass them is the dominance of English. The vast majority of laws and regulations are still written in English. The language of the High Court is also English. 

And the second reason seems to be that the English that is used in the law courts is not as fluent as that of word of mouth, newspapers, literature or stories and novels. This language is complex, convoluted, full of terminology and jargon. I think that some words, concepts, theories, legal language, procedures, terminology, etc. stand as obstacles in the understanding of the constitution, legal framework or judicial system of the country by people outside the world of law. It is important to explain these in a simple way. 

Independence of the judiciary, separation of powers—these are not just matters for lawyers and judges. Every citizen of the entire country has a fair share of daily life associated with these issues. Therefore, it is more than a responsibility to read and understand what these are. 

The citizens of this country acquired the constructive power to form a new state through the Liberation War of 1971. As a result, the constitution that was formulated in 1972 was drafted almost unilaterally. There was very little public involvement. There was no proper review and pressure from the intellectual community in the constitution-making process. Therefore, the unwavering principle of popular sovereignty did not reach the people. 

The leaders of that time established a system to eat the anti-people ants that had gained independence. When the constructive power came into the hands of the people of this country again in 1990, we may not have fully understood its importance. Its ultimate consequence is a fascist regime that is like a yoke on the neck of the nation. 

Law and courts, state structure, justice, these have to be guarded all the time. Otherwise, these rights will be lost to the citizens. Judges and lawyers who read the laws and regulations get their salaries and fees. And if the citizens are not aware, they will get into danger. In order to avoid danger, the judiciary, law and constitution will need to be studied and understood. Only then can constitutional fascism be prevented, and a democratic state structure will be created.

Headline_English: Why is BCS a condition for increasing the age of entry into employment?
Content_Enlish:
After a long-standing agitation by job seekers, the current interim government has decided to increase the age limit for entry into the job by two years to 32 years. Along with this, a condition has been added that a candidate cannot take the BCS exam more than three times. 

Since the protesters' desired demand of 35 years was not met, they rejected the government's decision. They expressed anger and frustration. Many job seekers posted on Facebook expressing their disappointment and anger. In particular, there is a heated discussion for and against why such a condition has been given that one cannot take the BCS exam more than three times. 

Shariful Hasan, convener of the 'Job Application Age Limit 35 Expecting General Students Coordination Council', said that the government's decision is contradictory to the demands they have been agitating for. The demands of the students have not been reflected in the government's decision. The agitating organization has said that the maximum age limit for entry into the job should be permanently increased to 35 years, excluding the condition. 

2. 
A young man named Rashedul Hasan became the first in the education cadre after taking the BCS exam six times. He started taking the BCS exam at the age of 35. He became a non-cadre in the 35th, 36th, 38th and 40th BCS; and Rashedul became the first in the education cadre (English) by participating in the last 41st BCS of his life (Source: Prothom Alo Online, August 6, 2023). 

Citing Rashedul's example, some are saying, then why would the authorities stop a job candidate after taking the BCS exam three times? The opportunity to give BCS should be kept open like other jobs as long as the age is there. 

Many questions arise from such a decision by the government. Many of those who have been agitating for raising the age limit for entry into the job to 35 years have already crossed the age of 32. What did they gain in this situation? 

Again, if the employment age is increased to 35 years, then if the children chase the expected job until the age of 35, when will they start a family? When will you work for your family, family, society and country? These issues are also being discussed. 

Read more 
Can the talented people be kept in the country by giving BCS three times 
30 October 2024 
Can the talented people be kept in the country by giving BCS three times 
3. 
A few days ago, the review committee recommended to the government to increase the age limit for entry into service. In that recommendation, the age limit for women was set at 37 years and for men at 35 years. There has been criticism for making the recommendation while maintaining the discrimination for which so much struggle has been fought. The demand was for the age limit to be the same for everyone. In the end, although the same age limit was set for both men and women, the agitators did not back down from their demand of 35. 

However, the demand for increasing the age limit for government jobs is not new. Job seekers have been making this demand for more than a decade. Many of those who first took to the streets in support of the demand are now over 40 years old. So even if the age limit for employment is now 35 years old, they will not get any benefits. Therefore, some people want the age limit for entry into the job to be lifted. 

4. 
In the new Bangladesh, it will not be enough to simply increase the employment age by two years. Realizing the pain of unemployed youth, government job application fees must be reduced. Earlier, during the Awami League government, job seekers demanded a reduction in the application fee many times but did not get any results. Therefore, they have become frustrated and have become silent about that demand. Before they become vocal again, the interim government should take initiatives to reduce the job examination fee. 

Currently, the BCS application fee is 700 taka. The application fee for 9th grade or higher (non-cadre) posts is 600 taka, the application fee for 10th grade posts is 500 taka, 300 taka for 11th to 12th grades, 200 taka for 13th to 16th grades and 100 taka for 17th to 20th grades. Which is like a 'sore throat on the back' for unemployed youth. Such increased fees must be reduced. Initiatives must be taken to reduce the burden of unemployed youth. 

New employment opportunities must be prepared. The government needs to think deeply about reducing job test fees, providing employment and economic security to unemployed youth, even if through subsidies.

Headline_English: Primary school: Let biscuits return to the new Bangladesh
Content_Enlish:
There are eight to nine types of primary schools, from satellite primary schools to PTI primary schools. There is also a system so that children from the nomadic or Vedic communities can learn even in a nomadic state. That is, there is a system of primary education for any child aged 5 to 10 years old, in all situations, anywhere in Bangladesh. Yet this year, seven lakh fewer children have been enrolled compared to last year. Why? 

The training that primary school teachers receive is not received by teachers in other institutions. There is also a qualitative difference between primary school teachers and kindergarten or madrasa teachers. Yet why do primary school children leave primary and go to those institutions? Lipi Devgupta, organizer and teacher of the Vigyan Chetna Parishad, said, ‘Earlier, students were always in school except for the working season. Now, there are none throughout the year.’ 

Two. 

Once upon a time, these primary schools were built by the people of the area. Yet why are they decaying from the inside out today? So are the schools unable to meet the needs of society? The teachers who teach in the schools are unable to build that relationship with the local people? For this reason, is the poor man sending his child to kindergarten even after paying 500 taka? 

People went to the moon. Bangladesh became a middle-income country by showing more exports. And the children of that middle-income country, the future leaders, go hungry at noon. 
Three. 

Earlier, the headmaster had an important role in the stipend. The headmaster could drop the name of a student who was regular in January but not regular in February. Now, he can send the name every six months. In this regard, Nafida Noreen (35), assistant teacher and poet of Sarangpur Government Primary School in Kaunia, Rangpur, said, ‘The one who does not get the stipend, does not get it. Even after repeated corrections, he does not get it. This destroys the respect and importance of teachers among the parents.’ 

And the child who gets the stipend once, does not have to come to school for the whole year. And the student who does not get it once, feels humiliated. He does not come to school again. On the other hand, instead of receiving money from teachers, teachers no longer have any psychological importance because money comes in mobile phones. 

Four. 

A research report was released on the improvement in children's health after eating biscuits. The reports showed improvements in several areas, including children's height and eyesight. Those biscuits were locked up due to the Corona restrictions, and there is no way to open them. 

After that, the ministers and bureaucrats of the former government argued for a few days about whether they would give eggs and milk or eggs and khichdi at noon. The biscuits never returned. The stipend money goes to the mother in three to six months via mobile phone, but the students get the biscuits directly. Midday meals are important for children. 100% of teachers unanimously said that midday biscuits can bring children back to school. A midday meal is important for children. 

Poor pregnant women also used to ask for biscuits from the neighboring school. This also benefited the unborn child. Farzana Jenny (30), an assistant teacher at Chilmari No. 1 Government Primary School, said, "Keep the khichuri, give biscuits for now. Otherwise, there will be no children in schools next year." 

Man has gone to the moon. Bangladesh has become a middle-income country by showing more exports. And the children of that middle-income country, the future leaders of the country, do not eat at noon. They come to school hoping for a packet of biscuits. That too has been discontinued now. At least the biscuits are available in the new Bangladesh.

Headline_English: Search for Hasina's resignation letter: A sign of trauma or an attempt at Awami rehabilitation
Content_Enlish:
Then why should Afghanistan's former Taliban president Ashraf Ghani, who fled Kabul in 2021, still be the legitimate ruler of that country? 

Even if dictator Ferdinand Marcos, who ignored the election results of the Philippines (1986), Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who failed to prevent the Iranian revolution (1979), and head of state Chiang Kai-shek, who failed to prevent the victory of the Communists led by Mao Zedong in mainland China (1949), were exiles, why shouldn't they be posthumously recognized as legitimate rulers in their countries? 

Many more fled the country without resigning due to public anger or revolution. Whether they regained their positions or not, Nanak Saheb, the alleged 'guru' of violence in the Awami League, probably does not know. 

Perhaps that is why 'he and they' have taken to social media to claim that Sheikh Hasina is the legitimate Prime Minister of Bangladesh. 

A few days ago, Hasina-appointed President Md. Shahabuddin, who was staying at Bangabhaban, said that he had not received a copy of the resignation letter of the fugitive Prime Minister, and the Awami League's boat seemed to be in the water. 

The 'hukkahua' began. On the other hand, there were demands for the President's resignation. 

The 'story' that the President told senior journalist Matiur Rahman Chowdhury not only belies the acceptance of Hasina's resignation in his address to the nation on August 6, but is also considered unacceptable in legal analysis. 

In his address to the nation, the President said, 'Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has submitted her resignation letter to the President and I have accepted it.' 

At that time, the chiefs of the three services were standing behind him. The entire nation witnessed that scene. 

Then he says that he does not have the resignation letter. The news of the resignation letter being submitted was published in the media and it was lost from Bangabhaban! What a terrible thing! 

Already, audio of several telephone conversations has come on social media. It is widely believed that Sheikh Hasina is heard speaking in those audios. 

Although the authorities or the Awami League have not officially confirmed that these telephone conversations are of Sheikh Hasina, almost no one has expressed doubt that it is Sheikh Hasina's voice. Even no one from the Awami League has expressed doubt. 

In one of the many 'leaked' audios, 'Sheikh Hasina' is heard saying that she could not go to Bangabhaban to resign from Ganabhaban before going to India. 

However, she did not clarify under what compromise formula she was allowed to leave Dhaka. Therefore, who cares whether she has signed the resignation letter now or not? 

Hasina's unannounced exit from the scene is a severe trauma for the beneficiaries of the power and supporters of the Awami League that has been in power for 15 and a half years. 

To overcome this trauma, they may want to believe that the 'Magic Lady' will surely enter the country saying 'Furung Farang Phaan' and something will happen. 

There is no doubt that that effort will be inspired from their side. However, the reality is that if Sheikh Hasina is confident that she has not committed any crime including murder, disappearance, corruption, vote theft, money laundering, and activities against the country's interests, then she can return to the country without a whisper and take on any challenge. 

If she does so, of course, the International Crimes Tribunal can take her into custody for questioning without the extradition process with India. 

The grief, fear, and pain of losing heaven at the defeat of the Awami League can be imagined. But it is a little difficult for the people on the side of the revolution to show sympathy for the opponent 'stronger than the coronavirus'. 

Because, Hasina's administration and party, which resorted to murder and force, did not leave the path open for peaceful transfer of power and coexistence. 

If Sheikh Hasina had been the legitimate Prime Minister after the farcical elections of 2014 and before the July 2024 movement, why did she and her party vanish in a single day on August 5? 

The workers and supporters of the popular party were supposed to hold a big procession. Why did the Prime Minister of the country where Hasina found refuge in the back-and-forth arrangement also congratulate the newly sworn-in Chief Advisor of Bangladesh, Muhammad Yunus? 

Because, Hasina's supporters have also seen the crowd of crores of people in Dhaka, processions of millions of people in big cities, triumphant celebrations in the towns and villages across the country. 

All those processions and rallies are the moments of final rejection of Hasina's illegal rule and the legitimacy of building a new Bangladesh and a people's state. 

This is the moment of drawing the beard ('period' or 'full stop') of fascist history. 

Looking back, if Hasina's Awami League had faith in the mandate of the people, it would have had the courage to confront the then opposition parties, including the BNP, in a fair election. 

If they had respect for democratic values, they would have accepted defeat even if they were defeated in the election. 

Let me remind those who are mistaken, after the abolition of the caretaker government system during the election in 2011, the results of 154 out of 300 seats in the 2014 election were determined without a vote, and not even 5 percent of the votes were cast in the remaining elections. 

In 2018, because the ballot boxes were loaded the night before, 'it is called a night election'. 

In 2024, in another one-sided election, 95 percent of voters boycotted the polling stations, proving once again what the elections of the Hasina era were like. 

Hasina, who once aspired to be the 'daughter of democracy', ensured a constitutional system that deprived the people of Bangladesh of their right to vote. 

Therefore, even before the student-mass revolution of July-August, the ‘popular legitimacy’ of Sheikh Hasina’s government was below zero or in the negative. 

Today, they are the ones who are questioning the constitutional legitimacy of the Yunus government and the student-mass uprising, which has destroyed a unique revolution of the century led by the young generation with the participation of the masses and political activists. 

Despite being defeated in this revolution stained with the blood of thousands of people, Hasina’s Awami League is threatening from unknown places on social media without showing any remorse. They are threatening to turn everything upside down. 

The beneficiaries of fascism certainly have the amount of money, network, manpower and energy to sabotage the ongoing reforms and future democratic processes. 

Through these counter-revolutionary activities, the Awami League is reminding us that the party’s ideology is indeed fascism. 

In 1975, Hasina's father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League had also established its own 'great death' one-party system. 

Perhaps because of the very history-conscious party's own fascist legacy, its student organization Chhatra League was immersed in crimes like terrorism, extortion and murder. 

Although the organization was banned, there is no strong argument against this decision. 

Now the devastated Awami League is not in a position to receive public, logical, legal and political sympathy. 

There are some isolated initiatives to revive that party, more specifically, to rehabilitate Sheikh Hasina politically. 

Yet, the Awami League may also face trials like Hitler's Nazi Party in Germany. 

Whatever the Awami ideology, post-August 5 Bangladesh is not only a matter of Dr. Yunus Saheb's advisory council. The future prospects and opportunities for good work that have been created for the nation in political change cannot be missed; rather, it will be the national responsibility of the good forces to bring those who want to obstruct it to justice. 
However, rumors have proven to be true most of the time in the political history of Bangladesh. 

For example, rumors of the military-controlled 1-11 government and the seizure of power by General Ershad in 1982 were already in the market. 

However, after enduring a decade and a half of fascist rule under the leadership of the Awami League with the support of his Jatiya Party, the nation paid the price for the political rehabilitation of the dictator Ershad even after the successful democratic movement of the 1990s. 

The Awami League has not yet admitted the mistake of following fascist policies, let alone apologizing to the nation. 

This time too, it is setting the pattern by undertaking a project to condemn the Yunus government. Fascist supporters are spending their days wishing ill for the country and the democracy-loving people.

In this regard, all the forces in favor of the revolution need to understand that the path to building a new Bangladesh state will not be smooth. If the revolution is given to someone, the counter-revolutionaries can target the ‘farmers’ to thwart the purpose of the revolution. 

Whatever the Awami League’s thinking, post-August 5 Bangladesh is not just a matter for Dr. Yunus’ advisory council. 

The future prospects and opportunities for good work that have been created for the nation through political change cannot be missed; rather, it will be the national responsibility of the good forces to bring to justice those who want to obstruct it.

Headline_English: How the independence of the judiciary ended in Pakistan
Content_Enlish:
The 26th Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan was passed. The independence of the judiciary was ended. It was a dark night in the parliamentary history of Pakistan. See through the eyes of two opposition lawmakers from Balochistan. One in a wheelchair and the other a woman member wearing a dark shawl. What a story their covered faces tell. 

These two were known to be missing for some time. Security guards did not allow any journalist to talk to them. Their votes helped the ruling coalition get the required number in the upper house. 

After the Senate vote, the National Assembly met at midnight. Half a dozen opposition MLAs appeared on the Treasury Bench. Interestingly, they had been missing for several days. With the votes of these defected leaders who appeared from the shadows, the required number was met in the lower house as well. This is how the threat of using a ‘brute majority’ by the Chairman of the People’s Party of Pakistan (PPP), Bilawal Bhutto, was realized. 

What happened on the night of October 20 and 21 has shattered a foundation of the Constitution. The leaders of the ruling parties are succeeding in one initiative after another to control the judiciary. And they are declaring this victory as a victory for democracy and parliament. They do not understand that they are just a pawn in a bigger game for the throne. Are they celebrating this victory knowingly at the cost of such a huge loss to the country? 

The independence of the judiciary is one of the foundations of the Constitution. As a result, questions are raised about the commitment of Bilawal’s party to democracy and the rule of law. What the so-called elected civilian government did to destroy the independence of the Supreme Court, not even the military government could do. A judiciary created to their liking will only strengthen the hands of extra-constitutional powers. 

In 2012, the then Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani was dismissed by Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry. The Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and its leader Nawaz Sharif supported the dismissal. Similarly, PPP leaders including Bilawal welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision to convict the then Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in 2017. None of this would have been possible without the support of the security forces. These two political parties are now members of an alliance. They have voluntarily become pawns in the game of the real power holders against their political rivals. 

The real power holders are now playing a new game. And these two parties are supporting them simultaneously. This new game began after six judges of the Islamabad High Court spoke about the interference of intelligence agencies in judicial matters and harassment of judges. 

Some clauses related to granting extensive powers to separate constitutional courts and security forces have been dropped. However, the draft did not change much regarding the move to subordinate the judiciary to the executive. The role of the executive in the constitution of the constitutional bench has further complicated the matter. The amendment has taken away the suo moto power of the Supreme Court. It has fixed the term of the Chief Justice for three years. And it has given the Prime Minister the power to appoint the next Chief Justice from among the three most senior judges of the Supreme Court. 

The government managed to pass this controversial amendment with the help of the security establishment and using coercive tactics. The way the opposition members were forced to switch sides was outrageous. These legislators were kept in detention for a whole week. 

There was no debate on such a controversial, such a far-reaching constitutional amendment. Most of the MLAs were not even shown the draft. They were not supposed to disobey the orders of their own party leaders. Our parliamentary history is not one to be proud of. But what happened last week is unprecedented. 

But the game is not over yet. Most of the time, the association has rejected the constitutional amendment. It remains to be seen how the new Chief Justice and other judges will react to this curtailment of the independence of the judiciary. It will not be easy for the government and those in power to bring the judiciary under control.

Headline_English: Why do European leaders want war?
Content_Enlish:
Anxiety and anger about the future of the European Union (EU) have been growing for some time. The lives of ordinary people are becoming miserable. And their leaders are trying to deal with the crisis with war. Its crises are not one, but many. And they are deepening rather than diminishing. The crisis of living, the housing crisis, the migration crisis. Economic growth has slowed down. 

And above all, there is the political crisis. The far-right is rising in countries. They are getting a mandate from the people in the elections. The sense of unity and liberal values ​​of the union are now under threat. 

Just a few days ago, the far-right Freedom Party won the Austrian election with 30 percent of the vote. Although they may be excluded from the process of forming a government in Austria. However, the rise of the right has also occurred in other European countries. Right-wing parties are in power or will soon come to power in nine of the 27 countries of the European Union. Internationally, the most significant challenge for the European Union is probably the ongoing war in neighboring Ukraine. The flow of weapons from Europe and the United States continues.

The war economy mantra is being preached with great force. Europeans are being pressured to believe that the European economy can be boosted by the military. In September, the liberal economist Mario Draghi, former president of the European Central Bank and former Italian prime minister, published a long-awaited report on the future of European efficiency. 
This war shows no sign of stopping anytime soon. Meanwhile, the shadow of climate change is growing longer and longer. One terrible natural disaster after another is occurring. What is the response of the European Union’s political leadership to this mounting crisis? 

It is no wonder that their response to the crisis has not come close to addressing the root causes of the problem. The destructive neoliberal policies they have so happily embraced have created countless boils. They are now seeking to escape this crisis by resorting to warmongering. Perhaps hoping that the excitement of war will make people forget their frustrations and anger. 

Over the past two years, it has been repeatedly said that Russia is the biggest threat to Europe’s security. And the solution is to defeat Russia in Ukraine. European weapons have been flowing into Ukraine. The European Union countries are gradually expanding their arsenals of more deadly, more destructive weapons. Now, it is being said that Ukraine will be allowed to use long-range missiles to hit targets on Russian territory. This is being emphasized by European leaders, including the outgoing EU foreign policy chief, Josep Borrell. 

On September 19, the European Parliament passed a resolution to allow countries that supply missiles to Ukraine to use them against Russian targets. Russia has repeatedly warned against such a move. Russia has even recently changed its policy on the use of its nuclear weapons. 

Not only are they continuing to increase the supply of weapons to Ukraine, they are also telling their people that countries need to be prepared to spend more on weapons. Because if the situation gets out of control while supplying weapons, the European Union is likely to be involved in a war with Russia. Andreas Kubilius is the candidate for the position of EU defense commissioner. The new post was created to counter the “Russian threat.” Andreas believes that the EU should become a “war-weapons warehouse” to counter Moscow. 

The war economy mantra is being preached with great force. Europeans are being pressured to believe that the military sector can boost the European economy. In September, Mario Draghi, a liberal economist and former president of the European Central Bank and former Italian prime minister, published a long-awaited report on the future of European efficiency. 

The report calls for deeper economic integration of the Union. Many have praised it. European leaders seem to be very fond of the Latin proverb, “If you want peace, prepare for war.” But there is a problem with applying this proverb in today’s world. And that is nuclear weapons. Once you get your hands on those weapons, human civilization could be wiped out. 

All this talk about war, preparations for war and the production of weapons for war is very effective in deflecting many of the European Union's crises and problems from their roots. The EU, which talks about human rights, freedom, democracy and justice, is essentially a neo-liberal institution. It is more concerned with the right of the rich to get richer. The health and development of ordinary citizens is not a concern of the EU. This is why the welfare state is retreating across Europe.

Headline_English: What I lost as a Palestinian in the United States
Content_Enlish:
This year has been a year of heartbreak. A year of fear. A year of hell. When I say, ‘This is the worst year of my life,’ I realize that I am not alone. 

This year, I have lost friends. I have lost my livelihood. The most precious thing I have lost is my faith in humanity. But before I say anything else, let me recite the mantra that I am required to recite to prove myself a good Palestinian in exile (Philadelphia, USA): ‘I condemn Hamas, I condemn Hamas, I condemn Hamas.’ 

You will notice that unless someone asks us to condemn violence; especially Hamas, we, the Palestinians, are usually not allowed to open our mouths. When the same person rejoices at the news of the murder of our brother and celebrates it incredulously, we are told to keep our mouths shut. Then we are told to remain completely silent. 

If an Israeli kills, it is an act of self-defense. And if an Arab kills, it is an act of terrorism. That is the rule here. That is what we have to accept. The United States has never been very secretive about its hatred of Arabs. But since October 7, this hatred has reached such a terrible level that I no longer feel safe in this country. 

I would have left if I had not built a life and a family in this country. Why would I want to live in a country where the Palestinians are treated so inhumanly that Senator Lindsey Graham can say that we should drop nuclear bombs on Gaza (where half the population is children) and not face meaningful criticism for making such a terrible comment? Why would I want to live in a country where my Senator John Fetterman openly mocks pro-Palestinian protesters and rejoices in our misery? 

And then there is more. The taxes I pay from my earnings are being spent on killing and starving my own brothers and sisters. Am I not indirectly participating in this infernal massacre? 

I am gradually losing my sense of reason for living in a country where a large part of our taxes are being spent on funding wars and on those who are being spent on our blood-drenched dollars, as Kamala Harris, with a beaming smile, describes as “the deadliest fighting force in the world.” 

I have been a victim of this hatred since long before October 7. Many times people here have told me that I cannot be Palestinian, because Palestinians do not exist. The amount of inhumane treatment we are subjected to here makes my body go numb. The bloodthirstiness of some people astounds me. 

I took a break from writing a column for the Guardian during the Hamas attacks. At the time, I was working on a corporate copywriting project with a large advertising agency. The agency’s internal office was filled with cheers from supporters of the Gaza bombing after Israel began its offensive. 

I was in no position to say anything to the agency officials about this. I admit, I was terrified. It’s hard to make a living as a freelance writer, and I usually rely on a few corporate jobs each year. I kept quiet for fear of missing out on future opportunities and waited for the bombing to stop. 

But no. The bombing didn’t stop. The number of Palestinians killed passed 10,000; then 20,000; then 30,000; then 40,000. Still, no number of Palestinian deaths emerged that satisfied Israel. There is still no one in American politics who will say, ‘Enough is enough, stop it.’ 

I once thought, like a fool, that the rise of Kamala Harris would bring about a positive change. But then I saw that she is also a cow in the same herd. She has already made it clear that she will not move away from President Joe Biden’s policy of unconditionally supplying arms to Israel. She has openly refused to recognize international law. 

When Kamala was crowned the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate last August, the party leaders did not invite a single Palestinian-American to the main stage for a single minute. 

The death toll in Gaza is rising. Now the humanitarian situation in Lebanon has become terrible. Seeing these hellish killings, politicians from both the Republican and Democratic camps in the United States are saying that we are responsible for our current plight. 

Let’s remember where this situation began: October 7. Kamala Harris mentioned this line in her debate with Donald Trump. It has been repeated in debates with vice presidential candidate Tim Walz and her opponent J.D. Vance. 

But the line creates a false narrative. Because history did not begin on October 7, 2023. While this date may mark a catastrophe for Israel, the truth is that every day for 76 years has brought some kind of catastrophe to the Palestinians. 

History did not begin on October 7. But when the world pauses to remember the day, it becomes clear whose lives are valuable to the world, and whose lives are worthless.

Headline_English: What is really happening with Hilsa?
Content_Enlish:
Farmed fish, such as Rui, Katla, etc., are sold for 200 to 400 taka per kg depending on the situation, after all the expenses, from buying them to maintaining them, feeding them, etc. 

However, the price of hilsa fish, which has no other cost except for catching them by fishermen and reaching the consumer, is 1,500 to 1,800 taka per kg! Hilsa does not eat grass, straw, rice husks or feed, and it is not necessary to hire daily laborers to raise hilsa! Why is the price so high? 

Research has also been done on whether hilsa can be cultivated in ponds or canned. Even then, the fish is getting out of the reach of the common man day by day. 

There is no logical reason for the skyrocketing price of this hilsa obtained from natural sources. However, the biggest reason for the price increase is the weakness of the supervisory organization in the hilsa market, which is a powerful syndicate. Apart from this, the movement of hilsa is being hampered by the impact of unplanned sand extraction, pollution, underwater platforms, dams and bridges in the river. This is threatening the reproduction of the fish, and production is declining. There is an impact on the price of daily commodities including fuel oil; in addition, the price of hilsa is increasing day by day as the supply is less than the demand. 

The Department of Fisheries, however, mentions in its statistics that hilsa production is increasing every year. In 2002-03, where hilsa was caught less than two lakh tons per year, hilsa production was 5 lakh 71 thousand tons in the 2022-23 fiscal year. In the 2008-09 fiscal year, hilsa harvest was 2 lakh 98 thousand tons. In one era, hilsa harvest has almost doubled. 
The question is, has the population doubled during this time? No. If we compare population and hilsa production, is the per capita supply of hilsa supposed to increase? It seems that with increasing urbanization, increasing income and wealth inequality, and the spread of ill-gotten money in the hands of some people, hilsa has become more elusive for the middle class than the lower class. 

Currently, some are inciting the price increase by using the excuse of hilsa export to India. An analysis of data from the last five years shows that the amount of hilsa exported from Bangladesh is only 0.29 percent of the total production. The Finance and Trade Advisor has rightly said, 'The amount of hilsa that is being exported is not even the equivalent of one day at Chandpur Ghat.' The question is, has this caused much loss in the availability of hilsa to domestic consumers or in the market price? 

Before thinking about solving this problem, some questions need to be answered. In particular, how much money from hilsa sold at high prices goes into the pockets of fishermen? Who is benefiting from the sale of this national fish? Apart from that, why is there a shortage of hilsa in the river? Why does Hilsa not reach the purchasing range of the common people even at some point of the year? 

The role of moneylenders, traders, traders and retailers is involved in the answers to these questions. After fishermen catch fish from the river or sea and bring it to the wharf, the control of the fish is no longer in their hands. It goes directly to the moneylender's box. The workers employed by the moneylender initially set a price and collect the 'dak'. The traders crowd around the fish box. After one after another, any trader buys the fish. 

Even if it is LC abroad, the traders buy the fish from here. The fish here is also sold in the local market. Then it is sent to wholesale traders or to the dak in different districts including the capital; especially to the fish traders in Karwan Bazar and Jatrabari in the capital. Here the dak is collected again. After the dak, the fish is sold to the buyers from the retailers in different markets. The four to five hands from the moneylender to the buyer, each of them, make a profit of 10 to 15 percent. This is how the price of hilsa is determined from the wharf to the retail buyer. 

At the beginning of the season, trawler owners spend three to four lakh taka to cover the net, trawler repairs and other expenses. Trawler owners often take a bribe from the shopkeeper. In return for this bribe, they have to give fish without paying. Trawler owners who take bribes can never get out of the net again. In a seagoing trawler, 16 fishermen spend 2.5 to 3 lakh taka, sometimes more, including fuel, ice, and market provisions, for 10 days. 

The trawler owner takes half of the profit from the catch. After that, what is left is divided into 20 parts. Out of these 20 parts, 16 fishermen take 16 parts, 2 parts for the boatman, and 1 part for the cook and engine driver. Again, if the fishermen do not get enough hilsa, the trawler owner has to count a huge loss. As a result, even if a trawler owner gets a lot of hilsa, he wants to make up for the previous losses. Meanwhile, fish is not available in the sea as before. And there is hostile weather. 

A lawyer of the Supreme Court has given a legal notice seeking to set the retail selling price of hilsa per kg at a maximum of 700 taka in the country. The National Consumer Rights Protection Department has conducted a special campaign against hilsa warehouses in various markets including Karwan Bazar and Jatrabari in the capital. Is it possible to reduce the price of hilsa through campaigns and laws? 

Although a kilogram of hilsa is sold for 1,800 to 2,000 taka in the domestic market, it is being exported to India for 1,200 taka. There is criticism across the country about how this is possible. However, a business source said that in reality, hilsa is not being exported to India at that price. They are sending this fish to India at a higher price, showing $10 or 1,200 taka in the books and pens. And transactions in excess of the government price are being carried out in hundis. 

Therefore, the first thing to do is to prevent smuggling to reduce the price. Break up the syndicate. Stop extortion. Apart from that, all the expenses of fishermen, such as the price of diesel, the price of nets, the price of yarn and rope, must be reduced. The entire country's Hilsa market is controlled through mobile phones from each Hilsa ghat. If the administration can truly control the ghats and ensure all kinds of facilities to the fishermen, then the price of Hilsa will come within reach. Research is underway on Hilsa. But what can be done to bring the price of Hilsa within the purchasing range of the common people, that research is more needed. Of course, market monitoring must be strengthened.

Headline_English: 'Seven Sisters' in the US election
Content_Enlish:
The phrase ‘Seven Sisters’ is found in Greek mythology, used to refer to the seven daughters of the Titan Atlas and the Oceanid Pleione. 

Readers are familiar with the phrase ‘Seven Sisters’ mainly centered around the states of the northeastern region of India. 

Considering the diverse culture and demographics of these states, the first Prime Minister of India, Jawaharlal Nehru, was the first to use the phrase ‘Seven Sisters’. 

In the case of the United States, the Seven Sisters refer to seven colleges. Barnard College, Smith College, Bryan Moore College, Radcliffe College, Vassar College, Wesley College and Mount Holyoke College are collectively called the ‘Seven Sisters’. 

These colleges play an important role in opening the path to higher education for women by overcoming economic constraints. In today’s article, the ‘Seven Sisters’ will be discussed about the seven ‘swing states’ of the US elections. 
The United States electoral system has been constantly adapted. Political parties have led this adaptation in response to citizen expectations and cultural changes. 

Initially, members of the Electoral College cast two votes each. The first two times George Washington received the most votes, he became president, and the second time John Adams received the most votes, he became vice president. 

From there, the number of states in the United States is now 50. And the Electoral College votes are 538. The Electoral College votes are assigned to each state. 

The highest number of Electoral College votes is 55 in California. The lowest number of votes is 3 in states such as Alaska, Washington, D.C., Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wyoming. 

The 50 states in the United States can be divided into three groups. Some states traditionally win presidential elections with Republican Party candidates. 

They are known as "red states." States like Texas, Florida, Ohio, Georgia, Indiana, Alabama are known as red states. These states are generally white-dominated. 

On the contrary, there are some states that traditionally lean towards the Democratic Party. These are known as ‘blue states’. 

Democratic Party strongholds like California, New York, Virginia, New Jersey, New Mexico, Massachusetts are ‘blue states’. The proportional rate of immigrants is comparatively higher in these places. 

Apart from these, there are some states where the number of supporters of the Republican and Democratic parties is almost equal. There is a fierce competition between the two parties in these states. 

These states are decisive in the election. The results of these states determine who will be the next four-year resident of the White House. 

These states are known as swing states. There are seven swing states in this election, the results of which will determine the fate of the two presidential candidates. 

In the last 12 elections, Georgia's winners have won the White House in 8 of the last 12 elections. Republicans have won all six elections in Georgia since Bill Clinton in 1992. 

Three decades later, in 2020, Joe Biden became the first Democratic candidate to win the state. He defeated Donald Trump by a margin of only 11,779 votes. This margin is 0.23 percent of the total vote. 

Joe Biden had to withdraw badly in the first presidential debate of 2024. That debate also took place in Atlanta, Georgia. 

Georgia is becoming more diverse. Support for the Democratic Party is also growing among women and young people. Similarly, the tendency of African-Americans to come out to vote is also increasing. 

The demographics here show hope for the Democratic Party candidate. One-third of Georgia's population is African-American. There are also about 5 percent Asians. 

As a result, although the Republican Party has won six of the last seven elections, this election is a swing state. Any candidate can win. 

Currently, Trump is ahead by 1 point in Georgia in the Emerson/Polara poll. He is ahead by 4 percentage points in the Marist poll and the New York Times/Sarina College poll. 

Kamala Harris is ahead by 1 point in the CNN/SSRS poll. 

Michigan was part of the three swing states that formed the 'Blue Wall' in the 2020 election, along with Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. 

Although Hillary Clinton lost these states in the 2016 election, Joe Biden was able to win these states. 

In the last two elections, Michigan has sided with the winners of two different parties. Candidates from both parties are visiting Michigan again and again in their election campaigns. 

Although the Democratic Party has won six out of seven elections since 1992, Democratic candidate Kamala Harris is worried about Arab-American voters here. 

Sympathy for Gaza is growing among these young voters, angry about the ongoing Israeli attacks on Gaza. 

The way President Biden has presented himself as a ‘pro-Zionist’ and has supported Israel has not been liked by many voters here. 

Both parties are eager to take advantage of the current situation. The 15 electoral college votes are here. The two candidates are tied in the Emerson/Polara poll in Michigan. 

Harris is ahead by 5 percentage points in the Marist poll, and by the same margin in the Quinnipiac poll. 

The main issue dividing the party in the US elections is immigration. Arizona is on the US-Mexico border, where Trump is always vocal about illegal immigration.

This state, with 11 electoral votes, is traditionally a Republican stronghold, but changing demographics have opened up opportunities for the Democratic Party. 

The state is 5.5 percent African-American, the same number are Native Americans, and 32.5 percent are Hispanic. 

In Arizona, the two candidates are also tied in the Emerson/Polara poll. The Marist poll has Trump ahead by 1 percentage point, and the New York Times/Sarina College poll has him ahead by 5 percentage points. 

The CNN/SSRS poll also has Trump ahead by 5 percentage points. Only the Emerson poll last week had Harris ahead by 1 percentage point. 

In Wisconsin, Democrats have won five of the past six elections. However, in the one that was won by a Republican, Republican Donald Trump is running again. 

More than 80 percent of the state is white. The Democratic Party has done well in recent times, but has won by very small margins each time. The only exception was Barack Obama - he won by quite a large margin twice. 

Donald Trump is targeting Wisconsin's 10 electoral college votes. This year's Republican National Convention was held in this state, and Trump also took the party nomination from here. 

Harris is leading in Wisconsin by 1 percentage point in the Marist and Quinnipiac polls. Trump is leading by the same margin in the Emerson poll. The two candidates are tied in the Emerson/Polar poll. 

She also attended the National Rifle Association event in February. She has intimidated voters on the issue of gun rights and the state's name. Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris is leading in the University of Massachusetts and YouGov polls. 48 percent of those who will vote support Kamala. Trump has 46 percent support. However, Harris is ahead by 6 percent in the Quinnipiac University survey. 
Pennsylvania 
Republican Party candidate Donald Trump has been assassinated twice so far, the first of which was in Pennsylvania. Trump was shot in the ear by an assassin. 

This incident became one of the election issues. This state with 19 electoral colleges regularly won Republicans in the 1980s. 

The next two decades saw Democrats win. The winner took the last two elections. It will play an important role in determining the winner this time too. 

Joe Biden visited this state several times before withdrawing. Kamala Harris is also coming repeatedly with her running mate. Donald Trump is not far behind. He has been to Pennsylvania repeatedly since the beginning of the year. 

He also attended the National Rifle Association event in February. He scared voters on the issue of gun rights and the name of the state. 

Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris is leading in the University of Massachusetts and YouGov polls. 

Kamala is supported by 48 percent of those who will vote. Trump is supported by 46 percent. However, Harris is ahead by 6 percentage points in the Quinnipiac University poll. 

She is ahead by 4 points in the New York Times and Siena College polls. Trump is ahead by one point in the Emerson College poll. 

Nevada 
The governor of the southwestern state of Nevada, with six electoral college votes, is a Republican. The two senators are also from the Democratic Party. 

In the last 12 elections, candidates from both parties have won 6 times each. The elected candidates here have had the opportunity to live in the White House 10 times. 

Biden defeated Trump in the last election by a margin of only 34,000 votes. The supporters of the two parties are almost equal among voters. 

But more voters than that have not affiliated themselves with any party. 40 percent of voters have no party affiliation. 

They will make their decisions based on issues such as abortion, the economy, and the prospects for a democratic future. 

The Emerson/Polara poll in Nevada has the two candidates tied. The Emerson poll also has the same result. CNN/SSRN has Kamala leading by 1 percentage point. 

North Carolina 
Barack Obama was the only Democratic presidential candidate to win North Carolina this century, winning in 2008. Republicans have won every other election since. 

Donald Trump won the last election. But that was by only 74,000 votes. 

In the last few elections, the gap between the Democratic Party candidate and the Republican Party candidate has been narrowing. At the same time, 22 percent of African Americans and more than 10 percent of Hispanics are unaffiliated. 

36 percent of voters are unaffiliated with any political party. 51 percent of voters are women. 

Although Democratic presidential candidates have repeatedly lost in the state, these equations give Democrats hope; North Carolina has become a swing state. For Republicans in the state, immigration is the main issue, and for Democrats, preserving democracy is the main issue. 

The two candidates are expected to have a close race in North Carolina. The Emerson/Polara poll and the Marist poll have the two candidates tied. 

Kamala leads by 2 percentage points in the New York Times/Sarina College poll; she leads by 1 percentage point in the Emerson poll.

Headline_English: Rohingya problem: Can action be taken before the 'time bomb' explodes?
Content_Enlish:
The Chief Advisor has termed the Rohingya crisis as a time bomb. This term indicates the severity of the Rohingya crisis. 

In the past years, many statements have been made by Bangladesh on the Rohingya problem in national and international forums. But there has been no progress in sustainable solutions. The Rohingya problem is not a bilateral issue. Days have passed in the hope that it will be resolved from within Myanmar by calling it a Myanmar problem. Due to such a wrong path, the solution to the Rohingya crisis has moved further away. 

The Rohingya problem was almost forgotten under the pressure of the Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Palestine wars and conflicts. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim came to Dhaka immediately after the UN General Assembly meeting. The Rohingya issue was highlighted at the event organized on that occasion.
