The Rohingya crisis came to the fore twice in a very short period of time in the international arena. Malaysia is an important member of the regional forum called ASEAN. 

Bangladesh has not yet been able to enter this forum. The chief advisor to the outgoing Malaysian ambassador said that Bangladesh will act as a bridge between ASEAN and SAARC if it gets ASEAN membership. But can the dying SAARC be pulled out of the cycle of India's one-sided policy? Hopefully, Malaysia is going to become the ASEAN chairman in 2025. But will this hope be able to defuse the time bomb of the Rohingya crisis? 

Bangladesh has not had a good neighborly fate since its birth. One neighbor considers it its fundamental right to interfere in everything in Bangladesh. The other neighbor feels proud to maintain distance. Bangladesh is a member of several regional and international forums. Some of them are dying. In others, Bangladesh is either very silent and inactive, or Bangladesh is not heard there. In such a situation, how much Bangladesh will benefit from gaining ASEAN membership is a question. 

Let's come to ASEAN's words in the context of the Rohingya crisis. Let's see why there is no reason for Bangladesh to hope for the Rohingya crisis under ASEAN's existing policy. 

One of the principles of this organization, established in 1967, is that they will not interfere in the internal affairs of any member state. This is good to hear. However, it also has some problems. ASEAN is not a military alliance. ASEAN started its work with the aim of helping member states resolve disputes and achieve regional economic progress through discussion and negotiation. At that time, the Cold War was going on in the world. There was a tendency for major powers to intervene in less powerful states. At that time, ASEAN was timely in order to stop such interference. At that time, only Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore were its members. Later, Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos, Brunei and Cambodia joined. 

Over time, ASEAN has given rise to some forums and agreements politically. The work of entering into free trade area agreements with some countries, holding dialogues on expanding trade and increasing investment, etc. can be called the success of ASEAN. But even though ASEAN's name mentions Southeast Asia, ASEAN has failed to play any role in stopping human rights violations, genocide or prosecuting them in that region. 

The Rohingya are scattered in different countries of the world. But the damage caused by the time bomb explosion will be Bangladesh's. And the damage caused to the Rohingya is still happening. Therefore, Bangladesh's activities to resolve the Rohingya crisis need to be accelerated by learning from past mistakes. 
ASEAN's member state Myanmar has been condemned by the whole world as a genocidal perpetrator. The matter has reached the International Court of Justice. But ASEAN has been and still is a silent spectator, except for a few official statements. The external reason for this is ASEAN's policy of non-interference in the internal affairs of ASEAN member states. Of course, there is also an undeclared reason, which is investment. 

Like Western countries, ASEAN members also have huge investments in Myanmar. According to the World Bank's 2023 data, among ASEAN members, Thailand's investment in Myanmar is 3.09 billion, Cambodia's 3.96, Malaysia's 7.92, the Philippines' 8.86, Indonesia's 22.09 and Singapore's 175.24 billion US dollars. Although they are on Bangladesh's side in the Rohingya crisis, they are their priority in practice, even if they are verbally. 

ASEAN had promised to implement five steps. They were - immediately ending the violence in Myanmar, dialogue with all partners, appointing a special envoy, providing humanitarian assistance on behalf of ASEAN, and a special envoy's visit to Myanmar to meet all partners. But there were so many differences of opinion among its member states on the Rohingya issue that in the end no steps were implemented. They neither pressured Myanmar to repatriate the Rohingya, nor did they want to take a few Rohingyas from Bangladesh for resettlement. 

No ASEAN member state has dared to say that ASEAN policy should be changed to save the lives of millions of people, stop genocide and ethnic cleansing. No one has said that interfering in the internal affairs of another state and speaking out to stop genocide are not the same thing. No member state has said that they will stop trade with Myanmar unless their own people are repatriated. No member state has said that they will cancel Myanmar's ASEAN membership until the international court punishes Myanmar for genocide. 

All in all, the question may arise, from what plan is the Chief Advisor trying to achieve ASEAN membership for Bangladesh? 
In 2025, Malaysia will assume the ASEAN chairmanship. If they take a firm stand on the Rohingya issue and redefine the policy of interfering in the internal affairs of member states in the light of reality, it will be a historic contribution to humanity. Malaysia also has an interest in this. Malaysia is also in trouble with the Rohingya, albeit in small numbers. 

However, Bangladesh has no choice but to take four-pronged steps to defuse the time bomb. Bangladesh has not taken the initiative to engage in dialogue with the Arakan Army on the Rohingya issue at the right time. Moreover, there is evidence of the Rohingya fighting against the Arakan Army and for the military ruler. However, given the direction the events are going, there will be no surprise if the Arakan Army takes over the country's governance. The previous government has consigned the Rohingya return to the museum. If the return can be implemented, it will be a great success for the interim government. 

The Chief Advisor has presented three proposals to the UN General Assembly—organizing an international conference to find a solution to the Rohingya crisis through discussion; raising funds for the Rohingya sheltered in Bangladesh; and prosecuting the genocide in the international court. Out of the three, action is being taken first on the second one. Although it will be like putting a band-aid on a huge wound. Because, while meeting the needs of helpless people for the time being, raising funds is not a solution to the crisis. Rather, it prolongs the crisis. So, has the first and third proposal been kept under official supervision so that it does not get lost? 

The Rohingya are spread across different countries of the world. But the damage caused by the time bomb explosion will be on Bangladesh. And the damage caused to the Rohingya is already happening. Therefore, Bangladesh needs to learn from the mistakes of the past and speed up its efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis.

Headline_English: What does Shishu Academy have to do?
Content_Enlish:
In 1972, Ahmed Safa wrote a new format for intelligence. After the mass uprising of 2024, our institutions also need a new format. This format will be based on what kind of people we want. It was also in Plato's communist state concept. In his state, children are also the property of the state. It is said that a child's personality develops through two types of relationships. For this reason, a person is also called a duality. The first is physical and the second is consciousness. And consciousness is associated with the formation of one's own perspective on life, active willpower and the quality of the intellectual situation around them. 

Children want to love and be loved. They imitate those they love, adopt their mannerisms. They want to borrow their evaluations of things, people and events. Children become familiar with the lives of adults in various ways—by listening to stories, poems, and fairy tales of adults. From the behavior of their friends' heroes, even from their own best friends. When it is clear to the child who is good and who is bad, then he decides how he will show himself in all similar situations. 

Pediatricians say that children are endowed with eight to nine types of intelligence. Some learn by observing nature, some learn rhythmically, some learn mathematically, some learn alone, some learn in groups, some logically, some learn by singing, some learn by touching, and some learn by going to a specific place. 

Two. 
A large area of ​​Shishu Academy in front of Curzon Hall in Dhaka city. And in the district towns, each Shishu Academy building is like a shack. In Rangpur or Kurigram or Barguna or Bogra, where is the Shishu Academy, it is impossible to find it. No one even knows its address. Who digs up a shack and finds out the address? Yet Shishu Academies are supposed to be the center of all schools, high schools, and madrasas in the entire district. 
The job of Shishu Academies is to provide learning facilities for children of all intelligence levels. Bringing children from the city to the village and children from the village to the city, taking all the children together by bus to visit places of interest, arranging for films, stories, poems, picture exhibitions and publications made by children. 

Regular children's fairs could be held in the district children's academies; where children of all nationalities could appear in their respective districts of the map of Bangladesh with the characteristics of their respective nations. There could be displays of fashion, food and other characteristics. In this, children would become interested in each other's culture and life. From childhood, they would know that Bangladesh is not just their village or city. They would know that Bangladesh is a country of many nations, multilingual and multi-religious. If a national unity and inclusive state is to be built, then there is no alternative to this fair. 

A book fair would gather with the participation of teachers-guardians-students. Where children would learn photography, cinema courses, singing, storytelling, dancing, recitation and everything else that can be learned. Just like Shilpakala Academy is not just for all types of artists, Shishu Academy is not like that. Shishu Academy is only for children, all children of the district. From there, they would build their own district, learn to love it. 

The District Children's Academy can procure double-decker buses for this purpose. They can build small museums inside the buses. Children will travel in those buses all year round. Each day, one school, sometimes several schools together. 

A Children's Academy must have the infrastructure and mentality to accommodate all children in the district's primary and high schools and madrasas. The database of the Children's Academy will contain information about all children in the district. With one click, you will know how many children in the district are interested in a particular subject and who they are. It will establish subject-based clubs. A cinema club for children interested in cinema. In that club, children will learn about cinema, make their own films and those films will be shown on a projector in front of the people of the district. 

The members of the cycling club will learn to ride bicycles and compete. The children of the literature club will listen to the best writers of the country on literature, write in magazines published in collaboration with the academy. A painting exhibition will be organized for those who draw. A photo exhibition will be held in the photography club. There will be discussions on scientific thinking and technology projects in the science club. The program will be held 365 days a year. 

Our rivers are lost, the Water Development Board office is skyrocketing. Bridges and culverts are lost, the LGRD office is in ruins. The DC-SP offices where clerical work is done, are full of wealth. And the hospitals where millions of people are suffering, have no beds. The Shishu Academy, which deals with several lakhs of children, is so small that no one notices it. 
Yet the Shishu Academy is supposed to be the largest institution in the district. Where are we pouring money if we don't develop children?

Headline_English: A new Middle East is coming, but it...
Content_Enlish:
A year ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took a map of the “new Middle East” to the UN General Assembly. The map outlined a vision for a regional order based on the Abraham Accords. The Abraham Accords are a process for normalizing Israel’s relations with its Arab neighbors. 

But instead of transforming the regional order through diplomacy and trade, Israel has chosen the path of destructive war and genocide over the past year. 

Israel’s open aggression in various parts of the Middle East over the past year has blocked any shaky path to peace there. The genocidal aggression in Gaza, the aerial bombing, drone and missile attacks in Syria and Yemen, and now the ground operation in Lebanon—all of these have completely shattered the relative stability that had been established in the Middle East at the beginning of this decade. 

In 2003, neoconservative thinkers wanted to create Iraq as a democratic beacon from which a new Middle East could spread. Two decades later, that transformation of the Middle East is taking place at the hands of a racist, settler state. That state is doing the transformation through genocide, invasion, and mass displacement. 

Israel continues to expand its borders as much as possible, and through a tolerable level of regional armed conflict. Israel is implementing this project by regularly violating international human rights law and testing Arab countries without pushing them into major tensions. 

The genocidal Israeli offensive has rendered much of Gaza uninhabitable. Regional governments have called for a ceasefire and de-escalation. So far, with the exception of non-state armed groups, most Arab states have been passive players. 

The red lines that Arab countries had previously drawn (such as mass displacement of Palestinians, targeted killings in hospitals and schools) have had no effect in stopping the Israeli aggression. But the year-long war in Gaza has sounded the alarm for the emergence of a new Middle East. This can be said in terms of the Middle East’s relations with Western countries. Here, the issue of American and European diplomacy is fully visible. 

However, Middle Eastern leaders’ trust in Western leadership is waning. In terms of mediating political agreements, countries there are increasingly turning to China. Countries are partnering with China for technological development and infrastructure reconstruction. 

Occupied Palestine was conspicuously absent from the revised map of the Middle East that Netanyahu showed. He has been showing for a year what is behind this distortion. 

From Israel’s perspective, a new regional arrangement means normalizing relations with Saudi Arabia. But Palestine is an obstacle to achieving that goal. Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recently said that his country will not normalize relations with Israel until a Palestinian state is established with East Jerusalem as its capital. 

Importantly, the Saudi crown prince said this, influenced by a demand that has become popular among young Saudis. Not only in Saudi Arabia, but also among young people throughout the Middle East, the Israeli genocide has created an absolute sense of solidarity with the Palestinians. 

In this regard, the Gaza war is truly changing the map of the Middle East. A strong sense of unity has been created among the people in the streets of Arab countries against the Israeli occupation and ethnic cleansing campaign. 

But to transform this new awareness into lasting change, Arab countries must establish their own authority in their future regional transformation. A single, settler, colonialist, and imperialist-backed power cannot be allowed to dictate that course. 
That can only be ensured by leading the way for a just and sovereign Palestinian state and a greater Middle East.

Headline_English: Where did the girls of the mass uprising go?
Content_Enlish:
Just three months ago, in the July Uprising, we saw how girls took over the streets. Thousands of girls of all ages came out on the streets. They were shaking everything with fearless slogans and graffiti. The participation of girls in the Bangla Blockade on July 7 was unimaginable compared to any other time. Since then, women's participation in the movement has gradually increased. 

Even in front of the procession, girls were not spared from police bullets and batons. Several women were even killed. The newspaper published pictures of the batons of the helmeted force jumping on two young women. Another young woman stood alone in front of the police prison van, as if she would block all aggression with both hands. All these pictures went viral at home and abroad, inspiring and giving courage to everyone. 

We saw pictures and videos going viral of a university teacher holding her student with both hands to save him from the police, letting her back fall under the police batons. I saw a mother patting her child on the back as she was being dragged into a police van. Our girls were also protesting in other parts of the country. From school girls to university students, garment workers, housewives, mothers, college and university teachers, employees, actresses, artists, singers—who was not in this movement? 

However, within a few months, it seemed as if girls began to disappear from the history of this uprising. Recently, the Department of Health published a list of those killed in July-August on their website. There are names of six women of different ages. However, although the report published in Prothom Alo on August 14 mentioned the killings of Maya Islam (60) and Nasima Akhter (24) with photos, they were left out of this list. 17-year-old Tanha or Nafisa Marwa, who was seen on Facebook, was left out. Perhaps many more who were injured or lost limbs were left out in this way. 

Naima Sultana, a class 10 student of Milestone School and College, could not become a hero like other students who died in the movement. No square was built for Naima, no wall was named after her. Even though we constantly remember Mughd and Farhan, we have forgotten about Naima. Coordinator Nusrat, who was detained in the DB office along with other coordinators, has also disappeared from the entire scene. Why did this happen? 

Since August 5, we have been witnessing a kind of patriarchal influence on the entire movement. The women who had filled the streets with slogans, protests and protests, without whom the leaders of the anti-discrimination movement had commented that this movement would never have been successful, are now seeing those same women disappearing. 
As Minal Srivastava gave an example in her article ‘Invisible Women in History and Global Studies’, 80,000 people were arrested in the Salt Satyagraha movement in India in 1930-31. Out of these, 17,000 were women. Yet, their place has not been found anywhere in the history of India’s independence. Thus, women disappear from statistics and data. Then it becomes inevitable to see the whole issue only from the perspective of men. Even after our recent mass uprising, we seem to see this happening. 

In an interview with Prothom Alo on October 3, Mahfuz Alam, Special Assistant to the Chief Advisor, said, ‘The involvement of women in this movement was huge. Although many people forget it now, it is true that without women, this movement would not have been successful in any way.’ 

Thank you to him for highlighting this truth. But the fact that women, like ten other activists, also took a stand against fascist oppression with ideological courage is somehow absent from this narrative. 

The torture and oppression that women were subjected to in various ways during the previous government’s tenure. The stories of Jagannath University student Khadijatul Kubra, Kushtia Islamic University’s Phulpari Begum, or actress Naushaba are worth remembering. Many of us have not remembered the contributions of those women either. 

Since August 5, we have been witnessing a kind of patriarchal influence on the entire movement. The women who filled the streets with slogans, protests and protests, without whom the leaders of the anti-discrimination movement have commented that this movement would never have been successful, are now seeing those same women disappearing. 

An opportunistic group has started stealing women's clothes. Street sex workers are being harassed, catcalling or bullying on the streets is suddenly increasing. The women participating in the movement were subjected to widespread bullying and trolling on social media then, and still are. The teacher Samina Lutfa, who played a courageous role in freeing the student coordinators from the DB office, was cornered by widespread trolling on social media. 

And it is quite surprising that despite the strong role of women coordinators in the entire movement, no women were included in the list of two members of the advisory council and three special assistants in the office of the chief advisor. The heads of the reform commissions are all men. 

There is no reform plan to change the status of women. It is seen that despite taking an active part in the movement, women are continuously lagging behind in achieving their rights. They are constantly disappearing from the scene. 

This time, a large number of ordinary women got involved in political activism, overcoming all fears and hesitations. But with time, they are disappearing from the scene. Not only ordinary women, but also those who were in the forefront of the movement. However, the reality is that more women should come into politics in our country, it is very necessary to create a situation where women's voices are heard at all levels. Will these invisible women, who make up half of the population, become visible in the future after the state reforms?

Headline_English: Huge money laundering ring of Bangladeshis in Dubai, what to do
Content_Enlish:
As a developing economy, Bangladesh needs a lot of foreign exchange to finance its trade and development. And one of the means to meet that foreign exchange requirement is expatriate income or remittances. However, people involved in the sector say that even though remittance flow through legal channels has increased, not all of the expatriate income is coming through banks. Our estimated or potential expatriate income is about $45-50 billion. 

Even though the expatriate income coming through legal channels has increased recently, the relevant people believe that it could be slightly above $24 billion per year. That is, slightly less than 55 percent of the potential expatriate income is coming only through legal or official channels. 

Expatriates are currently getting 121 taka against every dollar through the banking channel. On the other hand, this rate in the open market is a maximum of 123.50 taka. Due to the strict initiatives of the central bank, the hundi cycle has not been able to provide benefits to hundi recently. As the official rate and hundi rate are getting closer, expatriates are currently comfortable sending money through bank channels. As a result, if hundi is stopped, it is possible to bring in almost double the current annual income of 25 billion dollars. 

During the previous government's tenure, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Employment recommended taking steps to increase awareness about sending remittances. Ten obstacles were mentioned to prevent the violence of hundi traders to increase the flow of remittances from abroad to the country through banking channels. The obstacles are the difference in the remittance exchange rate in illegal channels compared to legal channels, the lack of valid documents of expatriate workers, the absence of branches of Bangladeshi commercial banks abroad or the lack of sufficient branches. 

Apart from this, the issues of absence of Bangladeshi money exchange institutions or lack of sufficient money exchange points in those countries, high fees or service charges and prescribed limits (ceilings) for sending remittances, violence of hundi traders, in many cases, expatriates or close relatives of expatriates not having bank accounts in the country, obstacles in sending remittances if they are not in line with income, lack of opportunity to send income from unauthorized business or work through legal channels, lack of awareness and enthusiasm for sending remittances through legal channels also come up. 

Many say that all efforts should be made to bring expatriate income into the country through legal channels. Bangladeshi missions abroad should be more active. Like some countries, the World Bank can also be taken for this. Action should be taken against some commercial banks or some of their officials involved in cleverly encouraging hundi. 

The supply of dollars in the market should be increased by all means, including the rapid repatriation of export earnings, and the stability of the exchange rate should be maintained. In addition to keeping a constant eye on the competitive exchange rate, more innovative and well-thought-out measures must be taken to bring in remittances through legal channels. We must go much deeper into determining the causes of hundi. At the same time, we must pay a new attention to the issues of incentives for expatriates. Proper investment of remitted money and even new types of investment products and services must be considered in this regard. The issue of easy investment by expatriates in the capital market has not yet been made easy. 

On the other hand, the means through which money is laundered, including under-over invoicing, must be identified. Finding out who the beneficiaries are and with whose help it is done is not a very difficult task. In addition to taking steps to increase expatriate income through the export of skilled manpower, initiatives must be taken to provide legitimacy to those who are currently abroad. The sufferings that exist must be resolved. 

According to the newspaper, Bangladesh Bank found new destinations for money laundering at the end of last year. A large group of 2,500 Bangladeshi citizens have set up a money laundering base in the European country of Portugal. They have also taken the country's citizenship to safely transfer the money. Out of this, they have laundered 14.5 billion taka to the country. The situation in Dubai in the Middle East is even more dire. Currently, the country is being used as the main route or 'safe haven' for money laundering. 

Bangladeshi businessmen have opened 13,000 establishments in Dubai to conduct money laundering. 65 billion taka has been invested there. Business groups are working as conduits for money laundering for politicians and bureaucrats. With the help of influential people of the fallen government, some industrial groups have built a huge empire abroad by laundering huge amounts of money under the guise of import-export and through hundi. 

It has already been proven that one of the main means of earning foreign exchange is collecting remittances through the export of manpower. Currently, remittances or expatriate income is also playing an important role in the formation of foreign exchange reserves. The continuous decline for a long time has stopped due to the increase in the flow of expatriate income. For this reason, many analysts, including the World Bank, are advising to take steps to gradually increase expatriate income. In this regard, the export of skilled manpower is being given utmost importance. 

Along with this, work must also be done to open the way for the export of manpower to new countries. Many have said that if at least 90 percent of the money currently being sent to the country by expatriates is brought through legal channels, there will be a surge in remittance flows. As a result, the foreign exchange market and reserves will return to a positive trend. 

A large amount of remittances are being smuggled through hundi and other means. The annual figure is at least 25 billion dollars. That is, more than half of the remittances sent to the country by expatriates are being smuggled. However, there is no official government announcement or written account on this. 

Although sending skilled workers abroad is time-consuming, it is possible to stop smuggling and create incentives for remittances through immediate action. This will quickly bring the ongoing dollar crisis and the decline in reserves under control. If the exchange rate is made competitive through an automatic process, there will be no need for additional government incentives. 

According to Bangladesh Bank, in January this year, remittances to the country through banking channels were $2.11 billion, $2.16 billion in February, $1.99 billion in March, $2.04 billion in April, $2.25 billion in May, $2.54 billion in June, $1.91 billion in July, and $2.22 billion in August. And in the 28 days of September, remittances amounted to more than $2 billion. 

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, remittances came in through banking channels of $23.92 billion. In the 2022-23 fiscal year, remittances came in at $21.61 billion. In the 2021-22 fiscal year, total remittances came in at $21.03 billion. During the Covid period, remittances came in at $24.77 billion in the 2020-21 fiscal year, which was the highest amount of remittances in the fiscal year. 

Many have already talked about increasing facilities for expatriates at the airport. Even the use of separate or special terminals for expatriates has been mentioned. This is a good proposal. With that, considering the amount of remittance brought through legal channels, the issue of issuing certificates and getting special services can be associated. Along with this, making air fares more affordable, sincere treatment of cabin crews on the plane towards them and even addressing them as 'Sir' can be introduced. Even at the immigration point. For these reasons, even if Mumbai or Delhi is transited, India's Indigo and Vistara airlines have already become favorite among Bangladeshi expatriates.

Headline_English: When will the poor board the intercity train?
Content_Enlish:
If a farmer enters Delhi with a sack of chillies by train for free, then a farmer also enters Delhi with a sack of chillies, which costs much more than the rail fare if it is brought by truck. The truck tires are saved, the road is saved, and the diesel subsidy is also saved. 

If an employee enters his office in Delhi by train from a distance of 50 kilometers, his vitality and living expenses are saved much more than staying in Delhi, which is a benefit to the country in one way. If a job seeker comes by train, he can give an interview much more refreshed than those who come by bus and give an interview. If a student can catch a train to college, he can be much more focused - this is what former Indian Railway Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav said. 

1. 
The railway factory established by the Indian government in Kapurthala, Punjab province, on 1,200 acres of land in 1987, produces 1,500 coaches every year. However, although the Saidpur Railway Factory was established in Bangladesh on 110 acres of land in 1870, it has not been modernized to this day. On the contrary, the equipment that is there is in danger of being destroyed due to disuse. 

And the planners of the last Awami League government approved a project of only 122 crore 22 lakh taka for the modernization of the Saidpur Railway Factory. Later, it was not fully implemented. The rehabilitation project, which was jointly funded by Japan's JBIC Bank and the Bangladesh government in 2007 at a cost of 146 crore taka to increase the production of the Pahartali Railway Factory, has not even started. 

80 percent of the machinery of these two factories is from the British era. They have lost their productive capacity long ago. We certainly cannot maintain the mark of British slavery by keeping these two factories running! Although the 'Central Locomotive Factory' was established in Parbatipur on May 14, 1992 with the aim of making locomotives (engines), no government has taken the initiative to make engines! 

The state will look after the poor, the rich will go by plane if necessary. About 30 to 40 intercity trains operate across the country. If two coaches are attached to each train, a total of 60 to 80 coaches will be required. These can be collected from local mails. 
The Saidpur Railway Factory, established by the British Raj around the Assam-Bengal Railway in 1870, was filled with the sound of hundreds of machines and the footsteps of several thousand workers and employees during its establishment. And in independent Bangladesh, under the 'Recovery Program' during the democratic government of 1991, the railway's manpower was reduced from 58,000 to 35,000. Especially the factory workers were reduced. For example, the sanctioned posts in the Saidpur factory at the time of establishment were 4,000, but in 2003 it came down to 1,621. 

The sanctioned posts in the Parbatipur Railway Factory are 1,036 against 1,699. And in Pahartali, there are 1,233 against 2,128. That is, all the factories are running with 40 percent less manpower. Only due to the shortage of manpower, although there is an opportunity to repair engines, carriages and wagons, they have to be repaired and imported from outside at an additional cost. 

On the other hand, among those who are working, 70 percent of the employees of the Saidpur factory and 90 percent of the workers are over 50 years old. This is in 2015. 

2. 
Currently, the railways can be made more profitable by adding 3 to 4 more coaches to the engines. A few days ago, there was a discussion with the Railway Secretary and DG. The Secretary said that the state will take care of the poor, the rich will go by plane if necessary. When the DG pointed out the technical problems in connecting local coaches with intercity trains, the Secretary suggested that the necessary repairs be done in the workshop. 

About 30 to 40 intercity trains operate across the country. If two coaches are connected to each train, a total of 60 to 80 coaches will be needed. They can be collected from those local mails. Only minor repairs will be done. As a result, there is no problem of additional costs. This is how Lalu Prasad Yadav made Indian Railways profitable. 

The shallow engines were for the so-called green revolution to extract groundwater, and our fishermen and boatmen have used them to cross rivers. 

Where 54 seats can be provided in a meter gauge luxurious or elegant coach, it is possible to make double that number of seats in a cheap coach. In this, where the fare in a luxurious coach is 600, the cheap one can be 300. These cheap seats will be allocated for the marginal people of the marginal areas of the country. This will prove once again that the current government is a government of mass uprising.

Headline_English: How terrible will Israel's retaliation on Iran be?
Content_Enlish:
Israel has been assassinating top political and military leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. In response, Iran launched missile attacks on Israel earlier this month. This has left many in the Middle East wondering what lies ahead. 

The attacks are a belated fulfillment of Iranian promises to avenge the Israeli killings. Similarly, the discontent that had been building among the country’s population has subsided. But there has also been concern about how Israel will respond. 

The mood in Tehran has become increasingly defiant, with Iranian government officials vowing to respond to any Israeli attack. Iranian President Masoud Pajhwok said earlier this month that “if Israel launches any attack, we will respond strongly and severely.” 

Another Iranian government official said that Tehran had communicated with Washington through an intermediary that any Israeli attack would be responded to by “non-conventional” means, including targeting civilian facilities. 

There has been speculation that Israel could attack Iran’s Kharg Island oil facilities. Israel could seek to weaken the sector by attacking Iranian oil refineries. If Israel launches a full-scale attack, Iran’s air defenses would be unable to stop it. 
The commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), General Hossein Salimi, warned Israel that “we are telling you that if any of our areas are attacked, we will give you a painful response in that area.” 

Observers say that if Israel retaliates, Iran alone will have to bear the brunt of the attack, as the United States and its European allies will continue to support Israel. 

For a year, the West has been aiding and abetting Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza. That war has now spread to Lebanon. 

Iran’s strategic allies Russia and China have so far been ambiguous about their position. They will only consider their national interests in taking further action. 

Iran’s Weaknesses 
Israel vowed to retaliate immediately after the Iranian attack. In a statement, Benjamin Netanyahu said, “Iran does not understand the extent of our determination to defend ourselves.” 

Iranian officials have given their citizens advice on how Israel could attack and what their targets might be. They have warned of possible attacks ranging from cyber sabotage to attacks on military bases and civilian facilities. They could also attack Iran’s oil and gas facilities. They could assassinate high-ranking military officials and even attack nuclear facilities. 

Behrouz Kamalvandi, a spokesman for Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization, said that an Israeli attack on Iran’s nuclear facilities was impossible. But if they did attack now, any damage would be quickly repaired. 

Iran’s foreign minister has warned that Tehran will retaliate if any Arab country uses Israel or the United States as a base to attack Iran. 

What kind of response Israel will give, of course, depends on future calculations and US cooperation. 

In any case, regardless of the nature of Israel’s response, or its extent, it can be said that Iran has had to deal with numerous such attacks in the conflictive relations that have existed between the two countries for decades. 

There have been one after another sabotages in Iran’s cyber system. Israel has carried out cyber attacks to disrupt the energy supply of gas stations in Iranian cities. Israel has also attacked the cyber system of Iran’s Shahid Razi port. 

Israel has assassinated Iranian nuclear scientists and military officers at various times. The recent assassination of Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was in Tehran on a state invitation, was a major setback. 

Another significant setback was the assassination of Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, the father of Iran’s rocket program, in 2011. He was killed in an explosion outside a military base in Tehran. Israel has stolen important documents from Iran and sabotaged nuclear facilities. 

Is this psychological warfare? 

Experts believe that attacking industrial and urban infrastructure rather than nuclear facilities could reduce the risk of an all-out war. 

Iran’s oil facilities, including the port of Asaluyeh and the terminal on Kharg Island, could be relatively easy targets for Israel because they are located in the south of the country. A major fire there would receive extensive international media coverage. 

Iran’s nuclear facilities are located deep underground and are located in the center of the country. Attacking them would require a major Israeli military effort and the availability of U.S. “bunker buster” bombs. However, U.S. President Joe Biden has opposed any attack on nuclear facilities. 

The Iranian government has also reacted to the Biden administration’s role in the conflict. The United States recently provided Israel with the THAAD anti-missile defense system. Iranian Defense Minister Brigadier General Aziz Nasirzadeh downplayed the issue, calling it “psychological warfare.” “This is not a new issue; it will not create any specific problems,” he said. 

Vaed Ahmadi, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security Committee, said Iran has the capability to attack the THAAD system. 

There has been speculation that Israel could attack Iran’s oil facilities on Kharg Island. Israel may want to weaken the sector by attacking Iran’s oil refineries. If Israel launches a full-scale attack, Iran’s air defenses would be unable to stop it.

Headline_English: Some suggestions and recommendations to stop ragging and torture in university torture cells
Content_Enlish:
The history of violence in educational institutions in Bangladesh is not new. There have been clashes between rival student organizations, conflicts between different groups of the same organization, and clashes with law enforcement agencies on campuses at various times. As a result of these incidents, activists of political student organizations, ordinary students, members of law enforcement agencies, and ordinary pedestrians have also been killed. 

But there are vast differences in character between the clashes between student organizations in the past and the incidents of student torture in the last 15 years. 

A recent study by the US-based human rights organization Sochhar-Torture Watchdog Bangladesh has revealed the various causes, types, locations, horrors, and indescribable suffering of the victims after the torture. 

The report was prepared by Sochhar researchers Dr. Shibbir Ahmed, Mehedi Hasan, and Rahnuma Siddika based on interviews with 50 students who were tortured at various universities between 2010 and 2024.

The study found that about 84 percent of the torture incidents occurred in university halls. In another 6 percent of cases, the torture began on campus but was later caught and tortured in the halls. 

These students who were tortured did not receive any significant support from other university students, the hall administration, the university authorities, or the state administration. 

There were even allegations that teachers directly or indirectly helped some of them in the torture. 

Failure to participate in political programs, being absent from night guest room meetings, failing to show sufficient ‘respect’ to senior leaders, liking Islamic or opposition party or opinion pages, posting Islamic posts or sharing waz on Facebook, posting or liking Sheikh Hasina, her father/family, anti-India or any political posts on Facebook, and suspicion of Chhatra Shibir or Chhatra Dal were the reasons for torture. 

Torture increased with seasonal political activity. Most torture occurred in the years preceding the elections, in August and before the formation of the Chhatra League committee. 

After the first-year students arrived on campus, the level of torture increased in the residential halls at this time in order to gain their full obedience and intimidate them. 

Various types of physical torture were carried out, including beating a person with sticks, stumps, GI pipes, rods, breaking the bones of the hands and feet, pulling out nails, giving them cigarette butts, beating them and torturing them again after they got tired, giving them soft drinks during the rest, threatening them with great harm if they revealed the torture, beating them to death and filing a false case with the police. Apart from this, various types of mental torture were carried out in the name of ragging or teaching manners, forcing them to do unwanted things, showing intimidation, forcing them to miss classes to participate in political programs, etc. 

University campuses are not only places of education, but also places for students to develop as creative, democratic and humane people. If we can ensure a safe campus by stopping torture, students will be able to achieve greater success in their personal and academic lives. 
Many victims have spent long periods in prison after the torture. Some have taken exams from prison, while many have fallen behind in their studies for a semester or a year. The victims are suffering from long-term physical disabilities and mental trauma, including being irregular in class, even dropping out of the university, being socially isolated, facing financial losses due to leaving the hall and messing around outside, and spending their days in fear and uncertainty on campus. 

This practice of torture was prevalent due to lack of justice, hall-centered student politics, public room-guestroom culture, housing crisis, and above all, fascist politics. 

The torturers were rewarded and later received high party positions, even high-ranking government jobs, which served as an incentive to create new torturers. 

Growing up through a corrupt process of student politics, the boy who was forced to leave because he had nowhere to stay in Dhaka city has one day become a terrible abuser. 

This culture of abuse has not only disrupted the learning environment at the university, but has also given students and their guardians a sense of fear and uncertainty. 

To try these past abuses and build a safe campus free from fear for students, 'Sochchar' has made 10-point recommendations: 

1. Form a government commission to investigate: Form a government commission to investigate the incidents of abuse that have occurred on campus and ensure justice. 

2. University investigation committee and institutional punishment: In addition to the state legal process, universities should form investigation committees and ensure institutional punishment against the students and teachers involved. 

3. Form a victim support cell: Form a permanent victim support cell, where any student can file a complaint if they are a victim of physical or mental abuse. 

4. Special security for first-year students: First-year students are the most vulnerable and are the main target of torture. Special measures should be taken for their safety. If necessary, separate halls should be built for first-year students, where only first-year students will be accommodated and those from second years will be transferred to other halls. 

5. Rules for student politics on campus: A strict set of rules should be formulated for conducting student politics on campus, so that students cannot be forced to participate in political programs against their will. 

6. Reforms and age limits for student politics: To reduce long-term leadership struggles or intra-party conflicts within student organizations, an upper age limit can be set for student politics. 

7. Declaring halls free from student politics: The most cases of student torture occur in halls. Therefore, to stop torture, halls should be declared free from student politics. If any kind of procession-meeting, guest room meeting or room occupation is prohibited in the halls, torture will come to an end to a large extent. 

8. ‘Inclusive Campus’-related training: Students and teachers can be given ‘inclusive campus’-related training to stop ragging and harassment. This training can be implemented under the orientation program in each department or by establishing a permanent training center on the campus. 

9. Solution to the housing crisis: If the housing crisis is solved by constructing new halls and buildings or by constructing high-rise buildings, the problem of ‘becoming a victim by playing politics to get a seat in the hall’ will be reduced to a great extent. 

10. Observing Campus Violence Prevention Day: Observing the martyrdom day of Abrar Fahad, a student who was tortured on the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) campus, on October 7 every year as ‘Campus Violence Prevention Day’ in all educational institutions across the country. 

By making students aware of the horrors of campus violence through various events on the occasion of this day, the tendency to become bullies will decrease and it will be possible to prevent violence by increasing the desire of ordinary students and teachers to unite against violence. 

University campuses are not only places of education, but also places for students to develop as creative, democratic and humane people. If we can ensure a safe campus by stopping violence, students will be able to achieve greater success in their personal and academic lives.

Headline_English: India's challenge with the new Sri Lanka
Content_Enlish:
The people's struggle, known as Aragala, brought down the all-powerful Rajapaksa brothers from the seat of political power in Sri Lanka in 2022. After achieving its goal, the struggle seems to have collapsed. Its source was economic chaos; but the enthusiasm for opposing the established political institutions that was then evidently not dissipated. Evidence of this can be found in the results of the recently concluded presidential election. The results of the election indicate a radical change in the country's political system. 

The people's struggle has yielded the fruits of the leftist National People's Power (NPP). It is led by the Janata Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP). The JVP began as an underground movement committed to armed struggle for the achievement of socialist ideals. However, they have later joined the mainstream. They have now come to power for the first time in the country's electoral history. NPP's Anuradha Kumara Dissanayake has been sworn in as President, promising to eradicate political corruption and bring about a renaissance. 

Minority wounds 
Anuradha Dissanayake has won. But his vote came mainly from the Sinhalese-dominated south of Sri Lanka. He did not receive unwavering support from the north or east, where Tamil Hindus and Muslims live. It is understood that he will have to work hard to fulfill his promise to unite the country. The three-decade bloody civil war ended only after the killing of Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam chief Prabhakaran by the Sri Lankan army in 2009; but since then, Sri Lankan governments have taken no special initiative to heal the wounds of the Tamil community. Anuradha will have to make a special effort to heal the wounds of the country's minorities. 

Anuradha himself is well aware of the concerns that the NPP's closeness to China and Anuradha's close ties to the Chinese Communist Party are causing for India. India will have to wait and see how the new president will balance his country's foreign relations with competing powers like India and China. 
Crowned with Thorns 
Dissanayake has indeed come to power wearing a crown of thorns. Sri Lanka has yet to recover from the economic collapse it faced in 2022. The country is now saddled with a debt burden of over $37 billion. Anuradha’s first task will be to come up with a fiscal plan to service the country’s debt. He will have to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for the next tranche of his nearly $3 billion bailout. Meanwhile, the IMF has ordered the government to impose heavy income taxes on the people and take other tough measures to bridge the country’s fiscal deficit. 

During the election campaign, Dissanayake promised that he would force the IMF to ease its conditions; but the IMF is not one to change its conditions easily. Moreover, the country cannot even function without their support. In a brief address to the nation after taking the oath, Dissanayake admitted that he was no magician and that “the common people and all sections of society have a great responsibility” to help and support him in recovering from the economic crisis. 

Tough election ahead 
With only three NPP members in parliament, Dissanayake’s first move was to dissolve parliament and call for fresh elections in mid-November. He appointed NPP MP Harini Amarasuraya as prime minister. Harini is a respected academic and women’s rights activist. The move will help women get the vote in the upcoming elections. 

The Anuradhapura party has promised to amend the constitution to curb the “excessive powers” ​​of the president and bring a fair balance of power to the provinces. For this, it is crucial for the NPP to win a majority in parliament. They will need 113 of their 225 seats to amend the constitution. That will be a tough task for the NPP, especially if the two opposition parties share seats. 

Pragmatist Anudha 
Despite his socialist leanings, Anudha is quite a pragmatist. He knows that he needs to attract foreign investors and domestic private investors to help the economy recover from the recession. In his speech releasing the party’s manifesto before the elections, he outlined three main priorities—maximizing the country’s economic output and creating jobs; supporting industrialists, businessmen and foreign investors in rebuilding the economy; and emphasizing the revival of key sectors including manufacturing, tourism and the maritime industry. He also promised to develop the education and health sectors. 

Strong foreign policy 
Foreign policy is a matter of interest and concern for India. The new president has promised to ensure ‘a strong and stable foreign policy’. He said this policy would ‘not allow any use of our territorial waters, land or air that threatens national security and ensure that all economic transactions are profitable for the country’. 

India had single-handedly supported Sheikh Hasina’s government in Bangladesh; But India has maintained good relations with all the major parties and their leaders in Sri Lanka. During Sri Lanka's economic crisis, India provided financial assistance of about five billion dollars. Anuradha has mentioned this with gratitude several times. He visited India this February and met National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar. He visited Gujarat and Kerala. He was particularly interested in the Amul dairy cooperative. He has previously spoken of bringing about changes in the Sri Lankan dairy industry. 

Challenges that India must consider 
In the 1980s, Anuradha participated in the movement and protest rallies against Indian intervention in Sri Lanka. Even so, his political lessons began with the Chinese Revolution. He and his party are known to be close to China. The possibility of China's renewed influence in Sri Lanka would be a matter of concern for India. 

Anuradha opposed the 13th Amendment to the Constitution. This amendment was made in 1987 through joint negotiations between India and Sri Lanka. There is talk of decentralizing power by forming a provincial council. India firmly believes that this will solve the Tamil problem. The current opposition party in Sri Lanka also wants the same. 

Before coming to power, Anuradha has said that he will reconsider Gautam Adani's wind power plant project in Sri Lanka. Because it is against Sri Lanka's 'energy sovereignty'. The size of this project is not small, 10 billion dollars. 

And all in all, what is understood is that the future of the 'Economic Partnership Vision' signed between Sri Lanka and India in 2023 during the time of Ranil Wickremesinghe is uncertain. 

Anuradha himself is well aware of the concerns that the NPP's closeness to China and Anuradha's close relationship with the Chinese Communist Party are a cause for concern for India. India will have to wait and see how the new president will balance his country's foreign relations with various competing powers like India and China. And public support is a very volatile thing. If he fails to deliver on the promises that brought him to power in 2022, it won't take long for the same public to turn against him. 

Taken from India Today, translated from English by Javed Hussain

Headline_English: What will the new student politics be like after the mass uprising?
Content_Enlish:
The kind of 'student politics' that exists in government educational institutions like BUET, Dhaka College, Government Bangla College, etc., is not the same in private institutions like NorthSouth or BRAC University. Would parents want all educational institutions to have such student politics in which their children, like Abrar Fahad, become victims of murder. Or would the children of those who killed Abrar Fahad also become murderers? Probably not. That is why the decision to ban politics in BUET gained public acceptance after the Abrar Fahad murder. 

Later, there was a call to reinstate student politics in BUET. The decision was appealed to the court. One reason for this is that participating in politics is a constitutional fundamental right of students. It cannot be denied that university students are free to join the student organization of any political party, except those banned voluntarily. It is said that if mainstream politics is not allowed and discussed on campus, attraction to banned political parties increases. For these reasons, perhaps, we see that student politics is being reinstated in BUET through a court decision. 

As a result, a dilemma or doubt arises. On the one hand, constitutional rights, and on the other hand, a system like creating a murderer for Abrar Fahad—there is a conflict between the two. Is this immobility inviolable? Are ordinary students not free from the cycle of lack of rights or insecurity? In many other countries of the world, students enjoy constitutional rights. But they do not have to face the consequences like Abrar Fahad. It would be difficult to find student politics like ours in any other country. How is that possible? 

Students can become members of student organizations as they wish. But they cannot force other students to become members of their organizations. The ‘protocol’ of serving or anointing senior student leaders and the ‘program’ of attending when ministers and members of parliament come to campus—is this participation forced by any law or right? This is a crime. Why won't he be brought to justice if he does this? 

If the leaders of the student organization take control of the hall and become the fate of ordinary students, why won't he be punished? 

There is no conflict between constitutional rights and the demands of the guardians. The problem is that a nasty and sick student politics is being continued by talking about law, constitution and rights. When the skilled workers of this student politics take away the fundamental rights of the majority of students, the administration, law and constitution just stand by and watch. Only extreme consequences like Abrar Fahad force the administration and law to budge a little. But they don't make any radical changes. 

Try to imagine, all the residential halls of the university are run by the administration. That is, the administrators are doing their job kindly. And willing students can freely join the student organization. By joining, they organize cultural and intellectual practices. They don't force anyone to participate in their party or program. Imagine, the elections for the student parliament are being held. All organizations and independent candidates are participating there. Some are winning, some are losing. Elections are held in the same way every year. What will students talk about in the student parliament? They will talk about the quality of food in the hall, the problem of collecting certificates. They will talk about problems like session jams. They will talk about getting proper attention and service from teachers and officials. 

In the history of student politics in Bangladesh, with few exceptions, has any so-called big organization protested for the needs of students? It should also be remembered that not implementing the student parliament is synonymous with not allowing professionals to form trade unions. 

Think about the purpose of student politics from the perspective of those in power. They want to 'control' the university and the students. Then any just movement against it can be easily suppressed. Maybe they think that they will get what they want through 'guest rooms' and 'political rooms'. 

A key issue in student politics is to capitalize on the needs of those who have to stay in the halls for accommodation. The central leaders need this violence. Is this why first-year students can be taken to inhumane public rooms, tortured in guest rooms, Abrar Fahad can be beaten to death in the ‘political room’? 

Some students from every batch choose student politics as their career. The economic aspects of this career include winning various tenders, taking bribes and extortion. Other benefits include eating in the canteen for free, receiving greetings from everyone, and being the ‘destiny controller’ of everyone in the hall with a thousand times more comfort than ordinary students. Such power and prestige are psychologically attractive. Therefore, there is no doubt that the larger economic structure is an important part of this discussion. 

Most student organizations and their core groups, which depend on the sick system, need manpower to ‘movement’ on the streets. The powerful university administrators work for those in power. It is difficult to expect them to take the initiative to establish normal administrative control. 

One of the major responsibilities of post-uprising Bangladesh is to develop a culture of genuine rights-protecting student politics. And for this, the right people must be appointed to residential halls and other administrative positions. Regardless of party affiliation, any student who commits any wrongdoing or crime should be brought to administrative and legal justice. This wrongdoing includes not only beating people to death, but also interference with personal freedom and any rights.

Headline_English: Will limiting the Prime Minister's term reduce his absolute power?
Content_Enlish:
After the student uprising, there has been a strong demand for state and political reform in the country. Regular discussions and reviews are being held on various civic platforms. People with different views of society are participating there. The participation of politically conscious youth is also noticeable. The interim government has taken several steps to reform the state. A separate commission has been formed to reform the constitution and the electoral system. Among the demands for reform, one discussion is gaining prominence, the term of the Prime Minister. There has also been talk about this from the political parties. 

The way for a government to become dictatorial in Bangladesh lies within our state system. Because, in Bangladesh, the Prime Minister enjoys unlimited power, and in addition to leading the executive branch, he also has absolute dominance in the legislature. Gradually, control of the other branch, that is, the judiciary, is also coming into the hands of the Prime Minister, along with control over the party. The limitlessness of power is so immense that supporters sometimes indirectly consider the Prime Minister as powerful as an 'avatar', above mistakes and receive immense loyalty. 

Bangladeshi prime ministers have become dictators at different times. According to the Variety of Democracy Index, the Prime Minister has led the two most autocratic regimes in Bangladesh. Sheikh Hasina surpassed even the military rulers of the 1980s in the severity of her dictatorship. 

After the July mass uprising, proposals to narrow the power of the Prime Minister are being vigorously discussed. There have been proposals to share the power of the Prime Minister and the President. There has also been a proposal to limit the term of the Prime Minister to two terms. The idea of ​​a two-term prime minister in the new political settlement is not a perfect proposal. 

Two terms do not mean 10 years 
In the UK, the country where the idea of ​​a prime minister came from, the Conservative Party entered parliament in 2019 with a majority of 365 seats. Boris Johnson, who led the Conservative Party, became the Prime Minister. In 2022, Prime Minister Boris resigned due to economic mismanagement, the Partygate scandal, and the non-cooperation of influential people in the cabinet. Liz Truss was elected Prime Minister through a party election. Liz Truss also had to resign after 45 days. Rishi Sunak took over as Prime Minister in her place. 

The 1996 general election in neighboring India can also be mentioned. The President first invited the BJP, which had won 161 seats, to form the government. Atal Bihari Vajpayee took over as Prime Minister. When national and regional political parties refused to form an alliance with the BJP for ideological reasons, Atal Bihari Vajpayee had to resign after 13 days. 

Then, with the support of the Congress, the United Front of 13 parties, including the Janata Dal and the Communist Party, formed the government. H. D. Deve Gowda took charge as the first Prime Minister of the government. When Prime Minister Gowda lost the support of the Congress, I. K. Gujral took charge as the Prime Minister in early 1997. 

The Gujral government also failed to bring stability. New general elections were called in early 1998. After gaining a majority in the elections, Atal Bihari Vajpayee of the BJP returned to the Prime Minister's office. 

In Bangladesh, the two-term Prime Minister is being talked about based on the five-year term of each parliament. The main reason for this is that since we have been seeing democracy in the country, elected Prime Ministers have generally led for five years. But from the examples of the UK or India, we see that the government is less stable in a parliamentary system. As a result, a two-term Prime Minister can never actually guarantee a 10-year Prime Ministership. Perhaps the only way to ensure this is to maintain the criticized Article 70 of the Constitution. 

Certainly, the most important thing is structural reform. Completely separate the executive and legislative branches. How will the legislative branch ensure accountability if important people in the legislature serve as ministers of the executive branch? Therefore, in addition to fixing the term of the Prime Minister, the important thing is to change the power distribution system. 
Countries where the term of the Prime Minister is not fixed 
Currently, about two-thirds of the countries in the world have democracies. The largest number of people in the history of human civilization now vote to form governments or regularly express their opinions. Despite globalization in democratic systems, nation-states have democratized by keeping their own economic, social and political structures in mind. Even then, democratic countries follow some basic values ​​and apply the examples of other countries in their own countries. 

In several countries where parliamentary systems of government are in place, the term of the head of government, i.e. the Prime Minister, is not fixed. Canada, the United Kingdom, India and Australia are examples of parliamentary democracies. In these countries, the Prime Minister remains the Prime Minister for as long as he can maintain a majority in parliament. Recently, Israel passed a law in the Knesset limiting the term of office of the Prime Minister to a maximum of eight years. Discussions are underway in Malaysia, Tunisia, and Sri Lanka to specify the term of the Prime Minister. However, it has not been successfully implemented in any country with a parliamentary democracy. 

It does not take 10 years to become a dictatorship 
The latest example of a dictatorial ruler in Bangladesh is Sheikh Hasina. As Prime Minister, she took advantage of unlimited executive power to eliminate opposition parties and opinions from the very beginning. She maintained her sole dominance by favoring some and oppressing others. Using populist propaganda and nationalism, state-sponsored killings, disappearances, violence, and judicial harassment were carried out against opposition parties. A knee-jerk foreign policy and anti-national agreements were made one after another. 

As a result, this process cannot be stopped by limiting the term. If power is not decentralized through a federal structure, even if the power of the Prime Minister is reduced, there will always be an opportunity to increase this power because there is a leadership of two departments. 
In the United States, we see that the executive power of presidents has been continuously increasing. The consolidation of power during the tenure of a president has given the next president continuity. But the federal structure has been able to handle the instability of Donald Trump's transfer of power there. 

As a result, the most important thing is definitely structural reform. Completely separate the executive and legislative branches. How will the legislative branch ensure accountability if important people in the legislature serve as ministers of the executive branch? Therefore, in addition to fixing the term of the prime minister, the important thing is to change the power distribution system. 

Why is the idea of ​​a two-term prime minister coming up? 
Bangladesh follows the Westminster format, like other former British colonies. Like the king, here the head of state lives, the symbolic president; the prime minister runs the government. Again, in a federal system, the president leads both the state and the government. Most countries that follow the federal system have limited the term of the president, following the example of the United States. 

The provision of limiting the term of the president has played a relatively good role in decentralizing power, which is what makes Bangladeshi politicians or statesmen want to limit the term of the prime minister. But the idea of ​​fixing the term of the prime minister has not been implemented in any country in the world so far. As a result, we cannot say for sure its results. 

But the idea of ​​fixing the term for the head of government is very positive. If we want to establish such an idea of ​​the head of government in Bangladesh, it should be done in a presidential federal structure. 

Presidential federal state structure 
In no country in a parliamentary democracy can the people directly elect the head of government. Locally, voters elect members of parliament, and they (members of parliament) elect the head of government. As a result, just as there is no opportunity for voters to give 'active choice' in the election of the head of government, there is no opportunity to give their opinion even if the head of government changes. 

Even if a member of parliament changes parties during the term of parliament, there is no opportunity for the people to give their opinion on it. In a democratic state, there should be an opportunity for the people to give a direct mandate on who will be the head of government or head of state, and that is provided by the presidential system. 

A common idea is that a federal structure should be adopted only if there is ethnic diversity. But if we look at the debates of the US Constitutional Convention, one of the examples of the federal structure, we will understand that the purpose of creating the US federal structure was to create a balance of power, formulate policies that are more suitable for the needs of citizens in different regions, and decentralize power. These reasons make federal rule relevant for Bangladesh after the military-civilian dictatorship. 

Through regional or provincial governments, the state will be able to reach the doorsteps of citizens, and the opportunity for citizens to be represented in the state structure will increase. While in the UK, on ​​average, one member of parliament represents every one lakh people, in Bangladesh it is six and a half lakh. By increasing public representation in the federal structure, centralization of power will be prevented. 

The federal structure will reduce pressure on Dhaka, and there will be opportunities to increase citizen facilities in this city, which is already burdened by the burden of population. Education, health, infrastructure, and law enforcement activities will be transferred to the provincial government, and regional economic centers will be created. Hopefully, social and political fears will also decrease.

Headline_English: Zelensky dreams of ousting Putin from power
Content_Enlish:
A friend of mine summarized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the UN General Assembly as follows: Force Russia to the negotiating table; take back the territory Russia has seized in Ukraine; prosecute Putin and his cronies for war crimes; give Ukraine more weapons and financial aid. 

I think that’s a fair summary. But that’s not the real point of Zelensky’s speech. In fact, Zelensky is thinking that he can extract a commitment from the US-led NATO to send air power and troops to fight in Ukraine. 

That’s why Zelensky is “campaigning for Kamala Harris” in swing states like Pennsylvania. This is because he knows full well that the only way to deploy US troops in Ukraine is if Harris wins the November election. 

The question is, how can Russia be brought to the negotiating table? Providing Ukraine with a large number of long-range missiles to attack Russian territory, so that Russian infrastructure can be destroyed and civilians can be killed. 

Behind this argument lies another explanation. That is, Putin is very weak and unpopular. Russia as a state is also fragile. If the situation worsens, then the way will be opened for Putin to be removed from power. 

Zelensky, the head of Ukraine’s military intelligence service, Kyrylo Budanov, and some of their friends in the UK and the US are promoting this theory. This theory came to their mind after the plane crash in August 2023, a few days after the ‘revolt against Putin’, killed the head of the group, Yevgeny Prigozhin. 

Prigozhin was the visible leader of the group. Prigozhin, who had made a fortune illegally, was a ‘friend’ of Putin. He started his march towards Moscow with a group of disgruntled soldiers. He claimed that the Russian armed forces did not provide his forces with enough ammunition during the Battle of Bakhmut. Because of this, hundreds of soldiers of the partisan army were killed in the Battle of Bakhmut. 

Similarly, attacking deep into Russian territory means creating the risk of nuclear weapons being used by Russia. So far, it is understood that Putin will not use nuclear weapons. But the fear remains if someone more extremist comes to power in his place. 
Prigozhin's forces were welcomed in Rostov-on-Don, Russia. They were national heroes because of their victory in the Battle of Bakhmut. Putin prepared to destroy Prigozhin and his forces as they wanted to lead the army towards Moscow. But after an agreement was reached with the mediation of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Putin finally backed down. 

But Prigozhin and his men did not keep that agreement. He eventually died in a plane crash near Moscow. 

Another person who wanted to overthrow Putin was Alexei Navalny. Navalny ran for mayor of Moscow in 2013, winning 27.2 percent of the vote. Navalny was injected with the nerve agent Novichok. He received treatment outside Russia. 

Navalny said he would never return to Russia. But he eventually returned to Russia. He was arrested and held in a high-security prison. There he died. Navalny used the anti-corruption campaign as a political tool. He directly blamed Putin and other leaders for theft and looting. 

Navalny certainly had Western support behind him. Although the extent to which it reached him and how it reached him is unknown. But neither Prigozhin nor Navalny was able to remove Putin from power. 

After these two died, there is no one left in the picture who could overthrow Putin. The strange thing about Zelensky’s theory is that it was developed with the help of UK intelligence and top political leaders. It is not clear how much support the CIA and the National Security Council (NSC) provided. 

The real threat from within Russia is assassins and murderers. These include terrorist groups. They have the ability to attack important military and civilian installations in Russia, and to kill politicians and military officials. They were the ones who carried out the brutal attack on the Crocus Theater complex last March, killing 60 people. 

In some cases, some Ukrainian organizations have the ability to recruit Russian citizens to carry out terrorist attacks. Although the attacker in the Crocus attack was associated with ISIS (also known as ISIS or a Pakistan and Afghanistan-based extremist organization), the Russians claim that Ukraine was behind the attack. 

But none of them has the ability to remove the current leadership of Russia. It is also unclear who will take over Moscow if Putin is actually removed from power or dies. When you hear the gloating from some Russian politicians and popular TV personalities, you wonder what the consequences might be if they come to power! Won’t they use nuclear weapons against Ukraine, the UK and the US? 

Similarly, launching an attack deep inside Russian territory means creating the risk of Russia using nuclear weapons. So far, it is understood that Putin will not use nuclear weapons. But the fear remains if someone more extremist comes to power in his place. 

Zelensky’s dream of removing Putin or putting him on trial is nothing more than political drama. In reality, the possibility of this is zero.

Headline_English: Palestine scores 5 goals against Bangladesh
Content_Enlish:
Bangladesh's start against Palestine in the World Cup qualifiers was not particularly bad. However, after conceding the first goal, the red-green representatives seemed to give up. The result was a 5-0 defeat to Palestine for Javier Cabrera's men. 

On Thursday night, in the joint World Cup and Asian Cup qualifiers at the Jaber Al Ahmed Stadium in Kuwait, Bangladesh fell behind 2-0 due to a defensive blunder in the first half of the match. Then, the team conceded 3 more goals in the second half. This was Bangladesh's biggest defeat to Palestine. 

However, Bangladesh fought hard in the first 40 minutes. However, Bangladesh conceded two goals in the last 5 minutes of the first half and was eliminated from the match. Ode Dabagh and Shihab Kambar scored the two goals in this half. In the 43rd minute, Musab Battah's shot was saved by goalkeeper Mitul Marma on the first attempt, but Dabagh did not make a mistake in scoring with the rebound. 

Bangladesh fell behind again in added time. When the ball hit Sohel Rana's foot from the corner, Shihab Kambar easily doubled the lead. 

After coming back from the break with two goals behind, Bangladesh was disorganized from the start. Palestine took advantage of that opportunity and scored the third goal in the 49th minute to knock Bangladesh out of the match. Shihab Kumble received the corner and created space and scored the third goal for the team with a strong right-footed shot. Three minutes later, Ole Dabagh hit the net with a great shot from the corner. 

In the 72nd minute, Bangladesh's Spanish coach brought Sumon Reza, Chandan Roy and Rabiul Hasan onto the field. This did not change Bangladesh's game. On the contrary, Ode Dabagh completed his hat-trick by scoring his third goal. Towards the end, Zayed Ahmed and Shakil Hossain came on to pass the time of the game.

Headline_English: Where Bangladesh is the first in South Asia
Content_Enlish:
It used to take one and a half to two hours to reach Chittagong city by road via Shah Amanat Bridge. Now, it takes only two to two and a half minutes to reach that route via the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Tunnel built under the Karnaphuli River. This tunnel has reduced the distance from Dhaka to Chittagong by at least 40 kilometers. This shows the importance of the Bangabandhu Tunnel. It is a matter of pride that this is the first tunnel built under a river in South Asia. Bangladesh has made history here. However, this bridge was not built just like that.
