The arrested are - Joint General Secretary of Chhatra Dal Central Committee Maksudur Rahman, former Joint General Secretary of Jagannath University Branch Chhatra Dal Md. Shakhawat Hossain Khan, Kalabagan branch Chhatra Dal members Md. Robin Khan and Md. Sagar. 

Earlier, Justice Manik alleged that he was attacked by a BNP procession on the way to his car. 

Justice Manik told Samakal, "I was ambushed by a BNP procession at Fakirapul intersection. My car was also vandalized and the miscreants beat me on the forehead, nose and mouth, and the driver and gunman of the car with punches and kicks." 

Police constable Rafiqul, who was in charge of Shamsuddin Chowdhury's security, filed a case with Paltan Police Station at around 11:30 pm on Wednesday in connection with the attack. 40 to 50 unidentified people have been named as accused in the case.

Headline_English: Bus search: 7,432 grams of gold found on 12 passengers
Content_Enlish:
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Department has seized 7,432 grams of stolen gold from the custody of 12 passengers after searching two separate AC buses bound for Darshan in the capital. 

The passengers involved in the gold smuggling are Rahat Khan (33), Mohsin Al Mahmud (37), Syed Amir Hone, (34), Shamim (23), Mamun (37), Bashir Ahmed Kamal (37), Mamun Sarkar (37), Atiqur Rahman Meena (42) and Indian citizens Nabi Hossain (46), Shahzada (47) and Mohammad Imran (37). 

Customs intelligence officials said that all this gold was seized from their anus and luggage after searching them. A case was filed against the gang at the South Keraniganj Police Station on Saturday. 

Customs officials further said that based on a secret tip-off, a raid was conducted on two AC buses of Royal Paribahan and Purvasha Paribahan in Chulkutia area of ​​South Keraniganj at around 3 am on Friday under the leadership of Deputy Director Sanjida Khanam. During the search, all these gold bars were seized from the custody of 12 passengers of the transport. 

In this regard, Deputy Director of the Customs Intelligence and Investigation Department Sanjida Khanam told Samakal that this gang smuggled gold worth crores of taka by posing as passengers of AC buses. A departmental investigation is being conducted against them along with a criminal case at the police station. Those who are also involved in this will be brought under the law during the investigation.

Headline_English: The helmeted man in the militant robbery has not been identified.
Content_Enlish:
The helmeted man who was abducted from the court premises in Old Dhaka has not yet been identified. On the day of the incident, the militant, wearing a helmet, fled on a motorcycle with his two accomplices. Investigators say they have received information about three motorcycles purchased by the militants, but have not found any clear clues about the perpetrators. Although investigators have received some information about some of the people involved in the abduction, detectives are in the dark about their whereabouts. 

DIG Md. Asaduzzaman, head of the police's Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit, told Samakal that the name and identity of the helmeted man has not yet been found. Multiple teams are working to find out the details of the abduction operation. 
Meanwhile, an accused named Eid Amin surrendered to the court on Sunday in the case filed in the abduction of two death-sentenced militants. The court granted him a four-day remand after the police applied. Dhaka's Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Tofazzal Hossain gave the order yesterday. 

Court sources said that Eidi Amin surrendered to the CMM Court in Dhaka around 2 pm yesterday through his lawyer. Then the lawyer applied for his bail. The accused claimed innocence in the court. However, the court ordered him to be sent to jail instead of granting bail. When the surrender came to light, the CTTC officer applied for a 10-day remand in the militant kidnapping case. After the hearing, the court granted a four-day remand. 

Lawyer Md. Rabiul Hossain, who applied for bail for Eidi Amin, said that Eidi Amin surrendered to the court voluntarily. Now the police will investigate whether the accused is guilty or innocent. 

In Eidi Amin's remand application, the police mentioned that on November 20, 10-12 members of Ansar Al Islam were stationed at the main gate of the court. Then they attacked the police and kidnapped two militants. Arrested accused Mehdi Hasan Ami alias Rafi told the police that Ami recruited members from the Ansar Al Islam military wing on the advice of Major (dismissed) Syed Ziaul Haque Zia. Ami was in touch with the top leaders of the organization and the accused arrested in various cases. The top leaders of Ansar Al Islam informed about the militant kidnapping plan. Police claimed that Eid Amin played the role of coordinator on the day of the incident. 

Meanwhile, a constable named Noor Azad, who was injured while trying to stop the kidnapping from the Dhaka court premises, was suspended yesterday. Earlier, 5 more police members were suspended in this incident. They are Dhaka Court Inspector Matiur Rahman, SI Nahidur Rahman in-charge of the jail, ATSI Mohiuddin of the police who was in charge of taking the accused to court, Constable Shariful Hasan and Abdus Sattar. 

On November 20, their accomplices abducted Mainul Hasan Shamim and Abu Siddique Sohel by attacking and spraying chemicals on the police in a crowded court premises in Old Dhaka. At the same time, they tried to abduct two other militants named Abdus Sabur and Arafat Rahman but failed. After this incident, the CTTC arrested Mehedi Hasan Ami alias Rafi. He is currently on remand. However, it has not been possible to arrest the two abducted militants yet.

Headline_English: Sometimes a journalist, sometimes a detective, drug dealing behind the scenes
Content_Enlish:
Mukul Hossain alias Maqbul Ahmed. Introduces himself as a crime reporter for Narayanganj newspaper Dainik Matribhumi Khabar. Sometimes he disguises himself as an intelligence officer. Behind these identities, he mainly runs a drug business. He used to bring consignments of ganja in private cars from different areas of Comilla and Narayanganj and sell them in different areas of the capital with three associates. His main associate Md. Faisal is the personal driver of an official of Bangladesh Bank. He used the car to transport drugs on holidays or during his free time. 

RAB-3 gave this information on Tuesday after arresting four members of a gang involved in drug trafficking. The other two arrested are Abdul Shahin alias Noman Hossain and Al-Amin Hossain. The operation was conducted in Bangshal area of ​​the capital on Monday night. During this time, three bags filled with 50 kg of ganja, specially hidden in the back of a private car, were recovered. 

A press conference was organized at the RAB-3 office in Tikatuli in the capital this afternoon to provide details. In it, RAB-3 commander Lieutenant Colonel Arif Mohiuddin Ahmed said that Mukul, the mastermind of the drug ring, worked as a driver for various transports for 25 years. In 2016, he got involved in the drug trade in the hope of earning a lot of money illegally. Although he was employed in various transports, he was repeatedly fired due to his involvement in drugs. Most recently, from June this year, he adopted a new strategy. He took a job as a driver for the Daily Matribhumi. In this, he could easily continue smuggling drugs using a 'journalist' sticker. But the authorities fired him two months ago after learning about his misdeeds. At that time, he secretly brought a microphone with the newspaper's logo. Using it, he was driving a vehicle carrying drugs, introducing himself as a senior crime reporter. In addition, he has established a syndicate for selling drugs by posing as a journalist. He has multiple drug cases against him, including a murder case for causing the death of a man in a road accident in 2008. He has been arrested in multiple cases and has also spent time in jail. 

RAB said that the arrested Faisal is the personal driver of a bank official. He had been regularly transporting large quantities of drugs using a car with a 'Financial Intelligence Unit' sticker used by the owner of the car.

Headline_English: ACC chargesheet against Mirza Abbas and his wife
Content_Enlish:
ACC sources said that the assets worth Tk 20 crore 74 lakh 47 thousand 828 in the name of Mrs. Afroza Abbas were actually acquired from illegal sources with the help and assistance of her husband Mirza Abbas Uddin Ahmed. Since Mirza Abbas was a member of parliament, mayor and minister, the accused (husband and wife) acquired assets worth Tk 20 crore 74 lakh 47 thousand 828 in the name of Afroza Abbas through bribery and corruption and later through various illegal means until August 16, 2007 and concealed the information about the assets. In accordance with the sanction order of the Anti-Corruption Commission, the investigating officer submitted the charge sheet to the court on Tuesday based on the charge sheet number 66 of the Anti-Corruption Commission, Integrated District Office, Dhaka-1. 

ACC Assistant Director Md. Salahuddin filed the case with Shahjahanpur Police Station in the capital on January 7, 2019 as the plaintiff.

Headline_English: Convicted accused in Bagerhat triple murder case arrested
Content_Enlish:
Rapid Action Battalion (RAB)-3 has arrested Subrata Kumar Paltu (35), a life-sentenced accused in the controversial triple murder case in Daivajhati, Morelganj, Bagerhat. He was arrested from the Sadar area of ​​Gazipur district on Tuesday night. 

Arrested Subrata Kumar Paltu is the son of Nirmal Pal of Daivajhati. 

RAB-3 commander Lt. Col. Arif Mohiuddin Ahmed confirmed this information. 

In October 2018, Daivajhati Union Awami League General Secretary Ansar Ali Dihidar, his wife Manju Begum and Jubo League leader Shukur Sheikh were hacked, beaten and shot and injured. They died while undergoing treatment. On December 4, the court sentenced 14 people to life imprisonment in the case filed in that incident. Khulna Divisional Speedy Trial Tribunal Judge Md. Nazrul Islam Howlader announced the verdict.

Headline_English: Sheikh Hasina assassination attempt: Escaped executioner Pintu arrested
Content_Enlish:
RAB has arrested a fugitive accused who was sentenced to death in the 1994 bombing and shooting case of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's train at Pabna's Ishwardi railway station. 

The accused, named Zakaria Pintu, was arrested from Cox's Bazar on Saturday night, said ASP ANM Imran Khan, assistant director of RAB's Legal and Media Wing. 

He said, "The arrested Pintu was sentenced to death in the attempt to murder case by attacking and shooting a train carrying Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 1994 28 years ago and is a fugitive accused who has been convicted in several cases including arms cases and is under warrant." 

He said that detailed information on this matter will be released at a press conference in Dhaka on Sunday. 

Zakaria Pintu, former general secretary of Ishwardi Municipality BNP, has been on the run since the beginning of the case. Eight others have been sentenced to death and 25 have been sentenced to life imprisonment in the case. 

Prime Minister and Awami League President Sheikh Hasina was the opposition leader in 1994. At that time, the BNP government was in power, with Prime Minister Khaleda Zia. 

On September 23 of that year, Awami League President Sheikh Hasina held a train march as part of her party program. She was supposed to stop at Ishwardi Station on her way to Syedpur by train from Khulna and hold a road rally. When the train reached Ishwardi Station, bullets and bombs were fired at Sheikh Hasina's coach. However, today's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina survived the incident. 

In the attack, Railway Police OC Nazrul Islam filed a case, naming seven people and showing more than a hundred others as 'unknown' accused. 

But the investigation into the case was stalled during the then BNP government. When the Awami League formed the government in 1996, the police were ordered to reinvestigate. After the investigation, the Criminal Investigation Department of the police filed a charge sheet in the case, accusing 52 people, including leaders and activists of Ishwardi's BNP, Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal. Later, the court framed charges and started the trial of the accused. 

Pabna Additional Sessions Judge Judge Rostam Ali sentenced nine BNP leaders and activists to death in the case on July 3, 2019. In addition, 25 people were sentenced to life imprisonment and 13 others to 10 years in prison. 

Apart from Pintu, the remaining nine defendants on death row are: BNP central committee member and former mayor of Ishwardi Municipality Moklesur Rahman, Pabna district BNP Liberation War Affairs Secretary AKM Aktaruzzaman Akter, former president of Ishwardi Municipality Jubo Dal Mustafa Noor Alam Shyamal, local BNP leader Mahbubul Rahman Palash, Rezaul Karim alias Shahin, Shamsul Alam, Azizur Rahman VP Shahin and Shahidul Islam Atal. 

These eight were sent to prison at the time of the verdict. Five of the 52 defendants in the case died at different times during the trial.

Headline_English: Over 100 'slanderous' IDs identified on Facebook
Content_Enlish:
In 2021, a man named Faiz Uddin went live on Facebook for the first time from a puja mandap on the banks of the Nanuar Dighi in Comilla. From that live, the rumours started spreading in various directions. In a video of a crowd of excited people moving towards the mandap with sticks, one person can be heard saying, 'Live, live' several times. 

In the same year, Sahin Uddin was hacked to death in front of his children in Pallabi in the capital. There was also an incident where it was circulated as the video of Jaton Saha's murder in Noakhali. In that incident, RAB arrested Ratan Shil from Chittagong and Ruma Sarkar, a teacher at Badrunnesa College in Dhaka. 

According to the law enforcement agencies, the purpose of these incidents was to send a negative message to the world about Bangladesh. An anti-national group is trying to create instability in the country by spreading rumors in cyberspace. 

The concerned said that more than a hundred such IDs have already been identified by the intelligence agency. To prevent them from spreading 'propaganda' in the future, the Digital Security Agency, Information and Communication Technology Division has started activities. A recommendation has been made to the BTRC to block these in accordance with Section 8(1) and (3) of the Digital Security Act-2018. 

Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal told Samakal that the BTRC has been asked to stop propaganda on social media. The agency is maintaining contact with the Facebook authorities. Facebook's Singapore representatives have returned from Bangladesh. They will implement this. Action is being taken against those who spread these things on social media, including Facebook. 

He also said that people are now gradually realizing that rumors are being deliberately spread on Facebook to destabilize the country. That is why people do not trust Facebook now either. People want to know the information and logic before believing. If someone is aggrieved and wants justice for propaganda, then legal action will definitely be taken. 

Sources say that in Bangladesh, incidents of incitement to extremism using social media, including Facebook, are increasing. Facebook is used to spread religious issues and rumors quickly and create violence. 

Relevant sources say that political rumors are more common before and after national or local elections. However, the incidence of spreading rumors on religious issues has been increasing recently. In 2017, 5 percent of the rumors circulated were religious, while in 2020, this rate rose to 40 percent. Again, 82 percent of extremists are vocal on social media. Incidents of incitement to extremism have increased at different times. In that case, social media is a big area for inciting socially educated youth or students. A large portion remains active in extremist activities. 

In 2016, the Dawalillah Forum, a platform for extremists, had 550 members. Three years later, this number has increased to about 4,000. Not only Muslims, but also followers of other religions are practicing extremism using social media. Some pages are being run on social media from outside the country. It is known that the number of Bangladeshi followers of this page is not very small.

Headline_English: Accused in North South embezzlement case missing, family claims
Content_Enlish:
Amin Moha. Hilali, the managing director of Ashalaya Housing from Uttara in the capital, has gone missing, his family has claimed. His brother Rafiqul Islam Hilali has filed a general diary (GD) with Uttara West Police Station in this incident. 

Rafiqul Islam claimed that Amin Hilali did not return after leaving his house in Sector 10, Uttara at 8 pm on Friday. Family members could not contact him. 

Amin Moha. Hilali is an accused in a case of embezzlement related to the purchase of land for the North South University campus. He is accused of embezzling Tk 303.82 crore by showing an additional expenditure of Tk 303 crore for the purchase of the campus land. The Anti-Corruption Commission filed a case against him on May 5 in this incident. Amin Moha. Hilali is the sixth accused in the case filed against six people, including four trustees of the university. 

Rafiqul Islam said, Amin Hilali left his house in Sector 11 of Uttara at 8 pm to go to his house in Sector 13. As soon as he left, he spoke to his driver Jamal Uddin. Then he told the driver to go towards the office and to contact him after 15 minutes. Since then, Amin Hilali has not been found. His mobile phone is also switched off. 

In this regard, Uttara Paschim Police Station Officer-in-Charge Shah Md. Akhtaruzzaman Ilyas said, A GD has been filed stating that Amin Hilali is missing. No information has been found about his whereabouts. The matter is being investigated.

Headline_English: Student politics: A pillar of democracy, or a tool of power?
Content_Enlish:
In the political history of Bangladesh, student politics was once a driving force of change. The role of students in every historical mass movement was immense. But over time, student politics has moved away from idealism and gradually become entangled in party politics. Today, it has become just a young wing of the mainstream political party, where loyalty to the individual and the party is gaining more importance than ideology. As a result, violence, tender manipulation, extortion and the tendency to suppress ordinary students are increasing. 

The character of student politics was different before and after independence. Students played a strong role in the 1952 language movement, the 1969 mass uprising, the 1971 liberation war and the 1990 anti-dictatorship movement. These movements were based on just demands and the students maintained morality and ideological consciousness. But student politics after the 1990s gradually fell into the trap of partisanship. The dominance of the student organizations of the ruling party is seen in educational institutions, while the student organizations of the opposition party are almost inactive. As a result, the development of free thought in universities and colleges is hindered, and participation in politics means establishing links with power. The mass uprising of 2024 has dealt a major blow against the dominance of party politics. The participation of the younger generation and students in this uprising was noticeable, which clearly indicates that they are looking for new alternatives outside the conventional party politics. But the question remains, will this change be permanent? What will the new political settlement be like? Or how can student politics be restructured? 

Currently, student politics in most universities means seizing and controlling power. The main goal of student organizations is to protect the interests of political parties and suppress the opposition. As a result, violence has increased in educational institutions, the space for free thought has narrowed, and the development of political awareness among ordinary students is being hindered. Party loyalty is now considered a qualification for leadership, where talented and qualified students do not get the opportunity to lead. The 2024 mass uprising has added a new dimension to Bangladeshi politics. It was mainly a youth-led mass uprising, where distrust in conventional party politics became clear. Along with the general public, school, college, madrasa, and university students actively participated in the movement. This made it clear that young people want change and are looking for a new trend outside the conventional political structure. 

Looking at student politics in other countries of the world, it is seen that it is very different from Bangladesh. In universities in the United States and Europe, student politics mainly works to protect the rights of students, where party politics does not have direct control. Although student politics in India is party-centered like in Bangladesh, democratic practices are quite active there and students can directly elect their representatives. In those countries, student unions and clubs play a role in the academic, social, and political development of students. In China, student politics is practically banned. Only organizations approved by the Communist Party can conduct activities. On the other hand, student politics in Bangladesh has now become a tool for protecting party interests, where principle-based politics is absent. As a result, it is used to protect the power of a specific group instead of the welfare of students. 

If student politics can be brought back to a healthy course in Bangladesh, it will strengthen the foundation of democracy. For this, several structural changes are necessary. First, the influence of party politics in educational institutions must be reduced and independent student organizations must be developed. Second, regular student parliament elections must be reintroduced, so that students can directly elect their representatives. Third, strict measures must be taken against violent politics, so that student organizations truly work to protect the interests of students. 
Strong student politics is very important in the development of democracy. But if it is used only for party interests, the future leadership will become weak and self-serving. The popular aspirations of the July mass uprising will fade. 
The participation of the masses in the mass uprising of ’24 has basically shown us that the people no longer trust the existing political structure. If this can usher in political reforms in the long term, it has the potential to create a new trend in student politics. Now is the time to restructure student politics and instill genuine democratic practices to ensure that it is. Instead of party-based partisanship, principled leadership can be the foundation for building a future Bangladesh.

Headline_English: Reforms can come even at the age of voters
Content_Enlish:
Although the minimum voting age has been 18 for a long time, there has been talk of lowering it recently. The issue has been under discussion since January this year when the chief advisor suggested that it should be raised to 17. The National Citizens Party (NCP), a student group that led the 24-day uprising, recently proposed lowering the voting age from 18 to 16. At the same time, the NCP has also proposed lowering the minimum age to stand for election from 25 to 23. The party argues that if the voting age is lowered, the generation in whose role the uprising was mainly successful will also participate in the voting field. 

It is true that in most countries of the world, including our neighboring countries, the initial voting age is 18 years. However, voting can be done at 17 years, or even at 16 years in some places. In Latin America, Austria and even Germany, citizens vote at the age of 16. However, in Bangladesh, I personally think that the voting age can be raised to 17 without lowering it by two years. This will also attract a large number of students who participated in the uprising. Those who were 16 years old in July-August 2024, and even those who were 15 years and five-six months old; if the election is held in December or later, they will also be able to vote at the age of 17. However, to make them voters, it will be necessary to update the voter list anew just before the election. We know that this list has already been updated in January, based on the age of 18. 

Citizens express their political opinions through voting. The age and maturity of the person are important in expressing this opinion. The rationale for setting the age of 18 for voting is that at this age, people have the power of judgment and intelligence. There is less risk of being influenced by others. Education is also an important issue here. If they do not drop out, higher secondary education is completed within 18 years. The same reasoning behind the reason for raising the voting age to 18 can now be raised to 17 years. That is, the maturity that used to come in a person at 18 for various reasons is now possible at 17 years. Due to internet technology, a person's eyes and ears are opened earlier. Due to the environment and increase in education rate, political awareness is born in a person at the age of 16-17. Therefore, the voting age can be raised to 17. What impact can 17 have on the next election? Voters can increase by 5 percent. This will add half a crore new voters. According to the draft voter list, the country's current voter population is 123.6 million. Since a large part of the country's population is young, even reducing it by one year can make a big difference. The latest census conducted in 2023 shows that 57 percent of the total population is young. Of these, the number of people between the ages of 15 and 19 is high. However, the slight complication in raising this age to 17 needs to be resolved first. Internationally, the maximum age of a child is considered 18 years. According to Bangladeshi law, a child is a child up to 18 years. This age of a child must be reduced. Plans to reduce the age of a child have been underway since 2022. The government's Law and Order Committee had proposed reducing this age. Their argument was that many people are seen getting involved in serious crimes at the age of 14-15. That means, not everyone will remain a child or a minor or immature until they are 18. However, the proposal was not accepted at that time due to controversy. 

Since determining the age of voters is an election-related matter, the Election Commission will take this decision. But political consensus is needed in this case. The discussion that took place after the chief advisor's statement on this issue in January showed that BNP has rejected the issue of reducing the age. On the other hand, Jamaat-e-Islami has spoken in favor of it. However, the Reform Commission formed by the interim government has not recommended reducing the voting age. While BNP has recommended raising the minimum age to contest elections to 21 years, it has taken a stand in favor of keeping it at 25 years. On the other hand, the National Citizen Party has suggested raising it to 23 years. 

In light of reality and the need of the time, change is the law of nature. The minimum voting age of 18 years has been the general rule, but reform can come here too. Change can come in the age to contest elections. Just because it has been around for a long time, it is not the case that we should cling to it. Our youth have achieved a lot at a young age. The story of the mass uprising of 24 is also about the youth. Since they are the majority and an important part of the country, it is important to give priority to their education, training and employment at the state level.

Headline_English: Is the United States going to become North Korea?
Content_Enlish:
There are a handful of 'pariah' states in the world today. States that are largely isolated. North Korea, Afghanistan, Belarus, etc. are at the top of these. Is the United States also going to become a pariah state? The way President Trump, who came to power just three months ago, is running the United States, the fear of the world's most powerful country becoming isolated cannot be ruled out. Trump has pushed long-time allies and neighbors Canada and Mexico away on various issues since coming to power. He has torn apart the trusted friendship of countries on both sides of the Atlantic. Most recently, on April 2, he imposed excessive taxes on products from 184 countries of the world, a move that angered the enemies and allies of the United States equally. 

Trump took a swipe at Mexico and Canada immediately after taking office as president on January 20 of this year. On the day he took office in his second term, he initiated the implementation of the 'America First' policy by renaming the 'Gulf of Mexico', which was named after its neighbor, the 'Gulf of America'; the gulf is located west of the US state of Florida and south of the states of Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas. Trump did not stop at this step; on March 4, he imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on the two large neighbors of the United States to the north and south, Canada and Mexico. In addition, Trump faced strong reactions from the country's citizens by suggesting that Canada become the 51st state of the United States. 

Meanwhile, immediately after winning the presidential election, Trump announced the establishment of US control over the Panama Canal. He alleged that Panama was collecting excessive fees from US ships and other vessels. Angry at Trump's announcement, Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino made it clear that every square meter of this canal and the surrounding area belongs to his country; not to the United States. Just two months after Trump took office, Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison, the owner of the important trade route, agreed to sell a majority stake in two Panama Canal ports to US investment firm BlackRock for $22.8 billion. The Trump administration has adopted a tough immigration policy for the United States since coming to power. President Trump has distanced himself from European leaders by seeking to buy Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark located in the Arctic or North Ocean region, and by making controversial comments about NATO and the war in Ukraine. 

Meanwhile, President Trump has sparked global criticism by announcing a plan to take control of the war-torn Gaza Strip and relocate about two million Gaza residents to Egypt and Jordan in order to rebuild it. Arab leaders have expressed anger at his bizarre plan and publicly criticized it. A rare unity can be seen among Arab leaders in opposition to Trump's proposal. In addition, the US administration has distanced itself from Middle Eastern countries over the threat of bombing Iran's nuclear facilities. After Trump announced the bombing of Iran on March 30, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait made it clear to the United States that they would not allow US warplanes to use their airspace or territory to attack Iran. Even US aircraft involved in the attack on Iran will not be able to take fuel from these countries. This decision by the Persian Gulf countries is being seen as a major setback for the Trump administration. 
Since Trump took office, US relations with South Africa, the dominant country on the African continent, have also been deteriorating. In February, the US stopped aid to South Africa, accusing it of supporting Palestine and 'unjust racial discrimination' against white Africans. The US president alleged that the South African government's new law included provisions for taking land from whites. On March 15, South African Ambassador Ibrahim Rasul was declared 'persona non grata' and expelled from the United States. As the saying goes, if you throw a stone, you get stoned. Trump is not discerning between friends and enemies in his 'unorthodox' or non-conformist way of running the country. It remains to be seen how much of a difference there will be between the United States and North Korea if Trump does not change gears in his second term.

Headline_English: Dhaka-Delhi relations should be based on respect and equality
Content_Enlish:
The bilateral meeting held on Friday between Bangladesh's Chief Advisor Professor Dr. Muhammad Yunus and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the BIMSTEC summit in Bangkok, Thailand, is undoubtedly significant. Bangladesh-India relations are not the same as before after the coup last July. We see that now the relationship is moving forward at some levels, while at others, especially at the political level, the relationship has fallen into a kind of inertia. I think that inertia has been overcome through this meeting. Our Chief Advisor Dr. Yunus and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi got the opportunity to discuss and discuss through this meeting. Through this communication at the highest level of the two countries, mutual expectations and a way to take the relationship further forward have been created. One thing has come to the fore through this meeting - although there are differences of opinion, discussions are needed. They spoke from that understanding. It did not seem that the positions of the two countries have changed since then. However, an opportunity has been created to move forward. The relationship should be taken forward in accordance with the decision that will be taken in the context of the discussions between the two heads of government at the political level.

It cannot be denied that Bangladesh and India, as the closest neighboring countries, are dependent on each other in many ways. However, it is important to move from the kind of relationship that existed between the two countries in the past to a respectful and equal relationship as neighbors. In this regard, a kind of expectation has been created, but in principle, the matter must be worked on to make that expectation a reality. For this, a vision must be created, a framework must be created in light of that, and there must be coordination. Along with this, public support is also important. Now we have expectations. 
Chief Advisor Dr. Yunus himself has also said that relations with India will be based on fairness and equality. We see this as a reflection of public expectations. But to implement this, we have to do internal work. As I have said about the vision. This vision must be 'consistent'. 

Our multidimensional relationship with India; where there is trade, border, security, common river. It is important whether we are able to coordinate between the ministries concerned in managing these issues. After the July 24 coup, it is important to take creative, sustainable and efficient initiatives to implement the public expectations that have been created among our people in their relations with India, that is, the principles of equality and fairness. 
Before this meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, we saw that Chief Advisor Professor Dr. Muhammad Yunus visited China. Due to the reality of Bangladesh, we have to work with everyone. Just like India's relations with Bangladesh; there are also relations with China, the United States, and the European Union. We have to work with all our bilateral and multilateral partners in our interests. India has a kind of rivalry with China. That is a matter of their relations. We have nothing to see in their differences. Earlier, we saw that relations with India were very one-sided; in that sense, there was no normal relationship. Now, in the reality of Bangladesh, it can be said that relations are moving towards normality. Therefore, as a normal thing, we can maintain cooperative relations with everyone in the interests of the country. 

The Rohingya crisis is our big problem. Since China's role in dealing with the Rohingya crisis is important, Bangladesh has had a kind of trilateral communication with China on the issue for a long time. During the Chief Advisor's visit to Beijing, China also gave a hint that it would cooperate on the Rohingya issue. They said that we should also work with Myanmar on the Rohingya issue. The Rohingya crisis is a complex issue. The situation in Myanmar has changed in the past seven to eight years. When the Rohingya came to Bangladesh after being persecuted in 2017, there was a kind of democratic rule there; Aung San Suu Kyi's party was in power. After that, after the military coup in Myanmar in 2021, various armed groups rebelled. As part of that, we have seen that the armed group Arakan Army has recently occupied a large part of Rakhine, where the Rohingya are inhabited. That is why the repatriation of the Rohingya has become more complicated. If we want to move forward on this issue, we have to be strategic and also look at the humanitarian aspect. 
Narendra Modi's meeting with Muhammad Yunus focused on the BIMSTEC summit. BIMSTEC, established in 1997, is working as a platform for regional cooperation; of which India is also an important member. Bangladesh has been given the responsibility of chairing this regional cooperation alliance of the Bay of Bengal countries for the next two years. Thai Prime Minister Phatthana Shinawatra has handed over the responsibility to Dr. Muhammad Yunus. It remains to be seen how successfully the goals and objectives of BIMSTEC will move forward under the leadership of Bangladesh. If we can do something good in BIMSTEC with the help of regional countries, people will undoubtedly remember it. 

Anyway, coming to the Yunus-Modi meeting. A lot was said there. From India's side, expectations of stability, liberal policies, and an inclusive society have been expressed. Democratic expectations are also important. In the last one and a half decades, dictatorship has emerged in its absence. The current government is also working to maintain stability after the changes of 24. We want to build a sustainable society. Our other partners also expect everyone to strengthen the institutions and create a sustainable governance structure through democratic elections. Those whom the people will elect by voting should be accountable to the people. That should be the priority now. We have to work in that way. I believe that the stronger Bangladesh is able to form a responsible government based on the consent of the people and the more peaceful the system is established in the social structure, the more we will be able to build relations with everyone, including India, based on respect and equality.

Headline_English: What are the chances of getting an H-1B visa in the United States?
Content_Enlish:
The annual H-1B visa application season in the United States began on April 1. Past experience shows that more than 20,000 employers can get permission to sponsor one or more foreign nationals in their businesses. A total of 85,000 H-1B visas are issued each year. These are mainly allocated to specialist professionals, many of whom are graduates of US educational institutions. Of these, 65,000 visas are open to all and 20,000 visas are reserved for foreigners with a master's degree or higher from a US university. Bangladeshis can also take advantage of this opportunity. 

In January 2025, there were more than 175 million people working in the United States, so these highly skilled workers make up less than half of the workforce. All of them are paid at or above market rates. The 2022 report shows that the average salary of H-1B workers increased by 52 percent between 2003 and 2021. At the same time, the average salary of all US workers increased by 39 percent. In other words, H-1B workers are not cheap substitute workers, but do not contribute to the decline in the salaries of US workers. 

H-1B visa holders contribute to the U.S. economy and have helped drive innovation in nearly every industry. They are doctors, technologists, engineers, professors, accountants, financial analysts, researchers, geneticists, quantum physicists, data scientists, and more. Many of these skilled workers are at the forefront of innovative technologies like artificial intelligence, which is critical to maintaining U.S. leadership in information technology. 

In fact, in an executive order dated January 23, the Trump administration acknowledged that artificial intelligence technology will be critical to the future of the United States and that with the right policies, the country can maintain its global leadership. In addition, studies have consistently shown that the H-1B program has had a positive impact on labor demand in the United States. Two recent studies have found that as the number of H-1B workers in a given occupation increases, the unemployment rate in that occupation decreases. 

Another study found that restrictions on H-1B visas and high rejection rates have forced many U.S. multinational companies to increase employment overseas and reduce the number of jobs at home. A 2022 study found that industries with a high H-1B workforce also have higher patent applications. A large portion of these patents come from states and industries with a high H-1B workforce. 

Indian nationals receive the highest number of H-1B visas. This is why it is often a topic of bilateral negotiations between the US and India, but the visa is granted to citizens of almost all countries. Unfortunately, the H-1B visa program comes under fire every year. Critics say it takes away jobs from US citizens and reduces wages, even though in reality there are shortages and high wages in key occupational categories. 

Data suggests that H-1B workers are highly skilled, earn market-rate (and sometimes above) wages, and are people who support not only their employers, but also their clients and the US economy. It is currently believed that both the Trump administration and Congress may try to impose new restrictions on the H-1B program. Senators Chuck Grassley (Republican-Iowa) and Dick Durbin (Democrat-Illinois), who sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee, have advocated for tighter controls on the program for decades. 

President Donald Trump sought to significantly limit the program during his first term—by giving priority to higher-paid workers, increasing salaries, and increasing fees. Although federal courts blocked most of the proposed changes, the 2017 “Buy American, Hire American” executive order increased scrutiny of H-1B applications. The denial rate reached 20 percent and the number of requests for more information increased in 2018, increasing uncertainty and costs for businesses. 

Earlier this year, there was a significant shift in the way the H-1B program was communicated. But it takes a deeper dive to understand what it really means. After Trump adviser Elon Musk praised the program, Trump said, “I’m a supporter of the H-1B. I’ve used it many times. It’s a great program.” But in his first term, he made the entire process one-sided by rewriting the rules to favor certain businesses. The businesses, hospitals, schools, and other institutions that rely on the program are spread across nearly every state. If the proposed restrictions go into effect, they could create a long-term shortage of technologists, innovative engineers, science and language teachers, and local doctors. 

The United States is now struggling to attract highly skilled workers in a competitive global market. If the country cannot attract and retain skilled foreign workers, they will go elsewhere. The current “skills shortage” in the U.S. workforce is expected to worsen in the coming years. The H-1B program helps retain and grow jobs in the United States. The Trump administration and Congress should consider the consequences if they decide to change the program. The H-1B visa program is a highly effective mechanism for attracting and retaining skilled labor, while also protecting the interests of American workers.

Headline_English: Greenhouse gases and virtual water challenges
Content_Enlish:
Greenhouse gas emissions are the main cause of global climate change. Excessive emissions of gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, etc. are causing global warming – which is a serious threat to Bangladesh. In Bangladesh, greenhouse gas emissions are caused by nitrous oxide from industry and energy, the transport sector, the use of chemical fertilizers in agriculture, and methane from waste disposal and landfills. 

In the context of Bangladesh, Professor Muhammad Yunus's goal of achieving zero net carbon emissions is to achieve a goal that will reduce Bangladesh's contribution to the increase in the amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted into the atmosphere. This goal is particularly important for Bangladesh, as the country is at extreme environmental risk. A large part of this densely populated and low-lying country is less than one meter above sea level, which makes Bangladesh vulnerable to the effects of climate change, especially sea level rise and devastating floods. Despite contributing only 0.3 percent to global carbon emissions, Bangladesh is one of the first and most serious victims of climate change. Experts predict that by 2050, sea level rise could permanently submerge about 17 percent of Bangladesh, displacing millions of people. Here are some examples and possible steps for Bangladesh to achieve net zero carbon emissions: The renewable energy initiative of Grameen Shakti Samajik Bishara Limited has reduced dependence on fossil fuels by providing solar home systems to over 1.8 million households in rural Bangladesh, where the national grid does not reach. It has ensured clean, affordable and reliable energy for families, schools and businesses. Improved stoves, biogas plants provide a sustainable energy solution by reducing the need to cut down trees for fuel. Environmentally threatening projects, such as the government’s plan to build a coal-fired power plant at Rampal near the Sundarbans, run counter to the net zero carbon goal and raise environmental concerns. 

Adopting clean energy solutions, i.e. prioritizing and investing in renewable energy sources such as solar, wind and sustainable hydropower. Harnessing the hydropower potential of neighboring countries such as Nepal through regional cooperation. The international community can play a key role by providing Bangladesh with cutting-edge clean energy technologies and financial support, which will help the country reduce its dependence on polluting energy sources. Encouraging green entrepreneurship. Increasing the use of clean technologies and practices at the local level by supporting and expanding eco-friendly social businesses such as rural energy. Avoiding environmentally harmful projects. Projects like the Rampal coal-fired power plant should be reconsidered and avoided, which pose a threat to the environment and long-term sustainable development. Technological leapfrogging. As a developing country, Bangladesh has the opportunity to directly adopt more efficient and cleaner alternatives by avoiding old and polluting technologies. Focusing on sustainable practices. Measures such as promoting sustainable agricultural policies, preventing deforestation and managing waste will help reduce the overall environmental impact and move towards zero net carbon. Achieving zero net carbon emissions is not only an environmental imperative for Bangladesh, but also important for its long-term economic stability and the well-being of its people. 

The concept of virtual water, known as hidden water in products, was popularized by J. A. Allan, a British geographer and professor at King’s College London. Virtual water can be seen as the water ‘embedded’ in a product. It is an indicator that indicates the amount of freshwater that evaporates or is contaminated during the production and transportation of a product. For example, it takes about 2,500 liters of water to produce one kilogram of rice, or about 10,000 liters of water to make a piece of cloth. The question is, how? This water is not directly visible, but is transferred ‘virtually’ through the product. Water availability is a major challenge for Bangladesh and climate change has made it even more important. We should be aware of the hidden transfer of water through our export products. Virtual water trade can be an important policy tool for Bangladesh to address water crisis and climate change. 
With globalization, Bangladesh is exporting water-intensive products (such as jute, leather, ready-made garments, agricultural products), which is causing a huge loss of virtual water. 8,500 liters of water are used to produce a pair of leather shoes, which disappear from the country through exports. 

Bangladesh needs some plans and strategies to address the virtual water problem. The import-export balance of virtual water must be ensured by calculating the amount of water used in the production and trade of products. If Bangladesh produces crops that use less water (such as corn) instead of wheat, then it is possible to maintain the virtual water balance. Citizens also have an important role to play in addressing the virtual water problem. The import of virtual water must be reduced by using locally produced products. Buy local products instead of foreign fruits and vegetables. This will cost more water due to transportation. However, the government itself must raise awareness about virtual water. Organize workshops in schools and colleges, where students will learn about preventing water waste and the concept of virtual water.

The government should make citizens aware and formulate some policies that will force citizens to comply. The following are the things that the government should do: Make it mandatory to mention water and carbon footprint on every product package so that citizens can make informed decisions; Provide subsidies on organic and eco-friendly products and increase taxes on chemical fertilizers and plastic products; Formulate policies for water reuse and energy conservation in homes and offices; Develop policies to improve public transport systems and reduce the use of private cars; Provide instructions from the government to reduce water and carbon footprint and motivate citizens to comply with them. 

Finally, it can be said that Bangladesh needs to adopt a sustainable development strategy to deal with the negative effects of globalization. It is possible to prevent environmental disasters through greenhouse gas control and proper management of virtual water. For this, the coordinated efforts of the government, private sector and civil society are essential. In this regard, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus, the father of the three-zero earth theory, is a suitable leader to establish Bangladesh as a global environmental leader.

Headline_English: Why the situation in Gaza is more serious than in Ukraine
Content_Enlish:
The two most horrific conflicts going on around the world are the ‘Ukraine-Russia War’ and the ‘Gaza War’. These two wars have become a reflection of brutality due to different locations and geopolitical reasons. However, while the first one is balanced in comparative military standards, the unilateral attack and the clang of deadly weapons in the second one are changing all calculations. The biggest question is, why is the number of casualties in the Gaza war so much higher than in the Ukraine war that started 19 and a half months ago, and why are the residents of Gaza unable to go to safe shelter? On the other hand, how have the Ukrainians been able to move? 

The international politics and humanitarian crises of the 21st century have raised another question before us. Do all wars make us cry in the same way? The images of the two battlefields of Ukraine and Gaza make it clear that the standards of global reaction and sympathy are not the same. On the one hand, there is a tide of sympathy for human rights, democracy and regional sovereignty surrounding the Ukraine war; on the other hand, the hellish massacre in Gaza is evaluated as a mere ‘security issue’. 

A comparative review of the two wars shows that the number of civilian casualties in Gaza is much higher than in Ukraine. The main victims are women and children in the besieged territory. According to UNICEF and the World Health Organization, more than half of the deaths in Gaza are children. On the other hand, the ratio of military to civilian casualties in Ukraine is relatively balanced. The civilian casualty rate is relatively low in most areas of Ukraine. This is because people have been evacuated from there in advance. European countries have welcomed Ukrainian refugees. On the other hand, there is no such thing as a safe haven in Gaza. Refugee camps, hospitals, schools – all types of facilities are constantly targeted by attacks. Israel controls and prohibits borders, electricity, water, medicine supplies – everything. 

At the beginning of the Ukraine war, millions of people moved westward. Countries including Poland, Hungary, and Germany received them with reverence. In contrast, Gaza is known as an 'open air prison', which is blocked by air, land and sea. Even after the war began, no humanitarian corridor has been created through which unarmed people can move to a safe place. 
The Western world (NATO, EU and the United States) has condemned the attack on Ukraine. A large amount of military, economic and humanitarian aid continues to be provided to Kiev. Most media outlets have portrayed Ukrainian fighters as national heroes. On the other hand, the Western powers continue to clearly support Israel in the barbaric attack on Gaza. For political reasons, the people of Gaza are often shown as a security threat in the Western media, along with Hamas. 

The number of deaths in the Gaza war, which began on October 7, 2023, has exceeded 50,000. The Russia-Ukraine war that began on February 24, 2022, has lasted for more than three years, but according to the United Nations, 10,000-15,000 people have been killed in Ukraine so far. Gaza is a narrow and enclosed coastal territory of about 365 square kilometers. With barbed wire fences, military posts and a blockade in place along both borders, civilians have no way out. At the same time, both air and land routes are controlled. 
It was much easier for Ukrainian citizens to leave the attack area. But the residents of Gaza are actually like prisoners trapped under the open sky. Women and children in Gaza are forced to remain there under the indiscriminate airstrikes of the occupying Israelis. To leave Gaza, visas, safe corridors and permits from the regime are required, which are almost impossible for them to obtain. This has turned the Gazans into a helpless and besieged population, cut off from the outside world. 

On the other hand, the political guardian of the Ukrainians, President Volodymyr Zelensky, did not use children and women as human shields. He did not try to blame his opponent for human rights violations, this politically immature Zelensky. The Kiev government and the European Union jointly arranged for the safe evacuation of Ukrainian women and children. 
The fundamental difference between the massacre in Gaza and the war in Ukraine is the right of ordinary people to evacuate and the type of weapons. While the citizens of Ukraine had the support of a state and international structure, there was no such respite for the people of Gaza. Gaza has now become a completely besieged city of death, where people are constantly being wounded not only by aerial bombing but also by the silence of parts of the Muslim world and the West.

Headline_English: New situation in Europe with the end of the old world order
Content_Enlish:
Across Europe, US President Donald Trump is seen as a troublemaker with the inverted Midas touch. That is, whatever he touches, the consequences tend to be worse. Yet, despite his outdated views on most matters, he is the perfect embodiment of our age. 

In 2021, I wrote a book called The Age of Untouchability. In it, I argued that hyper-connectivity requires a rethinking of the rules of international relations. I saw that the institutions and systems that used to unite us were being used as tools. Trade, the internet, energy sources, supply chains, migration, critical raw materials, and cutting-edge technology could be used to exert geopolitical influence and inflict suffering. 
In this new world, I saw that the boundaries between war and peace were blurred. We thought we had entered a golden age of peace after the Cold War. We were wrong. In reality, violence was everywhere. But it came with sanctions, export and energy controls, electoral interference, and immigration as tools. All of this led to the formal war being halted. 

Just a few months after my book was published, Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. US President Joe Biden, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Olaf Scholz tried to restore the old order in response to Russian aggression. Especially since Trump’s reelection, it has become clear that we need a new way of looking at the world. The Trump administration has thrown together all the old rules and made them liquid. There are no clear distinctions left between war and peace, allies and enemies, national and private interests, or left and right. Trump has launched a trade war against the rest of the world. He is also trying to plunder Ukraine’s mineral resources and threatening the territorial integrity of Greenland and Panama. The old rules of international order are no longer valid. 

Unfortunately, it is not just a matter of chaos. There would be some basic consensus on what ‘order’ looks like in this case. There is none here. Thinking about international order has been completely overshadowed by events. For years, governments have muddied the existing crisis of hyper-connectivity and interdependence, from the 2008 market crash to the Syrian refugee crisis and the pandemic. Policymakers have also been unable to win the trust of citizens. Many have resorted to emergency and exceptional measures. There are now so many exceptions that international rules look like Swiss cheese with holes. It has become an exception-based order rather than a rule-based order. 
Trump understood this. He played into the public’s frustration with the elites. These elites pretended to have all the answers. But they failed to deliver on their promises. Americans are playing into the hands of many around the world who have always believed that the liberal international order was a fraud. It is much like the Holy Roman Empire, which was not holy, not Roman, not even an empire. The liberal international system cannot be called liberal after the atrocities at Abu Ghraib or Guantanamo Bay. It cannot be called international when many parts of the world are immersed in civil war. It cannot even be called a discipline because of this failure. 

Mark Leonard: Director of the European Council on Foreign Relations; European Council on Foreign Relations 
Translated by Iftekharul Islam

Headline_English: Methane gas can also be a driving force for a green economy
Content_Enlish:
Climate change is no longer just a scary prediction of the future; it is our current reality. One of the most harmful greenhouse gases responsible for global warming is methane. A large part of it comes from the stomachs of our most familiar livestock, namely cows, goats and buffaloes. Yes, you read that right. These hardy animals constantly emit huge amounts of methane gas through their belching, breathing and waste during their digestive process. Globally, about 100 million tons of methane are emitted from such livestock every year, which has a global warming potential of about 80 times that of carbon dioxide. The methane produced in this way accounts for about 16 percent of the world's total greenhouse gas emissions. 

The question may arise, what is Bangladesh's role in this global situation? Surprisingly, our country's livestock sector emits about 30 million tons of methane equivalent to carbon dioxide every year, which is about 1 percent of global emissions. From a financial perspective, this loss amounts to about 3 billion US dollars per year. It is conceivable that our economy is facing such huge losses just from the digestion process of cows! 

This is where modern science shows hope. Studies have shown that it is possible to reduce these emissions by up to 50 percent through the right technology and management. While the price of one ton of carbon reduction according to Australia's 'ACCU Scheme' is 35 Australian dollars, in the open market this price can be up to 100 dollars. Accordingly, if Bangladesh is able to reduce methane emissions by half, then this 'green economy' will potentially have a market value of about 1.5 billion dollars! 
A novel discovery is playing an important role in making the potential a reality. Dr. Abed Chowdhury, a scientist at the Australian research institute 'Lom Bio', and his research team have recently discovered a special type of natural fungus, which is capable of reducing methane production by up to 90 percent in the digestion process of cattle. Most surprisingly, the fungus works without any genetic modification and does not have an adverse effect on the health of the animal. When mixed as a feed additive in animal feed, methane emissions are virtually stopped. 

This research was published in the journal 'Biotechnology Reports' in March 2025. A new company, 'Rome Agriculture', has been formed based on this discovery. The company is developing a model in which farmers themselves can produce this fungus in small units, much like a microbrewery. This will reduce costs and make it easier to spread the technology from farm to farm. The results at the experimental stage are promising. If it is proven effective in real farm management, it could be a breakthrough in protecting the climate. 

The idea that livestock gas only means a threat to the climate is starting to change today. With the right technology and science-based management, methane gas can be the main driving force of a green economy. This is like a silent revolution. A single drop of fungus in animal feed is becoming one of the tools to save the world from global warming. 
This innovation has shown us that through the proper application of science and technology, we can not only protect the planet, but also benefit economically. It is hoped that this fungal-based feed additive will spread to farms worldwide in the next few years. Every such discovery gives us courage – with science in hand, we can still dream of a healthy, green and beautiful world.

Headline_English: The key reform is to replace the relationship between the people and the state.
Content_Enlish:
For almost a decade and a half, the independence and accountability of the state's democratic institutions have been in jeopardy. Sheikh Hasina and her bureaucracy have effectively established an authoritarian regime by controlling the constitutional structure, democratic institutions and administrative system of the state for a long time. Instead of independence and accountability, loyalty to power, repression and political bias have become the mainstay everywhere. As a result, the relationship between the state and the people has broken down; the people have become alienated from the state and distrustful. In this context, the main political and social task now is to re-establish the relationship between the state and the people. This relationship must not only be reformed in words, but replaced with a real structure - where the people will be the real owners of the state and the state will be the servant of the people. The most important thing for this change is a free, fair, competitive and participatory national election - which will be the only means of legitimate transfer of power and the first step in rebuilding democratic relations. 

The relationship between the state and the people is the fundamental basis of the state system. If this relationship is not based on mutual trust, accountability and participation, the state becomes an instrument of monopolistic autocracy – where the people are no longer the owners, but rather the subjects. Then the relationship through which the state is supposed to be accountable to the will and welfare of the people turns into a repressive and authoritarian exercise of power. In this reality, the need has arisen not only to reconstruct, but to replace the relationship between the state and the people on a completely new basis – this is the most fundamental and essential reform today. 

The idea of ​​​​this replacement occupies an important place in political and moral philosophy. In philosophical analysis, the relationship between the state and the people is fundamentally related to the questions of freedom, justice, authority and the legitimacy of power. It needs to be founded on a political and moral framework – which legitimizes the state on the basis of the consent, rights and dignity of the people. 

After independence, the people of Bangladesh expected that the state would fulfill their dreams. But as a result of long military rule, one-party politics, partisanship in the judiciary, administrative bias, and mismanagement of the electoral system, the state has gradually become isolated from the people. Power has been concentrated in the hands of political and economic elites, rather than being vested in the representatives of the people. As a result, the state system has become a bureaucratic-party machine without stakeholders – where policymaking and resource allocation are external to the people. This isolation has created political distrust, electoral aversion, and a crisis of democracy. 

This crisis has been exacerbated by a series of illegal, one-sided vote thefts, voter fraud, and sham elections. After the caretaker government system was abolished through the 15th Amendment to the Constitution in 2011, the country’s electoral system has lost credibility. In the January 5, 2014 election, ruling party candidates won 153 seats unopposed, which is unprecedented in history. The 2018 11th National Assembly election was called the ‘night vote’ – where ballot boxes were filled in advance. The 12th parliamentary election of 2024 was a complete ‘dummy election’, the outcome of which was predetermined. The opposition parties and the people boycotted the election and accused the government of deceiving the people. Then the final resistance of the people arose and on August 5, 2024, the autocratic Awami League government fell through a student-public uprising, Sheikh Hasina was forced to leave the country and move to India. 

In this context, BNP Acting Chairman Tarique Rahman presented a new state philosophy, the main basis of which is an inclusive democratic system; returning the state to the people and re-establishing democracy. According to him, ‘I think, as a political activist, I can say that I have achieved something only when I can return the voting rights of the people of Bangladesh.’ This is not just a political commitment, but a reflection of a new state ideology. 

In such a situation, some talk about reform of the Election Commission, impartiality of the administration or anti-corruption measures. However, these efforts are only partial and symptomatic. Because, if the entire structure is disconnected from the will of the people, it is not possible to bring about the desired change by changing only the parts of the structure. 

The way in which different countries of the world have redefined the people-state relationship in response to their political crises and questions of state legitimacy is instructive for Bangladesh. For example, in Germany, the ‘Basic Law’ was formulated in 1949 to re-establish democracy after the Nazi period. In this, the people were specifically mentioned in the constitution as the sole source of state power and the administration, judiciary and executive were brought into a structure of accountability to the people. 

The event of Nepal abolishing the monarchy and transitioning to a republic in 2008 is important. There, the centralized structure of state power was broken, the constitution was written with the active participation of the people, and the state was transformed into a service-giving structure formed with the consent of the people. These countries have proven that democracy, stability and public trust can only be achieved by establishing a new relationship between the state and the people. 

In Bangladesh, a national consensus-based interim political agreement is needed to build a relationship between the state and the people – where the people will be the center of the state structure. A framework is needed – where the constitution will be popular, the administration will be impartial, the judiciary will be independent and policy-making will be based on public participation. In order to build a state that is transparent, accountable and humane for the people, public hearings, citizen participation in policy review, public consultation in budget formulation and political accountability must be ensured. The state is not just a collection of laws and institutions; it is a living social relationship, the life of which is the people. 

Until the relationship between the state and the people is re-established, the legitimacy of the government will not be achieved through elections, and distrust and deprivation will increase in society. Therefore, now is the time not only to repair the relationship, but to completely restructure the relationship through inclusive democratic and political transformation – where the state will be of the people and the people will be the sovereign owners of the state. Elected public representatives will be forced to be accountable to the people. Because, we know that hegemony in dictatorship or fascism cannot be stopped with bookish reforms or textbook laws. 

The foundation of democracy is elections. National elections are very important; they are one of the ways to restore democracy, establish the political rights of the people, and ensure the participation of the people in the rule of the people. Without elections, no government can be a true representative of the people. If power changes outside of elections, it gives rise to an illegitimate regime - which undermines political stability and the rights of the people. 

Therefore, there is a dire need now to organize a free, fair, and acceptable national election. The government should immediately announce the specific date and roadmap for the election. The people are ready - they want to see their future, rights, and dignity reflected through the ballot. In this reality, progress in state reform will be meaningful only when it is legitimized through elections. Without elections, there can be no effective basis for reform. Taking the initiative of national elections to protect the promise of good governance and ensure the re-establishment of democracy has now become an inevitable demand of the time.

Headline_English: What kind of budget do you need for the garment industry?
Content_Enlish:
The ready-made garment sector is the lifeblood of Bangladesh's economy. This sector, which is the largest private employment generator, is currently facing various local and international challenges. The industry is particularly under pressure from US counter-tariffs, India's transshipment ban, high bank interest rates, wage increases, and frequent increases in gas and electricity prices. 

Bangladesh is moving from an LDC (least developed country) to a developing country in 2026. At that time, the garment industry, which contributed 84 percent to exports, will lose many international trade benefits, which will directly hit the industry's competitiveness. According to an Asian Development Bank (ADB) report, Bangladesh's exports may decline by 5.5 to 14 percent after its transition from a least developed country. The main reason for this decline will be the loss of duty-free market benefits (such as GSP). 

In this context, this year's budget is very important for the garment industry. Among the policy measures that we are expecting from the government at the moment, the corporate tax rate for the garment industry will be maintained at 12 percent. The withholding tax applicable against exports will be reduced to 0.50 percent as before and will be maintained for 5 years. 

Although it is said to be 12 percent, in reality we pay more corporate tax. The government collects advance tax from entrepreneurs, although that money is not refundable. Currently, we have to pay withholding tax at the rate of 1 percent against our exports. Initially, it was 0.25 percent, then it was reduced to 0.50 percent. From here, it was reduced again to 0.60 percent. Then, in a leap, it was reduced to 1 percent, which reduces the capacity of the industry. 

Our industry remains dependent on cotton. However, the demand for non-cotton products among buyers in the global apparel market as sustainable and environmentally friendly clothing is constantly increasing. Currently, 52 percent of the global apparel trade is non-cotton. Our non-cotton clothing exports are only 26 percent. Efforts to utilize our huge potential in non-cotton products continue. The government's policy support will accelerate this effort. We believe that there will be special incentives for non-cotton garment exports in the budget to encourage investment and exports in this sector and maintain competitiveness. This will increase employment. There will be vast opportunities in the related service sector. Above all, the amount of direct and indirect revenue collection of the government will increase. 

BGMEA is working on the implementation of the Four R concept - Reuse, Reduce, Recycle, Recover to gift a clean world to the next generation. Our factories are reducing waste through the use of new technologies and process upgradation. Every year, about 500,000 tons of jute is produced from the textile and garment sector. We export a part of it, through which we earn about $ 400 million annually. If we recycle the jute, we will be able to produce products worth about $ 5 billion, which will bring our domestic growth. Therefore, all processes, products and services related to the recycling industry need to be kept free from customs duties and VAT. Investors will be attracted to this sector. 

Due to the significant increase in the cost of living, workers are disoriented with their families. If rationing and fair shop are provided for them, at least to some extent, that crisis will be reduced. They will work with satisfaction. 

The expected steps to reduce business operating costs to maintain the competitiveness of the garment industry can be – 1. Making 100% VAT-free various products and services of the 100% export-oriented ready-made garment industry. 2. To make the factories modern, safe, risk-free, environment-friendly and cost-effective, allowing the import of some fire-fighting equipment and materials that are not on the list duty-free/concessional. 3. Providing duty concessions on the import of all equipment for solar PV systems for setting up environment-friendly industries and saving energy. 

If import-export activities are not made easier, we will lose customers. Because this business is fashion and time-based. If you are late for one day, you will face problems. If you are late for two days, the order is canceled. Simplification of rules and regulations is necessary to quickly clear the imported goods and reduce the export time. HS codes need to be simplified to eliminate complications during the clearance of imported goods in bond management.

Headline_English: Why are the agreed reforms not being implemented?
Content_Enlish:
Two major events are expected to happen on the day the article is published. One. The National Budget will be presented by the Finance Advisor. Two. The second round of dialogue between political parties and the National Consensus Commission will begin. Some ideas regarding the interim government's budget have already been made public. There is a lot of doubt about what will ultimately be achieved in the dialogue on state reforms. 

In most cases, political consensus was not established in the first round of dialogue on what the Consensus Commission calls 'fundamental reforms'. Despite holding multiple meetings to establish a consensus, no results were achieved. Among the parties in the field, Jamaat and NCP appear to be close, but BNP's differences are clear in this regard. Their views also differ on the means of implementing the reform proposals. A 'charter' in this regard is expected to be published by July. 

Initiatives for state reforms were, of course, taken during the first and eleventh governments. Most of them were abandoned during the elected government. This is our experience with reforms! 
In the final stage of the July mass uprising, demands for state reforms were raised along with the resignation of the government. When the interim government was formed under the leadership of Muhammad Yunus, they also emphasized reforms. The government moved forward with the agenda of justice, reform, and elections. Initially, there was little objection to it. However, after a few months, differences began to grow among the main political parties regarding whether elections should be held 'early' or late. 
It is worth noting that within two months of the formation of the government, the army chief told Reuters that they would support the government in completing reforms and elections within one to one and a half years. The role of the army was positive in the last part of the popular uprising. They also played an important role in forming the government. Therefore, everyone took the army chief's statement seriously. After that, the chief advisor also said that elections would be held after the reforms by December this year or June next year. Political dialogue is underway on the formation of the reform commission and its recommendations in this context. 

In the meantime, two sides in politics have gradually become clear. One side wants elections by December. The other side has no objection to elections in June or later. There is also talk that a section of the second party wants to keep the Yunus government for a long time. However, this does not seem to be realistic. Muhammad Yunus has also clearly said that they will not be in power even for a day after June 2026. In the meantime, the demand for elections by December has been strengthened. The army chief himself has expressed his clear intention in this regard. Recently, the acting chairman of BNP has also demanded that elections be held by December. The chief advisor even wanted to resign over this. After all that has happened, the question of specifying a deadline for elections instead of reforms seems to be more present. 

How interested is the government in reforms? This question may arise from the news that the government is delaying the implementation of 121 recommendations that are 'immediately implementable' in a Samakal report. The government separated those recommendations from the Reform Commission report and said that there is no need for political dialogue on them. There is also consensus in the public sphere. But there is no news of progress in the implementation of the recommendations even after two and a half months. Initiatives and arrangements are also absent.
