Even then, why don't the two main political parties want to make a solution to end the violence and complications? In 1996, the BNP did not want a caretaker government, arguing that the law was not in the constitution. After the one-sided elections in 1996, the BNP, led by the Awami League, added the caretaker law to the constitution in the face of public demand. In 2006, the caretaker government in the hands of the BNP became controversial, and it was later canceled. Now the ruling party, the Awami League, is saying that the caretaker government's law is not in the constitution. They forget that in 1996, the Awami League launched a strong mass movement because the BNP said the same thing. The caretaker government law is added to the constitution. 

Democracy and democratic institutions in this country are not strong. Therefore, elections are not fair and free under any government party. There is no example of fair national elections under the government party. That is why the provision of the caretaker government during the election was added to the constitution. Its relevance is the same today. Elections are for this country and the people of the country. The last two elections were not participatory without the participation of the two main political parties, and they will not be in the future either. The reality of One Eleven certainly raises big questions about the relevance of the caretaker government, but there is no opportunity to hold a single election by canceling it. The neutral caretaker government during the election will hold fair elections and step down from its responsibilities – this decision is currently the responsibility of the two main political parties of the country to make logical and practical. However, since the leaders of the opposition party are under arrest, under house arrest, and in hiding, it is now the responsibility of the government party to resolve the chaotic equation of politics.

Headline_English: Those who are not graceful are not lovable.
Content_Enlish:
A railway lineman had just gotten married. He was talking to the Shalids, and when he raised his hand, the train stopped. The Shalids rolled their eyes and said, "Babbah!" 

Dulabhai, in compliance with the Shalids' demands, took them to show them his immense power. He raised a red flag with his hand. The train stopped. Suddenly, the train stopped and the passengers got off in a huff and puff and realized that a newly married lineman had stopped the train to show the Shalids his power. Hearing everything, the passengers caught the lineman and beat him up. 

In response to the Shalids' question, Dulabhai replied, "I showed my power. Won't they show their power?" The Shalids knew that the common people also have a little power in their hands. 

The question may be, do the people of Bangladesh have a way to show such power? In the past, sometimes even a street sweeper could see an MP's reckless car and say, "We will see your power during the election, come then." Is there that opportunity now? 

Intellectuals say – No, no. 

Our ministers and MPs get angry from time to time. So writing about them is quite risky now. The situation is a bit like Germany in the 1960s. 

East German Stalinist leader Walter Ulbricht and leftist journalist Willy Brandt meet. Ulbricht asks – ‘What are you busy with now.’ 

Brandt replies, ‘I collect jokes about myself. And you?’ 

Ulbricht replies, ‘I collect information about people who make jokes about me!’ 

In Bangladesh, it is not acceptable to tell jokes like this. Here you will find a group of nationalists who will say that you are defaming the government or the party. At the same time, they will claim that they do not interfere with freedom of expression. There are such nationalists in the opposition parties too. As a result, leaders and workers of both parties are like a conch shell for intellectuals. 

An American and a Russian are arguing about which country has more freedom of speech. The American says, “I will go straight to the White House and shout ‘Down with Joe Biden!’ Nothing bad will happen to me.” The Russian gentleman replies, “I will go all the way to the Kremlin. And I have the freedom to shout ‘Down with Joe Biden!’ Nothing will happen to me either.” 

These stories are universal across countries. When satirists feel threatened in their own country, they change the name of the country. Reporters Without Borders says that press freedom is gradually deteriorating in Bangladesh. However, this is not a matter of concern for Bengalis at all. The reason is that we have to think so much about oil, rice, pulses, and many other things that the thought of running a family seems to be our biggest problem. Freedom of speech is a luxury for hungry people. 

The only Bangladeshi politician went to conquer the Himalayas with 9 European politicians. Ten adventurers fell into great danger while climbing the mountain. The rope to climb up has become very weak. If one person is not let go of the rope, everyone will fall together. No one is willing to let go of the rope. The Bangladeshi minister saw that the situation was not very convenient. They will force him to let go of the rope. 

Then he started a speech to everyone, why the lives of great scholars like them are much more valuable than the lives of insignificant people like him and how blessed he feels to be able to sacrifice his life for these 9 European politicians. The scholars became emotional during his speech. Everyone clapped their hands with emotion. After that, only he survived. The real thing in politics is to survive yourself. Sometimes it happens that others will not let you survive, they will want to overthrow you. Then you may get angry, what is wrong with them trying to overthrow the government! 

This is basically a European story. In Europe and America, making fun of MPs, ministers and heads of state is considered a high level of humor. But that doesn't happen in our country! Yet, even a few years ago, cartoons were drawn in newspapers about the Prime Minister, and there was criticism. Namasya cartoonist Rafiqunnabi (Ranbi) drew cartoons, Shishir Bhattacharya drew cartoons, Manik Ratan drew cartoons. At that time, a lot of political humor was written in newspapers. People enjoyed it. Politicians from all countries enjoy this joy. I don't know what the leaders think in our country, but even if you write a funny joke on Facebook, you read hundreds of offensive comments under it now. Are we becoming more intolerant day by day? 

Cartoons in newspapers are funny but also a matter of branding. Cartoons or humor are written about someone who is extremely popular. Politically conscious Bengali politicians have probably forgotten the A, B, C of politics. Who will teach them the liberality of politics, the humor of politics? There is no school to learn politics. 

A young man came to learn politics by hand. The leader took him to the roof of his house and said, "Jump."

The young man said, ‘What are you talking about! If you jump from here, you will be killed.’ 

‘There are fake leaves below. Nothing will happen. Jump.’ 

The young man believed the leader’s words and jumped. As usual, he fell limp with broken arms and legs. 

The leader came down. 

‘You said nothing would happen.’ 

The leader said, ‘This is your first lesson. Never trust any leader in politics.’ 

The young man learned politics. 

He might stand in the next election too! We common people are also preparing for the election. Elections are a matter of joy for us. Every time we vote, believe, and get lucky. We forget all this again. Forgetting everything, we laugh and have fun.

Headline_English: China's influence on Myanmar's rebels
Content_Enlish:
On January 12 this year, China announced that it had brokered a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and three ethnic groups known as the Three Brotherhood Alliance. However, the agreement applies only to the northern Shan State. The region is where opponents of Myanmar’s military government have made the most progress in the ongoing civil war. According to media reports, the alliance has captured one town in Shan State every three days since it launched a new operation against the Myanmar army on October 27 last year. 

In fact, the agreement signed under Beijing’s mediation aims to protect China’s interests rather than bring an elusive peace to Myanmar. Beijing is very concerned about the threat of the conflict in Myanmar spilling over into China. Myanmar’s volatile northern region has become a haven for Chinese criminal gangs, who smuggle people and drugs and are involved in online crime from across the border. The ongoing conflict has already blocked trade routes and put the safety of Chinese citizens in border towns at risk. A statement from the Chinese Foreign Ministry said both sides in the conflict “committed to not harm Chinese nationals working on projects in Myanmar and Chinese nationals living along the border.” 

However, the ceasefire is unlikely to fulfill China’s expectations. In fact, a large-scale resistance movement has developed across Myanmar, which the generals have failed to suppress. The recent ceasefire has not stopped violence, and threats against China remain. A day after the ceasefire was announced, the Arakan Army, a member of the Three Brotherhood Alliance, captured the town of Paletwa in western Myanmar, on the border with India. Meanwhile, the Kachin Independence Army shot down a Chinese-made fighter jet. This was the third such attack in just a few weeks. In addition, the Myanmar army lost control of one of its division headquarters in an area where there is a ceasefire. 

As the civil war in Myanmar escalates, China has been caught off guard. In the past, China has been able to exert influence in Myanmar politics. But the country has been thrown into turmoil by the emergence of new resistance groups in the civil war. Most members of the People’s Defense Force are younger than the state troops and have refused to sign any agreements with the Myanmar military, despite Beijing’s requests. These new groups have established strategic and logistical links beyond Myanmar’s borders, allowing them to smuggle weapons and other goods. 

As a result, China’s influence in Myanmar has been limited. This has been possible because the resistance has spread across most of Myanmar’s fighting, which has made China’s efforts to end the conflict ineffective. 

In fact, the main goal of the nations in the Three Brotherhood Alliance is to defeat the Myanmar army. Therefore, a ceasefire agreement with the army cannot ensure the safety of Chinese citizens across the Myanmar border. The army has not been able to show its ability to deal with criminal gangs in Shan State before the civil war. As a result, the region will become a threat to China in addition to the war. The civil war has already affected China’s relations with the ethnic groups in northern Myanmar. Beijing’s ability to influence Myanmar’s ethnic resistance groups is limited. However, another reason Beijing-brokered ceasefires have not worked is that Beijing also has limitations in providing any support to the military government. 
China’s patience with the Myanmar military is running out. It has failed to crack down on criminal gangs targeting Chinese citizens. Criminal gangs have smuggled about 120,000 people into Myanmar to run online scams. China’s position on Myanmar is to support the traditional ruler. Before the 2021 coup, Beijing also had good relations with the democratic government led by Aung San Suu Kyi. Since then, corruption and ungovernability in Myanmar’s border towns have threatened the security of Chinese citizens. This has also eroded China’s trust in the military. 

The Myanmar military’s failure to bring stability to northern Myanmar means that China is in a difficult situation. The Myanmar military will have to maintain the status quo with them as they remain in power, but their inability to suppress resistance movements will pose a threat to China.

Headline_English: The scars of war on nature
Content_Enlish:
Ukraine is burning. 700 days of aggression have passed. Gaza is burning. 100 days of burning have passed. Yemen's Houthi-dominated areas have begun to tremble under the relentless bombardment. Since these regions are in the Middle East or on the Black Sea coast, perhaps the sound of bombs, the cries of the wounded, or the wails of the bereaved do not reach the well-decorated living rooms of the Western world. The atmosphere of the sophisticated closed media rooms of the so-called developed countries of Asia may be able to stop this urge at its luxurious doors. 

However, people in this modern society forget that the effects of war ammunition and heavy or chemical weapons are not confined only to the place or time of application. This blazing fire belongs to Ukraine; this countless death to Gaza; this endless destruction began in Yemen, but this undeniable act of environmental degradation belongs to all of us. Its impact leaves a far-reaching global imprint, from which it may take centuries to recover. Who will make the warlord or the aggressor superpower realize this? 

There has been much discussion on military theory, especially the nature of war versus its character. Prussian Carl von Clausewitz is considered one of the most influential military theorists in history. According to him, the nature of war never changes. People go to war motivated by the desire to gain land, economic oppression, cultural aggression, or sometimes spirituality. The addiction to conquest and the determination to resist it characterize the nature of war. From the Akkadian or Assyrian wars to the Liberation War of Bangladesh or the nature of the current conflict has therefore revolved around the cycle of conquest and resistance. 

However, the nature of war changes and has changed. Tactics, weapons used, technology – all these change with time. The Assyrian wars in Mesopotamia, the conflicts during the expansion of the Roman or Ottoman empires, and the invasions of Genghis Khan's conquerors did not use ammunition. They fought with open swords in frontal battles. Although explosives were invented during the Chinese Tang Dynasty in the 9th century, it was only used in cannonballs in the 14th century. This was followed by modern weapons, devastating nuclear weapons, and the latest state-of-the-art hydrogen bombs and chemical weapons. Therefore, the war team was forced to change its tactics. However, this transformation of war-innovation has certainly moved in one direction. That is, to be immersed in the competition to stay at greater and greater distances, cause maximum damage in less time, and wreak havoc over a wide area. The results are also clear. Loss of life is an inescapable fact of war. Along with this, the level of negative impact on land, water, air, livestock, and vegetation; that is, the level of negative impact on the natural environment has increased geometrically. We all have to live with the reality that any modern war can spread its harmful effects beyond the borders of our own countries and occupied territories. 

The environmental impact of war is extensive. From preparation to the production and supply of weapons, especially during war, non-renewable resources are used extensively. This includes metals needed to make weapons (such as titanium or nickel used in missiles) and fossil fuels needed to operate weapons and deploy troops. A research article published on January 5, 2024, says that during the 60-day Gaza war, Israel emitted the equivalent of burning 150,000 tons of coal; Hamas only emitted 300 tons. 

It should be remembered that one ton of coal can be burned to produce 2,200 kilowatt-hours of energy. In other words, the energy consumed in the Gaza offensive could have met the energy needs of 50,000 Israelis or 750,000 Bangladeshis for a year! Modern warfare is therefore accelerating global warming without hesitation. Even if the helpless cries of children in Gaza cannot be heard in New York or Miami, the United States, they too have no way to escape the global impact of global warming. However, countries like Bangladesh are in the crosshairs of global warming! That is our fear. 

In addition, due to changing war tactics, it has become possible to cause damage to large areas in a short time. This tactic was first used during the First and Second World Wars. At that time, just as city buildings could be demolished in an instant by dropping shells from bomber planes, thousands of hectares of fields could be burned to ashes in an instant. The destruction of buildings pollutes the air. The smokestacks created by dust cause extensive physical damage to the surviving wounded and unfortunate war victims. On the other hand, land damage is undoubtedly economic and inevitably environmental. During the Second Indochina War, which lasted from the 1960s to the 1970s, the United States sprayed about 170 kg of the chemical dioxin in South Vietnam to damage arable land. This destroyed one million hectares of cropland. That land remained uncultivable for the next two decades. 

Even more profound damage to arable land was caused by the use of nuclear weapons in World War II. The famous American military scientist Arthur Westing showed in an article that if a 20-kiloton atomic bomb was dropped (Nagasaki's 'Fat Man' was 23 kilotons), all the trees on 500 hectares of land would be wiped out; no vegetation would remain on 43 hectares of land. In addition, all the livestock on 1700 hectares of land would die. 

We know about such widespread and long-term effects of nuclear weapons. The bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 and the Chernobyl nuclear accident in 1986 have posed an extreme health risk to the people of those areas for decades. They have made cropland uninhabitable. They have poisoned livestock. It is as if the world will never see the use of these deadly weapons again. 

Although the nature of war has not changed, its character has changed. Although the roar of world war has subsided, the frequency of local conflicts has increased. This new form of war continues to disrupt the environment through the use of weapons, extensive damage to infrastructure, and even the use of chemical substances. No one is immune to its effects. While the fires are burning in Gaza, Ukraine, and Yemen, it is imperative to extinguish them. It is imperative not only for humanity, but also for the global environment to strengthen this anti-war tone.

Headline_English: When technology is a threat to women
Content_Enlish:
On December 22, a news report in Samakal showed that four or five young men had stripped a young woman naked and made the video go viral after not receiving the money she was owed. These news reports are no longer isolated incidents. However, what was said in another news report in Samakal on December 29 – that the parlor authorities had installed a hidden camera in the service room of the Women's World Beauty Parlor in the capital and recorded sensitive videos of at least 3,000 women in six months – is something that really surprises us. Where women from many influential families in society use the service, how can such heinous crimes be committed day after day? 

With the development of science and technology, there have been major changes in the lives of the people of this country. Technology is now within everyone's reach. From boys to old people, from women to men – everyone has a smartphone. Thanks to excessive digital technology, women are able to make their lives more enjoyable than before; it may seem so at first glance. But are women really better off in society because of digital technology? Rather, violence against women in society has increased violently than before. Starting from home to workplace, women are constantly being subjected to torture at every stage. 

News of rape and sexual harassment from the media all over the world is getting stuck in our eyes every moment. These videos are going viral every moment in our country too. These viral videos are no longer just about sharing information. For many, these videos are quite enjoyable. Because a kind of rapist and pleasure-seeking eyes are constantly being created thanks to social media. In the online world, it seems like hunters are constantly lurking in the hope of prey. Helpless girls are the victims of these. 

Thanks to digital technology, women are taking attractive selfies with expensive smartphones. Again, those cameras are secretly capturing their private or secret moments by creating uglier and uglier reels. Lovers are making their lovers' naked scenes viral, pictures and videos of private moments are coming out of the bedroom. Many teenagers to middle-aged women are committing suicide for fear of these videos going viral. There is a booming business of creating ugly reels and spreading them on social media. 

In the capitalist world, technology has become such an easily available product that it is easy to make a profit from it. Its first and main victim is women. No matter how much women's participation in the economic and social spheres of society increases, in the current era, digital technology has not been able to provide women with the same level of security as it has given them the opportunity to enjoy life; rather, it is failing in many cases. Because cybercrime is running very fast; it is two steps ahead of the law or administration. Despite the creation of new laws, dangerous cybercriminals are getting away with it due to the lax implementation of these so-called laws. Digital technology has made women's bodies much more accessible, from which it is easy to make a profit. So, are women really better off in the era of digital technological development? Or has their personal security in society become more restricted than before - we need to think about this issue.

Headline_English: Ways to fulfill our collective dreams
Content_Enlish:
A major change can be observed in our past and present lifestyle in terms of festivals, celebrations, and formalities. By adding new festivals to our social life, we are being pushed towards consumerism; which can easily be identified as capitalist activity. 

Such festivals have been associated with our national life, the existence of which we have not seen in the past. The fuss about December 31 was not so intense before and after independence. It was limited to a very limited scope and unostentatious arrangements and formalities. Now, on that night, the disorder goes to an unimaginable level; as if December 31 means unlimited arbitrariness, free freedom of disorder. 
When the new year comes, we expect to fulfill unfulfilled dreams and aspirations along with exchanging greetings. But in reality, even though the year comes and goes as usual, no change occurs in our collective life. Since that distant adolescence, I have seen that we are going around in the same circle. Far from being positive, the experience of collective life has gradually increased in the negative. As if this is the fate of our collective life. 

Our ancestors used to praise the British era by comparing it with the Pakistan era. They used to talk about the happy memories of the past in unbelievable stories of buying and selling for money. However, the infatuation with which Bengali Muslims believed in the creation of Pakistan and the two-nation theory from a part of Pakistan; it collapsed soon after the establishment of Pakistan. 

After hearing the accounts of the failures of the elders due to the change of regime, I thought that good times would surely return at the end of the Pakistan era. Therefore, Bengali Muslims did not waste much time in discovering their roots. The 23-year Pakistan era ended in the armed liberation war; through defeating the Pakistani occupying forces. But even in independent Bangladesh, the dreams and aspirations of the countrymen remain unfulfilled. The people of the country have not achieved independence and empowerment – ​​this is a fact. Power and independence are under the control and control of a few. In terms of the situation, the majority of the people are nothing other than the subjects of the ruling class of the country. Neither Pakistan of the Hindu-Muslim religious division nor Bangladesh of the Bengali-Non-Bengali division – could fulfill the dreams and aspirations of the people of this country. This is certainly disappointing. But what is the underlying reason for this? 

The main reason for this is inequality. Inevitably, class discrimination. Contrary to the establishment of equality of rights and opportunities for all citizens, the extremely discriminatory system persists and gradually strengthens. Special classes, those who are small in number, have become rich with the opportunity to become rich. Since this class discrimination has intensified, it has penetrated even into the family. Whether or not there is a relationship between siblings and relatives has also become determined on the basis of class position. 

There has been and is a lot of analysis and historical research on the 23 years of Pakistan's rule. But compared to that, we have not been able to do enough analysis and judgment on the Bangladesh period. We have only heaved a sigh of relief at the achievement of independence. The number of those who stood by the nation at the crossroads of the nation and gave the nation the direction of liberation can now be counted on the fingers. Others have surrendered themselves to various greeds and desires in the party circle. And hybrid politicians have joined the profession called politics to build their own destiny. Politics is no longer under the control of politicians; it has gone into the hands of bureaucrats and businessmen. Those who truly want to change the fate of the people; want to change the society and the state, are so divided by disagreements and divisions that they have become isolated from the people. 

Why do we describe the good reputation of the past period? Surely in the disappointment of not achieving. We have failed to fulfill the collective aspirations despite defeating the opponent and achieving victory in the liberation war. Behind that failure, we want to forget the present by dwelling on the past. But the present is reality. There is no way to avoid it and it is impossible. Our collective dream and aspiration; after all, the only way to eliminate inequality is to radically change the existing system. Until that is done, years will come and go; our life span will decrease; but the desired expectations will not be fulfilled.

Headline_English: Series of dramas in Pakistani courts over elections
Content_Enlish:
The upcoming elections in Pakistan have seen fierce competition in the courts as well as in the political arena. The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has taken away the cricket bat from Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)'s election symbol. The party moved the Peshawar High Court against this; the court initially overturned the ECP's decision, but a few days later, on the commission's request, it reversed the ruling and refused to give the PTI the election symbol 'cricket bat'. The PTI then moved the Supreme Court against the Peshawar High Court's ruling. However, the party withdrew its appeal and again went to the Peshawar High Court, and the court overturned the ECP's decision and gave the PTI the election symbol bat. The Supreme Court, on an appeal by the ECP, on Saturday overturned the Peshawar Court's decision and upheld the ECP's decision. As a result, the PTI lost its election symbol and all its candidates now have to vote as independents. 

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court's earlier verdict disqualifying lawmakers for life for not being "honest and righteous" has recently been overturned by another Supreme Court ruling. In this, Pakistan Muslim League leader Nawaz Sharif won a huge legal victory. As a result, there was no obstacle to the participation of former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who was disqualified as a candidate in the 2017 elections on corruption charges. The Supreme Court's ruling also gave the country's new political party Istiqama-e-Pakistan (IPP) leader Jahangir Khan Tareen a legal opportunity to participate in the elections. Because he was also accused of the same charges. 

It seems that these court farces have also affected the election campaign. Although the election (February 8) is less than a month away, the election campaign has not yet begun. Whereas under normal circumstances, it should have progressed well by now. The only legal avenue open to the PTI to get a fair election. That too seems to be closed. Currently, most of the party’s leaders and workers are in jail and they are not able to hold much meetings due to the authorities’ restrictions. They are not even able to use online social media to raise funds or strengthen support. Their work is being hindered by shutting down the internet and other online facilities. 

The farce over the elections does not end here. Meanwhile, a strange attempt is underway in the Senate, the upper house of the country’s parliament, to postpone the election date. With the help of the Senate chairman, some members have moved a controversial motion calling for the postponement of the election citing weather and security conditions. The motion was adopted without any quorum, although it has no binding or legal value. 

The PML(N) is going to win the election. But so far, they have not launched any campaign. This is because of their assured position in the election field. Another reason could be that the party leaders are still busy distributing tickets; the seat-sharing program with other parties is not yet over. The PML(N) is working to resolve the ongoing issue with the IPP over seat-sharing. Meanwhile, the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) has entered the political arena with great force under the leadership of Bilawal Bhutto. They are hoping to regain some of the seats they lost in Punjab. But beyond that, the party is unlikely to gain much. As a regional party, they will get most of their support in Sindh. However, Bilawal Bhutto's party is ahead in the campaign in the country so far. 

The delay in starting the campaign by other parties means that voters are still waiting to know the positions of the political parties. Voters want to understand what the political parties stand on important issues for the future of the country. The PPP has not yet announced its manifesto. However, it has only given 10 programs, which promise 'financial assistance to the people'. However, there is no statement on how it will address the economic, security and foreign policy challenges. The PML(N) has not yet come out with a manifesto in public. It is expected to present it next week. A party leader said that the manifesto will be released along with the campaign. 

So, it can be said that February is going to be a lifeless and haphazard election so far. However, the common people of the country are expecting politicians to present solutions to the country's many crises, especially the economic issue, to the public.

Headline_English: Where will the young people go then?
Content_Enlish:
A private organization called Youth Matters Survey says in its report that 42 percent of Bangladeshi youth now want to go abroad. Does the number sound low or high? It depends on who the survey was conducted on. It could be urban and rural; young people from both sides were surveyed. If only urban youth were asked and if they were educated, not 42, but more young people would have said that they are looking forward to going abroad. What is the reason? The main reason is that there is no work in the country. Unemployment is increasing. Unemployment is of course higher in rural areas. Experts say that it is twice as high as in urban areas. But where do rural people have the courage and ability to go abroad? 

Still, they go. They want to go by selling their land and mortgage their houses. Because there are opportunities to earn money abroad, which is not available in the country. Now, however, it is seen that some of those who went abroad are coming back. Because there is now a shortage of work abroad too. The main reason for this is the economic recession; another reason is the lack of demand for manual labor in the development of machinery. Apart from that, fraudsters are also active. They also do their work, take them with false promises. Girls go too. There is a demand for girls in the Middle East, especially in Saudi Arabia. Many girls are in great danger there; some are sold. There have also been allegations that they are being forced into the sex trade. Who can say that slavery has disappeared? 

The youth of Bangladesh fought a war once. A war against the state. Not for a short time, but for a long time. During the British rule, during the Pakistani era. A great war took place in 1971. The youth were not afraid. They did not run away. They went to war in groups. They fought hard and forced the Pakistani occupation forces to surrender. Now it seems that those youth can survive if they can leave the country. As I said, unemployment has become terrible. There are no job opportunities. The government agency Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics is reporting that employment has decreased by about 4 lakh in the last three months. The Bureau of Statistics reports that the unemployed who have passed out of universities are now 8 lakh. Government data is not always accurate; There are various misconceptions. Private and real data will say that the number of unemployed is even higher – that is our assumption. Information from various sources indicates that 15 million Bangladeshis are now abroad. 

Why has the employment opportunities not increased within the country? There is no shortage of people to work hard. Young people who want to go abroad all go because they will work hard. Even those who are determined to go abroad for studies also go abroad knowing that they will have to work hard and work hard. No; the shortage is not of labor; the shortage is of capital. But why is capital not being developed; why is income not being converted into capital? The reason for this is that income is being smuggled abroad. The rich of Bangladesh take money abroad and some enjoy themselves, some buy houses, others invest in business and commerce. Huge investments have been made by the rich Bangladeshis in Singapore. Some products produced in our country are being exported abroad. Income is also generated from that. But $9 million of export income has not come to the country. Income is not coming to the country; it is staying abroad. And recently, Bangladeshis are doing what they call a "swift business" in Dubai. The growth rate of Bangladeshi businesses has matched that of Indians. The number of Bangladeshi businesses in the Dubai Chamber of Commerce is now 1,044. [Samakal, October 28] 

It's good that they are doing business, but where did they get this money? They certainly didn't earn it in Dubai. They took it from Bangladesh. There is no way to take it legally, there are prohibitions. They took it illegally. There are many problems with the legal route, the need to satisfy each step; the illegal route is smoother in comparison, as long as there is a satisfactory increase in production at two or four points, all doors open. The news of PK Halder's money laundering seems unbelievable; it's like magic. But it happened. PK Halder is not the only one, many others are active. Besides, there must have been big-name people behind and in front of Mr. Halder. Otherwise, how did he escape and why is his whole story not known even after he was caught? 

2 
Why don't the youth have the same feeling now as they once did? We know that the fight was against the state. The state was not an ally then, it was an enemy; that is why the fight became necessary. But has the state become an ally now, so there is no need for war? 

No; it is not like that at all. The state was an enemy then, it still remains an enemy; its hostility towards the people has not diminished at all; rather, it has increased. But this hostility is now much more clever and skillful than before. Moreover, it has the cover of the homeland. The hostility now pretends and propagates that its work is to increase the opportunities and happiness of the people, to improve the country and to make the state the news that the people have no conflict with the rulers of the state. They are people of the same country, of the same nation; everyone is everyone's own. The power of the media has always been invincible. With the development of technology and the capitalist occupation of property, the media has never been as powerful as it is now. It has the power to make half-truths and outright lies appear true, and it continues to do so. 

The media is never impartial. It always favors the powerful. So when two people die in a Russian attack on Ukraine, it is big news, but when 500 people, mostly children and women, are killed in a Gaza hospital in an Israeli bombing, it is just a number. The question posed in an ‘open letter’ by Palestinian-Israeli intellectuals to the US media would be raised by thousands of voices, if there were such a thing as a global conscience. The question in the ‘Open Letter’ is as follows: ‘Why are we not applying pressure from a journalistic perspective, why are we not questioning the fabricated images of the Israeli authorities to justify war crimes in Gaza?’ 

The Israeli Defense Minister has said that the Palestinians are not human beings, but animals in human form. The minister’s words have been propagated as if they were not the voice of a strange animal, but the words of a hero. 

3 
The major political parties are the most corrupt. This is not new information, everyone knows it. However, the real and fundamental truth is that the source of corruption lies in the imperialist capitalist system of this country. Elections themselves are speculative capital businesses. The bigwigs of the two major parties and alliances invest crores of rupees, which return a thousandfold when they come to power. This is why there is so much conflict and strife over power. The people's right to vote has become a joke. Therefore, eradicating corruption is not possible through reforms, the existing system needs to be abolished. 

The next election is being held under the leadership of the ruling government, which has thrown the main opposition party into prison. As a result, the people are panicking. The imperialist masters are trying to broker a compromise between the two major parties loyal to them. Because if there is a compromise, it will be easier to seize the country's natural and marine resources, including gas, coal. Apart from this, Bangladesh has geopolitical importance. It has the cheapest labor force in the world.

Headline_English: Election fraud a month before the vote
Content_Enlish:
Recently, the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has rejected the nomination papers of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) candidates without any due process. This has raised questions about the legitimacy of elections in the country, which has tarnished the entire process. The heinous incident of pushing former Foreign Minister Shah Mohammad Qureshi towards a police van has highlighted the scale of the ongoing atrocities against PTI leaders. It seems that the level of atrocities has increased with the February 8 elections in mind. 

The incident in the case of PTI candidate and former MP Jamshed Dasti is another example of thuggery. The aim of these activities is to suppress the opposition. In a video message widely circulated on social media, Dasti said that he is on the run to avoid arrest. He has also accused the security forces of vandalizing his house and stripping his wife in front of their children. Although the police have denied these allegations. 

Such allegations of atrocities were not raised even during the military regime. These incidents have made politics difficult at the beginning of the new year. The face of the security forces is becoming clear in such actions of a loyal caretaker administration. The situation in the country will not be normalized through such a farce in politics. 

The above-mentioned incidents are not only happening against PTI candidates. The nomination papers of many leaders from Balochistan like Akhtar Mangal have been rejected for trivial reasons. The aim of these is to weaken PTI and other political parties, which seem to be able to challenge this selection process of the establishment. In this situation, the possibility of reconsidering the nomination papers rejected by the Election Tribunal is very low. 

These incidents have raised questions about the independence and impartiality of the Election Commission of Pakistan. The commission did not allow PTI to choose its election symbol ‘BAT’, which has made the institution’s nefarious activities even more clear. Interestingly, the Election Commission has appealed against the ruling of the Peshawar High Court. Because the court has upheld the election symbol of PTI. It is not difficult to guess who is behind all this. In such incidents, only the state is being humiliated. The country is systematically heading towards destruction through electoral fraud. We are moving towards a shipwreck with the increasing breakdown of the entire political system. The Pakistan Muslim League (N) and some of the leading political parties have joined this game of conspiracy for their own interests. That is why they are equally despicable. 

However, if we recall the despicable history of power struggles, the power-hungry attitude of these politicians is nothing new. It seems that the Pakistan Muslim League (N) will come to power again. Despite this certainty, their leaders are busy forming alliances with the main rival parties to remain in power in the future. But the party has not yet been able to present any strong program to face the upcoming difficult challenges of the country. They have created this situation based on their unattractive past performance. The PML-N is preparing for the election campaign. The list of potential candidates has been filled with old people, but the members of the Sharif family are getting more prominence. There is no hope of building a new leadership, which highlights the party's past. There is no possibility of change in this. It will undoubtedly be a very difficult task for a political party to energize the youth as the majority of voters, who are 65 percent of the total voters. 

However, despite most of the first and second-tier leadership being in jail or absconding, the PTI's acceptance has not decreased, especially among the youth. Perhaps this is why so much oppression and persecution is being carried out on the party. The Election Commission of Pakistan has also taken away the party's symbol 'bat'. But an electoral process creates such political dynamics, the results of which are not easy for anyone to completely control. It is clear that there is no specific program or ideological position in the electoral contest, but rather the sole objective is to come to power and control the situation. The elections are only a few weeks away, and the first-tier political parties have not yet been able to reach the people. In the meantime, what we have seen are some popular slogans and promises of impossible achievements. In fact, there is no good understanding of the severity of the problem among the main political parties.

The economic plight of the lower classes, growing inequality, the devastating effects of climate change, and population explosion do not come up in their discussions. Even the rising tide of terrorism does not find a place in their discussions. These political parties have long handed over national security and foreign policy to the military. Because of this, the country is only moving in one direction. The security forces have deeply entrenched themselves at every level of the power structure, leaving civilian control unimaginable. Many fear that instability could increase due to the breakdown of political power outside the military. Moreover, no rigged system can solve the governance process and economic issues. It remains to be seen how much power the civilian administration can uproot in the future if it gains power. 

Only a desperate fight for power and a rigged election process can push the country towards further disaster. This situation can only be addressed through free and fair elections. But there is no such urgency to create this situation.

Headline_English: Both crises of Bangladesh's progressives
Content_Enlish:
The desire for development is the key to development. The desire for development leads people to a better life. Development is measured by the ability to enjoy in the Human Development Index; but American economist Walt Rostow adds another thing to it. That is – the people’s perspective on the world and life. 

Modern life should be defined in the light of Rostow’s development philosophy: a life based on science and reason is modern life. On the other hand, in the definition of happiness, Amartya Sen says, ‘People also find happiness in seeing others happy. If someone else is unhappy, their own sense of happiness decreases.’ Even though their own food, clothing, shelter, medical care and health are assured, they are a sensitive person. Therefore, they fight for an egalitarian society. 

In Bangladesh too, some people are continuously working under the banner of the Communist or Socialist Party. The ruling party has been ruling the country since 2014 by abolishing the democratic process. In 2014, the main opposition party did not participate at all, and even though they did in 2018, they came to power by rigging it extensively, just like in 2014. In the 2024 elections, almost 50 percent of the parties, including the main opposition party, are not participating in the elections. If the goal of the Left is revolution, then before deciding whether such elections should be held, one must understand why and when people revolt. The job of a political party is to awaken the consciousness of freedom among people. Only then will they feel deprived and rebel. A collective revolution is created from the rebellion of an individual. 

The logic of participating in elections is that when people are prevented from coming to the polling station or when they go to the polling station and find out that their vote has been cast, they will be boundlessly angry. Once, twice, three times, as anger accumulates, they will rebel. It must be remembered that the prerequisite for rebellion is anger. And anger is created when they realize that they are deprived of their just rights. That right may be of food, opportunity, or votes. 

What will those outside the political party do who want to lead the country towards progress? Where will they go? Who will they vote for? In fact, in the current political situation in Bangladesh, progressives are in a difficult dilemma. The Awami League had a close relationship with the workers and peasants. There were many promises. Bengali nationality would develop in a secular manner, the peasants and workers would be liberated under the socialist ideology. There would be a truly democratic state. The Awami League could not fulfill that expectation. No one in Bangladesh thinks that there has been democracy since 2014. All citizens will benefit from the extensive infrastructural development that has taken place in Bangladesh; but it is impossible to understand how much the quality of life of the people at the bottom has improved with the increase in per capita income; but it can be said without hesitation that most of the people in the country are unhappy. Because the gap between the rich and the poor in Bangladesh is now at the very top of the world. Inequality makes people unhappy. 

People have to make decisions based on the activities of the current Awami League, not on ancient traditions. Progressives cannot vote for a party that abolishes the democratic process, that removes progressive writings from textbooks under pressure from fundamentalists, lowers the marriage age of girls, and removes statues. 

Can progressives vote for BNP? The founder of this party imposed the first military rule in Bangladesh. He removed secularism and socialism, the essence of independence, from the Constitution of Bangladesh. The Constitution is a document with secular provisions, to which Ziaur Rahman added the revelation of a particular religion. The Constitution is an impersonal thing and it is for people of all religions. Giving the Constitution a religious character is tantamount to insulting the Constitution. It may take a long time for the people of this country to realize how giving the Constitution a religious character is a permanent loss for Bangladesh. It is an even greater loss because no party in this country of people full of religious emotions will dare to restore the Constitution to its original state. 

So what is the solution? The solution is to build new forces. In pre-revolutionary Russia and various European countries, there were initially parties called Social Democrats. Even today, many parties called Social Democrats are strong in South America and Europe, and in power somewhere. The same must be done in Bangladesh. The policy of this party will be flexible, so that the people are not afraid to get involved with it; but at the same time, the work of changing the psychology of the people towards a unified life consciousness must continue. One day, perhaps, it will be possible to form a party with a complete communist ideology and come to power.

Headline_English: New curriculum arrives, promises to make education 'smart'
Content_Enlish:
The most important thing for the youth is education. What is its condition? The British rulers introduced a system of education in our country, not for our benefit, but in the hope that we would benefit them. That system was in operation for 125 years. Then Pakistan came, and efforts were made to make the education system useful for the rulers of Pakistan. The 'revolutionary' Ayub Khan wanted to bring about a revolution in the field of education as in other fields. A capitalist one. The youth of East Bengal did not accept that. They protested. In fact, the movement against the education policy was the first public protest against Ayub. The uprising of '69 began from that protest, and then the country gained independence in the war of 1971. After independence, there have naturally been repeated attempts to bring about 'development' in the education system. But no development dared to step outside the capitalist genre. Rather, the distance between the three streams of education has increased further. Every attempt at educational reform has harmed the mainstream. That is, the Bengali medium.

A strange method called creative was introduced, so that it is not known what benefits have been achieved, but it is undeniable that harm has been done. Under the pressure of Hefazat-e-Islam, changes have been made to the Bengali textbook, the harmful aspects of which have been written about; it has been said; there have also been voices raised from conscious circles. But it has not worked. Now a new curriculum has come, which is said to make education 'smart'. It is heard that the so-called 'knowledge-based' education will be replaced by 'skill-based' education. We have not seen everything ourselves yet, but from the news that the newspapers have given, it is known that theoretical science, i.e. physics, chemistry and biology, will be brought into the same book. That is, the science education that was there before will also be reduced. Religious education will definitely remain as before. 

Various types of experiments are going on in education. This is certainly not the last step. Of course, we will go further. However, it must be noted that these experiments are not in the English medium curriculum. The same curriculum is being implemented there unchanged (one could even say undistorted) and the children of the country's affluent families have become skilled and 'smart' after being educated in that education. They are studying in private universities or going abroad. Those who fail to go abroad are left feeling depressed. English medium is not being given a hand; it cannot be given. If that education is going well, then what is the worry? The children of the ruling class study in English medium; they do not even come close to Bengali medium. The Minister of Road Transport and Bridges has said that when you get on the elevated expressway, you feel like you are in Europe. When you get down, you see the poor conditions; the same distance between English medium and Bengali medium; although they are operating in the same country and at the same time. There was no need to bring any 'revolutionary' changes in madrasa education either; however, arrangements have been made to give Aliya Madrasa degrees equal status to mainstream degrees, so that the growing attraction towards madrasa education will increase further. The poor mainstream is the culprit. 

However, it seems that there will be a big objection to the changes being brought this time. Objections have already been raised. In this case, one problem is that the government is saying that a 'terrible' false propaganda is being carried out about the new curriculum. Of course, it has not been made clear in the government statement who is doing this dirty work. However, what has never happened before has happened this time. Which shows that we are gradually becoming more 'democratic'. That is, critics are being punished. Very smartly, three teachers and a parent have already been imprisoned for criticizing the Cyber ​​Security Act. The government has filed a case against them under the Cyber ​​Security Act. There is hope of getting bail in other cases too, but there is no bail in this case. Bail is prohibited. The news of the incident was reported in the headline of a national daily as follows: 'Parents in trouble for criticizing the curriculum: NCTB case, arrest, homelessness in panic' (Ittefaq, December 2). 

The news is saying that there have been objections to the new curriculum. Even in the National Parliament, several members have spoken about its inconsistencies. Concerned parents have formed a human chain at Shaheed Minar and held a press conference at the Press Club regarding this. Parents say, “Since there are no written exams in the new curriculum, students are not sitting at home with books. When asked to study, they say there is nothing to study. The school is giving students various ‘group studies’ assignments, which students and parents are facing various problems to solve. These problems include: going to classmates’ homes after school to solve group studies assignments, taking a lot of time for this work, spending a lot of money on purchasing work materials, students using devices uncontrollably under the pretext of group studies, etc. 

Two news headlines in another national daily (Jayzaydin, December 3) are as follows: 1. Demand to cancel the morally destructive education curriculum; 2. New curriculum, a blueprint for destroying generations. The first news item is about a human chain; the second is about a seminar held at the National Press Club. The human chain was organized by an organization called Shachet Gargash Samaj; the seminar was held under the initiative of 
Child and Child Protection Movement and Sammilit Shiksha Movement. 

Parents who raised objections on the issue of morality The statement is as follows: What is being taught in the name of health protection and science education in the new curriculum in the sixth grade textbooks is clearly ‘sex education’. The topic of discussion of the seminar was, ‘Chronology of Planned Educational Destruction 1972-2022’. Its main statement was as follows: ‘Among the many curricula that have been implemented so far, the new curriculum is the worst and most unrealistic. As a result of this curriculum, many low-quality English medium schools will be created in the country. This will result in a lot of foreign currency going out.’ According to them, the national backbone is being weakened by frequent changes in the curriculum. They claim that instead of encouraging students to be device-oriented, they should be oriented towards studying theoretical subjects. There is no doubt that this demand is very reasonable. Knowledge makes people skilled, but knowledge is nothing but floating information, if there is no theory inside it. And making students smart by focusing on devices? That is the same as making students mechanical and lazy. Laziness is no longer a skill. And this is also a globally recognized truth – excessive use of smartphones Depression is increasing. 

Since the beginning, in education, it is not what the student learned, how much he learned; how he achieved 'results', that was made valuable in our country's education system. Evaluation will also be important in the new education system. But it will happen differently. There will be no marks, grades will also go up; values ​​will be given through triangles, circles, quadrilaterals. Even though science education has been reduced, it is understood that the shopkeeper of geometry will be quite powerful. 

On the other hand, the number of students is going down. It has been learned that this time three crore less textbooks will be printed. What is the reason? Because nothing else. The number of students from pre-primary to ninth grade has decreased by about 28 lakh. (Jayjaydin, September 21) The success rate in public examinations is also declining. The pass rate in higher secondary was 85.15 percent last time, this time it has come down to 78.64. In fact, all students are supposed to pass. Because they go to school assuming that they will succeed. has been sent for. The phenomenon of rising and falling exam results is also somewhat mysterious. For example, this time, Barisal board students have done better than Jessore board. The pass rate in Jessore is 69.88 percent; in Barisal it is 80.69. What is the explanation for this? Did the children of Barisal suddenly become more talented and focused? Or was there a flaw in the assessment? It doesn't seem like they worry much about these things. 

Sirajul Islam Chowdhury: Emeritus Professor, Dhaka University

Headline_English: The risk of global anarchy is growing
Content_Enlish:
The Cambridge School is a leading institution in economic thought in the Western world. But their role in global economic management in 2023 was not very positive. Surprisingly, the primary reason for this was not the emergence of a Chinese-led alternative economic system, although many predicted that it would. Rather, it was the internal crisis of the existing system, which further questioned its effectiveness and acceptance worldwide. 

However, no new international system is likely to be introduced soon. Instead, many countries have decided to adopt autonomous systems as an alternative to the Western-created economic system. This is increasing the risk of a breakdown in the global economic system and the role of the United States is eroding. 

Doubts about Western leadership in economic management have been rising long before 2023. In the last 15 years alone, its credibility and effectiveness have been questioned due to various wrong steps. As a result, there have been many disasters. An example is the 2008 financial crisis. The repeated use of business investment as a tool for sanctions, the uneven distribution of COVID-19 vaccines, the central bank’s continued “temporary” inflation, and the alarming increase in interest rates by banks. 

The system has proven incapable of addressing the most urgent global crises, such as the extraordinary borrowing of the global South and climate change. As a result, other mechanisms associated with it have also lost credibility. As the problems become more acute, Western institutions seem increasingly ineffective and less inclusive. 

Two events in particular this year have increased global disillusionment with the Western-run system. First, despite the sanctions imposed on Russia for using the international payment system SWIFT and the price caps on its oil exports, Russia has managed to maintain its international trade relations smoothly. Although the temporary system invented by Russian technologists for international trade and transactions is not at all cost-effective, it has significantly reduced the damage to the country’s economy and has been able to significantly help finance the war in Ukraine.
Russia has also received assistance from various countries to circumvent the effects of Western sanctions, although this number is still relatively insignificant. This limited success against sanctions has shattered the old belief in the world that ‘there is no alternative to the West in economic management’. 

Second, the US role in the war between Israel and Hamas has exposed the futility of the West’s commitment to human rights and international law. 
A few days ago, Joe Biden admitted that millions of people around the world believe that Israel’s excessive response to Hamas’s attack on October 7th has caused it to lose international support. The latest UN General Assembly debate on the ceasefire was held. 153 countries voted in favor of the ceasefire and only 10 countries voted against it. The number of countries that were absent was 23. 

Several countries expressed regret that Israel has not been brought to justice despite bombing civilians and ignoring international law. The UN aid official in Palestine, Philippe Lazzarini, has repeatedly called Gaza “hell on earth.” 
Whatever their position on these events, countries are questioning the effectiveness and acceptability of the Western-led global order. They are accelerating the pace of moving the world economy from unicentric to multicentric, even knowing the risks. On the other hand, the way middle powers are asserting themselves on the world stage may be successful in encouraging smaller allies of the West to become “swing states” or neutrals. 

The Western powers must confront this threat. Political leaders should keep an eye on the risk of a breakdown and take urgent steps to prevent an international catastrophe by strengthening existing multilateral strategies. This effort should begin by reforming the policies of key institutions and re-energizing them; this could start with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The primary task will be to appoint representatives and encourage them to express their views, and to abolish old appointments that are focused on Western interests. In addition, the process must be modernized. 

While the Western-led system has served the world well since World War II, it is urgent to reform it. If the current international framework is allowed to fail, the new Chinese system will not be able to take its place, but will cause even greater disaster. The result will harm us all, even in the short term. It will also hinder our collective ability to deal with increasingly complex and long-term crises.

Headline_English: How Iran is benefiting from the Gaza war
Content_Enlish:
The situation in the region has deteriorated at an unprecedented rate since Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel and the subsequent Israeli counterattack. The armed conflict between Israel and the Palestinians has been a source of concern for decades. The Iranian-backed Hamas attacks have done little to benefit civilians or Palestinians in Gaza; they have done little to bring peace or reconciliation there, even in the short term. 

Iran funds and trains Hamas. This means that Iran likely knew about Hamas’s plans in advance. The Hamas attack came at a time when a US-brokered normalization deal between Saudi Arabia and Israel was nearing completion. The deal included Saudi Arabia’s civilian nuclear program, further strengthening US-Saudi defense cooperation, and the possibility of a peace agreement between Israelis and Palestinians through Saudi influence. Moreover, the G20 summit in New Delhi, about a month before the Hamas attack, announced plans to build an India-Middle East-Europe corridor. This regional strategic connectivity project initially included India, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel. Both initiatives undoubtedly go against Iran’s long-standing regional ambitions. 

The ongoing conflict in Gaza has left the Arab world unwilling to accept a normalization agreement with Israel or greater economic cooperation. They are also pressuring governments not to take any concrete steps towards this end. This is fulfilling Iran’s objective. By stoking the flames of conflict and instability in the region, Iran wants to divert attention from its own economic crisis, socio-political challenges, regional ambitions and nuclear program. Iran is trying to position itself as a major regional power by controlling its proxy groups in the Middle East. The country could use negotiations and international diplomacy to make concessions on its nuclear program or to avoid scrutiny. 

The Gaza war also provides Iran with an opportunity to gain support from like-minded groups in the region, potentially expanding its network of allies. Iran could exploit the long-standing conflicts and tensions to destabilize neighboring Arab states, including Iraq, Syria, and Yemen. This has been evident recently in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis have been attacking commercial shipping for weeks, including a missile attack on a Norwegian tanker. Since October 7, the Houthis have also been launching drone attacks and missiles at Israel and commercial shipping, most of which have been intercepted by U.S. forces in the Red Sea. 

On another front, the rise of rebel and extremist groups in Iraq and Syria is a cause for concern. The current situation in the Gaza conflict has created an opportunity for Iran to expand its ties with such groups. 

Iran also poses a threat in the Strait of Hormuz. To counter Houthi attacks on ships, a multinational maritime task force needs to be established with increased intelligence sharing. In addition, the United States and Gulf states can play an effective role by adopting missile and drone countermeasures, increasing regional naval patrols, special operations forces, enhancing counterterrorism capabilities, and enhancing regional cooperation. Joint military measures are needed to counter the Houthi threat. This will help secure critical shipping lanes and contribute to stability in the region.

Headline_English: Bangladesh audit of the peddler of democracy
Content_Enlish:
There are only 10 days left for the 12th National Assembly elections. In the meantime, the attention of various media outlets has mainly been taken away by the election activities. Although the competition is mainly between the official and independent ‘dummy’ candidates of the ruling party Awami League, the arguments, conflicts and violence on both sides have created a lot of curiosity among the public about the vote. The main discussion almost everywhere in the political arena is now – who will win if the vote is ‘free’ and ‘fair’ as promised by the government and the Election Commission, and what will happen if it is not. 

But even in this, new rumors have started, especially on social media – the January 7 vote may not take place after all. Many people in favor of boycotting the ongoing elections, including a former female BNP MP who has become a political celebrity thanks to the media, are promoting the issue. Recently, the US ambassador to Dhaka, Peter Haas, went to Delhi to ‘spend the Christmas holidays’. Their speculation-based campaign is mainly based on this issue, that Peter Haas will stop the election without BNP by convincing Delhi at the last minute. Although everyone knows that the Indian government's position on the Bangladesh issue is strongly anti-US. This was publicly stated by the spokesperson of the Indian Ministry of External Affairs a few days ago. 

Not only that; US President Joe Biden was supposed to be the chief guest at India's Republic Day program to be held next January. On Friday, The Hindustan Times reported that Biden is not coming to the event. French President Macron will be his replacement. Although the White House did not officially say the reason, he is not attending the event mainly to avoid the discomfort caused by the Indian government's association with the recent assassination attempt on Sikh leader Pannun in the United States. In this situation, where the two top officials of the Biden administration, Foreign Minister Antony Blinken and Defense Minister Lloyd Austin, could not sway India from its position on the Bangladesh issue despite their simultaneous efforts, how can a mere ambassador like Peter Haas succeed! 
Why only these mediocre leaders of the BNP; A section of civil society is still loudly saying that not only is the BNP, the party of choice for a significant number of voters in the country, out of the election process; the election, which will be held with thousands of party leaders and activists from various levels in prison, will not be 'inclusive' or 'inclusive', nor will it be participatory. Therefore, it will not be acceptable in the country, at least not to the West. Referring to the latest labor policy announced by US Secretary of State Blinken, they are also predicting that after the election, the US will impose a trade embargo on Bangladesh, albeit a 'partial' one. Because in their words, the US does not easily release anyone it has captured. Although the potential target of this embargo is our ready-made garment sector, leaders say that according to the principles of the World Trade Organization (WTO), one member country cannot impose any trade embargo on another member country and our labor situation is not at the level of embargo at least at present. 
It is true that we once enjoyed Generalized System of Preferences (GSP) treatment from the US for various plastic products and other products, which the country suspended a decade ago without any valid reason. In December 2021, it imposed various sanctions on the RAB and some current and former officers of the force on charges of human rights violations. The country said last September that it had already started implementing visa policies on Bangladeshis who obstructed the democratic election process, including members of law enforcement agencies, the ruling party, and the opposition. In line with this, the US visa ban on some individuals here after the upcoming elections is not surprising. 

Does the Biden administration have sufficient justification to impose on Bangladesh the kind of US sanctions we saw on the socialist countries led by the former Soviet Union until the last decade of the last century, and the kind of US sanctions we still have on Cuba and Russia? 

Almost everyone who is aware of US policy admits that although the stated purpose of such sanctions is to establish 'democracy' and 'human rights', in reality the Biden administration wants Bangladesh to be free from the 'grip' of China and Russia. The current Bangladesh government has already taken steps to reduce, if not eliminate, this US 'concern'. Another big issue is that the US is pressuring Bangladesh to comply with its Indo-Pacific policy, which calls for keeping the India and Pacific region 'liberal and open', which is not being well accepted by India, the US caliphate in the region. Let's take the case of our neighbor Myanmar. There, India is supporting the junta government that Biden dislikes in harmony with not only Russia but also China. As a result, the implementation of the much-talked about Burma Act is also becoming difficult for the US. The fact that Europe's pro-China leader Makhon is replacing Biden at India's Republic Day celebrations is also quite indicative. 

In early September, Michael Kugelman, director of the South Asia Institute at the renowned US think tank Wilson Center, visited Dhaka. In an interview with UNB, he said that the Biden administration had chosen Bangladesh as a “test case or object of examination” for implementing its values-based foreign policy. Citing Kugelman’s words, many are saying that the US will not make concessions on the issue of democracy and human rights in Bangladesh. 

But the question is, within a month of the Bangladesh elections, national elections are going to be held in Pakistan on February 8, which everyone thinks is not only one-sided but also a farce. What is the US position on that? In April this year, the process in which the government of Imran Khan, who was once a pet of the army and later wanted independence, was forced to give up power is being called a parliamentary coup by many, and the Biden administration was the almost open sponsor of that coup, in which the Pakistan army provided support. Imran and his party, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), have been under a crackdown since the anti-military protests in May. The latest news is that Imran wants to participate in the elections despite the party being divided into several parts under pressure from the establishment. But he has been disqualified in a mysterious trial and his popular symbol has also been taken away. However, the peddlers of democracy around the world are not saying anything about this. On December 12, White House spokesman Matthew Miller, in response to a journalist's question, said that the United States is eager to work with whoever the people of Pakistan 'show' or 'elect' as their leader. But he did not want to see 'free, fair and participatory' elections there like in Bangladesh. Everyone knows that Imran joined the China-Russia camp before his overthrow; he visited Russia at the beginning of the war in Ukraine, ignoring US prohibitions. That is why the Biden administration is completely unresponsive to the trial of his party's leaders and activists in military courts, while trampling on the principles of democracy and human rights. 
Pakistan is not a country in Africa; Bangladesh is a neighboring country in South Asia. Will the Biden administration's hypocrisy on the issue of democracy and human rights be acceptable even to the people of the United States?

Headline_English: Increase the age limit for employment.
Content_Enlish:
Highly educated job seekers in Bangladesh have been protesting for the past 10 years demanding that the age limit for applying for government jobs be increased from 30 to 35. Although ordinary students of the country have been holding non-political and non-violent programs in order to achieve their demands, there has been no positive response from the government so far. On the contrary, the police have repeatedly dispersed the students by beating them with batons during these programs due to the spontaneous participation of ordinary students. 

Is the demand to increase the age limit for applying for government jobs completely unreasonable? The age limit for applying for government jobs in Bangladesh was increased from 27 to 30 in the early 1990s, when the average life expectancy of Bangladeshis was only 57 years. Although the average life expectancy of Bangladeshis has increased to 73 years today, the age limit for applying for jobs has not been increased. Although the retirement age for government jobs was increased by two years from 57 to 59 years in 2011, the age limit for entering the job has not been increased. On the other hand, the employment of government employees at the end of the contract has become another obstacle to the normal employment process. 

During the COVID-19 pandemic, almost all types of job recruitment exams were closed. This resulted in the loss of about three years from the lives of job seekers. While in many countries of the world, the age of entry into the job was permanently extended by another two-three years to compensate for the damage caused by the Corona pandemic, in Bangladesh, the opportunity to apply is only given with a 'back-date', which was discriminatory and unplanned. 

Despite being citizens of the same country, our students are being discriminated against. Although the age limit for applying to the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) is 30 years, the age limit for applying to the Bangladesh Judicial Service (BJS) is 32 years, and in government nursing and private schools and colleges, it is 35 years. 

It is sad but true that various private institutions or organizations have also been following the age limit for applying to jobs as per the government standards of 30 years, which has put job seekers in another dilemma. Because, on average, a student is 25-26 years old by the time they complete their honors-masters. If they fail to get a job within three to four years of preparing for the government job exam, this age limit also becomes an obstacle to entering private institutions or organizations. 

A review of international standards on the age of entry into employment shows that the age limit for applying for a job in 162 countries of the world is 35 years. In some countries, it is open. Among the South Asian countries, the age limit for applying for a job in our neighboring country India is 35-45 years in different states, 45 in the Maldives, 35 in Sri Lanka, 35 in Nepal, and 35 in Afghanistan. In South Asia, only Bangladesh and Pakistan have an age limit for applying for a job. 

Although the National Youth Policy of Bangladesh calls 18-35 years old as youth, they are not given the opportunity to apply for a job at the age of 30. So far, the demand to increase the age limit has been raised 71 times in the Bangladesh National Parliament and the Parliamentary Standing Committee of the Ministry of Public Administration has recommended in writing to increase the age limit for applying for jobs to 35 years, but it has not been implemented yet. 

The demand of the job seeker is that the age limit for entering the job should be increased from 30 to 35 years. If necessary, the retirement age should also be increased. 

Zubair Hossain Zahir: Job Seeker

Headline_English: The name of the AL is involved in all the achievements of Bangladesh.
Content_Enlish:
Bangladesh Awami League Joint General Secretary and Information Minister Hasan Mahmud has commented that the name of Awami League is associated with all the achievements of Bangladesh. He said this while speaking as the chief guest at the triennial conference of Atrai Upazila Awami League in Naogaon on Sunday. 

Hasan Mahmud said, "In just a few days, we are going to celebrate the golden jubilee of 50 years of independence. We are celebrating the birth centenary of Father of the Nation Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. In the meantime, on the eve of the 50th anniversary of independence, another achievement was achieved under the leadership of Sheikh Hasina on the night before yesterday. That is, Bangladesh transformed from a least developed country to a developing country. The name of Bangladesh Awami League is associated with all the achievements of Bangladesh. Bangladesh Awami League is not only the organization that led the war of independence, everything in this country has been achieved under the leadership of Bangladesh Awami League.’ 

After the meeting, the 67-member Atrai Upazila Awami League committee was announced with Nripendra Nath Dutta as the president and Akkas Ali as the general secretary. 

Atrai Upazila Awami League President Nripendra Nath Dutta presided over the conference organized at the Sahebganj Football Field in the upazila.
